items.title: Socrates went nuclear: Comparing Interaction Strategies for AI systems in a Learning Context using Brain Sensing

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Students are adopting LLMs at scale. This poses a question: does unrestricted AI access bypass the cognitive effort required for learning, or does it streamline knowledge acquisition? This paper reports on a study where we compare three designs for user-AI interaction in a learning context: (1) an unrestricted conversational bot like ChatGPT, (2) a pedagogically constrained bot that guides through hints without giving final answers, which we refer to as the Socratic mode; and (3) a non-conversational adaptive tutoring system that adjusts difficulty in real-time based on the user’s cognitive engagement derived from the brain signals. Fifty study participants were tasked with learning about nuclear safety protocols, a domain chosen for its zero-prior knowledge baseline. The participants progressed through an instructional video, a pre-test, an AI-driven assessment phase, which varied in the three conditions, and an immediate post-test. The nature of the questions centered primarily on factual knowledge acquisition, but it still required participants to have a global understanding of the concepts in order to answer the questions correctly. A Muse headband was used to derive the cognitive engagement of all users in all conditions. The unrestricted chatbot produced higher learning gains (delta) than both constrained modes ( p <.03, d > 0.80), while the adaptive condition generated significantly higher EEG engagement ( p =.018). The cluster analysis of chatbot usage and discussion patterns by users showed that most participants in the unrestricted-mode adopted a direct answer-retrieval strategy, while participants in the Socratic-mode initially attempted to reason through the hints before progressively disengaging. Consequently, this also suggests that the success of the unrestricted AI is not an evidence of deeper learning, but rather a result of the immediate post-test evaluation after the training phase.

items.title: AI-powered human action recognition of functional activities in stroke: a systematic review

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI)-based human activity recognition (HAR) is a promising approach for detecting functional activity in individuals with stroke, potentially enabling objective and ecologically valid assessment, monitoring and treatment. We aimed to synthesize current evidence on AI-based HAR for functional activity recognition after stroke, focusing on sensing technologies, target activities, settings, and model architectures. PubMed, Embase, WOS, and Scopus were searched and seventeen studies involving 224 individuals with stroke met the inclusion criteria. Inertial measurement units were the predominant sensing modality (12/17, 70.6%), with several studies demonstrating the feasibility of recognizing relevant functional activities using a single device. Single-sensor approaches were also used in home-based and simulated-home settings, suggesting potential for scalable and unobtrusive monitoring outside clinical environments; however, most studies were conducted in controlled clinical settings (11/17, 64.7%), with limited real-world validation to date. Convolutional neural networks were the most frequently used deep learning architecture, while Random Forest was the most common traditional machine learning method. Multimodal sensing may enrich activity characterization, although greater sensing complexity may reduce feasibility for prolonged home monitoring. Methodological and reporting limitations, including concerns regarding confounding and reproducibility, should be considered when interpreting the current evidence. Overall, single-sensor AI-based HAR appears promising for low-burden, continuous, and ecologically valid monitoring. Future research should prioritize longitudinal validation in everyday environments, transparent reporting of code and data availability, and inclusion of acute and severely impaired stroke populations to facilitate clinical translation toward objective monitoring, personalized rehabilitation, and remote care.

items.title: Human tutoring, generative AI tutoring and independent internet search: A randomised between‐subjects experiment on students' responses to academic challenge
items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

analysis.methods: The study was conducted in a large sixth-form college in England with a well-established digital infrastructure, including a bring-your-own-device policy, a dedicated digital leadership team and prior experience with custom-built educational GenAI tutors. Participants were aged 16-18. A total of 160 students volunteered and took part, representing approximately 5% of the college's population of around 3000. Recruitment was college-wide. The Director of Digital Strategy circulated invitations by email at several points during the academic year and a two-minute video in which the researcher explained the study and invited participation was shown during morning tutor time. Recruitment did not occur through particular subject lessons, although participation was self-selecting. Eleven participants were excluded because technical disruptions resulted in incomplete sessions or unusable data, yielding a quantitative analytic sample of 149. Usable post-task questionnaire responses were available for 154 participants (Human, n = 52; GenAI tutor, n = 52; Internet, n = 50) and were retained in a separate questionnaire dataset. Current A-level subject data were available for 144 of the 149 participants in the quantitative analytic sample. The most commonly studied subjects were Mathematics (n = 94, 65.3%), Psychology (n = 69, 47.9%), Biology (n = 43, 29.9%), Chemistry (n = 38, 26.4%), Physics (n = 37, 25.7%), Further Mathematics (n = 34, 23.6%) and Computer Science (n = 28, 19.4%). Participants could report multiple subjects. To assess baseline comparability following random allocation, participant characteristics were compared across the three conditions. Kruskal-Wallis tests identified no statistically significant differences in perceived socioeconomic status, GCSE mathematics grade, perceived mathematics ability or perceived mathematics ability relative to others (all ps ≥ 0.917). Chi-square tests likewise identified no significant associations between condition and baseline trait challenge-seeking category (p = 0.446), gender among female and male participants (p = 0.307), Mathematics participation (p = 0.606) or Further Mathematics participation (p = 0.871). The study used a single-site, three-condition, randomised between-subjects experimental design. Each participant had only one form of support and remained in that condition throughout. Random allocation was used to reduce the likelihood of systematic baseline differences between the condition groups and thereby strengthen the internal validity of the comparison (Clark et al., 2026) . Participants were individually allocated using a randomnumber generator to one-to-one human tutor, GenAI tutor or independent internet search. The quantitative analytic sample comprised 52 participants in the Human condition, 50 in the GenAI tutor condition and 47 in the Internet condition. All participants were presented with the same fixed sequence within a 90-min session: two 20-min sections of increasingly challenging mathematics problems ( S1 and S2 ), inspired by the PERC task (Porter et al., 2020) , followed by a behavioural challenge-selection task adapted from Rege et al. (2021) . Materials, task order, timings and outcome measures were held constant across conditions. Participants were instructed to use the support for guidance and not to seek direct answers. Participants in the GenAI tutor condition additionally received verbal and written guidance on using the tutor, including instructions not to enter personal data. The two-section structure was designed to examine how students responded when required to return to a new round of challenge after an earlier encounter with substantial difficulty. Effort, perceived difficulty and the number of questions attempted were recorded for each section. Task-related stress was assessed after the problem-solving sections, and behavioural challenge-seeking was assessed through the subsequent selection task. Students attended a single 90-min session conducted in a small teaching room within the college and completed the study individually on their own devices using a standardised Qualtrics platform. After instructions emphasising that tasks were intentionally challenging and optional, participants completed S1 with their assigned support, followed by effort and difficulty ratings, then S2 and the same measures. They then completed the challengeseeking task and a post-task questionnaire. The researcher was present to ensure procedural consistency. As an incentive for participation, all students were entered into a prize draw to win one of five £20 gift vouchers.
analysis.results: Findings are reported first for condition differences in perceived difficulty, effort, attempts and challenge-seeking, followed by task-related stress and changes across the two task sections. Tables 1 and 2 present the descriptive and inferential results, with significant omnibus differences examined using Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons.
analysis.discussion: The capacity of generative AI to independently complete many traditional academic tasks calls into question the educational value of using such tasks as primary indicators of learning (Corbin, Dawson, et al., 2025; Corbin, Walton, et al., 2025) . In response, there is growing consensus that evaluations of AI in education should move beyond grades to attend more closely to how learning is enacted and to the development of higher-order human capacities in human-AI interaction (Luckin, 2018 (Luckin, , 2025;; OECD, 2019 OECD, , 2025;; Wegerif & Major, 2024) . By foregrounding learners' effort, perceived difficulty, behavioural engagement and affective responses, the present study responds directly to these concerns by examining how learning is experienced and regulated under different support conditions. Even with identical tasks, the Human, GenAI tutor and Internet groups differed in their patterns of perceived difficulty, effort and attempts, while stress-response distributions varied descriptively. Consistent with long-standing critiques of performance-based assessment (Bjork & Bjork, 2011 , 2020; Marton & Saljo, 1976; Wegerif & Major, 2024) , the present findings further underscore the value of examining how students travel through learning, not just where they end up. As calls grow to prioritise the development of wider human capacities essential for learning (Luckin, 2025) , understanding these behavioural trajectories becomes critical. The findings did not support the preregistered directional hypothesis overall, as support from the GenAI tutor used in this study did not produce consistently higher effort, a greater number of attempted questions or greater challenge-seeking than the comparison conditions. Given the differences between the preregistered and implemented study, the precise outcome-and section-specific findings are interpreted as exploratory. The variation in effort, perceived difficulty and attempts across conditions suggests that some aspects of students' responses while working through challenge may be shaped by the form of interactive support available during learning, consistent with prior work on the role of framing and interaction in shaping engagement with difficulty (Duckworth, 2016; Duckworth et al., 2007; Dweck, 2006; Hadwin et al., 2018; Young et al., 2024 ). Crucially, these findings extend prior accounts by showing that these response patterns may also differ when support is provided by a GenAI tutor. Students working with the GenAI tutor used in this study reported the highest and most stable effort across sections, although the between-condition difference was significant only in Section 2, when effort was higher than in the Human condition. This higher effort co-occurred with greater perceived difficulty than under human tutoring. One possible interpretation is that the GenAI tutor used in this study helped students continue investing effort despite finding the tasks difficult, suggesting that this form of GenAI support may help sustain engagement during challenging independent work. However, higher effort could also reflect the additional exertion required when difficulty remained unresolved. Self-reported effort is not inherently positive or negative. Higher effort may indicate willingness to persist, but it may also reflect unresolved difficulty or a greater need for exertion. Conversely, lower effort may indicate disengagement, but it may also mean that less exertion was required because support made the task more manageable. The findings therefore cannot determine whether this effort represented productive persistence or difficulty that the support had not adequately alleviated. Effort was therefore interpreted alongside perceived difficulty and attempts, rather than as a standalone indicator of the quality or success of students' engagement. In the separate post-task questionnaire, the GenAI tutor condition descriptively contained a lower proportion of stressed responses than the Internet condition. As no inferential comparisons were conducted, this pattern cannot establish that GenAI tutor support reduced stress, but it is consistent with prior work suggesting that AI-supported struggle may reduce frustration, support motivation and help regulate cognitive load (Bassner et al., 2026) . The GenAI tutor condition also showed the largest descriptive increase in attempts from the first to the second section. Although co-regulation was not measured directly, the combined pattern of reported effort, perceived difficulty, attempts and stress responses is consistent with the possibility that interaction with the GenAI tutor contributed to students' regulation of behavioural engagement and affect as they worked through unresolved difficulty. This interpretation aligns with conceptual accounts that position generative AI as a potential participant in distributed co-regulatory systems (Lodge et al., 2023; Nguyen, 2025) . Consistent with expectations from scaffolding and co-regulation theory (Gaffney & Rodgers, 2018; Hadwin et al., 2018; Vygotsky, 1978; Wood et al., 1976; Wood & Wood, 1996) , the Human condition produced the most favourable difficulty profile, with students reporting the lowest perceived difficulty in both sections. Students also attempted significantly more questions than those in the GenAI tutor condition in Section 1 and the Internet condition in Section 2. Post-task responses also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses and the highest proportion of calm responses in the Human condition, adding an affective dimension to this more favourable profile. While these patterns do not establish greater conceptual progress because response accuracy and learning were not assessed, they may reflect more extensive scaffolding and co-regulatory support under human tutoring. Within this broader pattern, lower effort in the Human condition may indicate that less exertion was required to continue when support made the tasks feel more manageable, rather than reduced engagement. Viewed through this theoretical lens, the pattern observed in the GenAI tutor condition is consistent with accounts of a distinct and partial form of emerging co-regulation, rather than the fuller scaffolding and co-regulatory capacities associated with human tutoring. In contrast, the pattern under human tutoring was more consistent with scaffolding and coregulation operating together. Comparable dissociations have been observed in recent experimental studies of AI-supported learning, where improvements in affective experience under AI support were not accompanied by gains in conceptual understanding (Bassner et al., 2026) , and where AI support was associated with motivational and affective benefits while lacking the social presence and collaborative depth of human interaction (Fan et al., 2025) . Together, these patterns are consistent with positioning generative AI between human support and independent internet search along a continuum of scaffolding and coregulation. Because conceptual progress and learning were not assessed, this positioning concerns engagement with difficulty rather than comparative learning effectiveness. Effort, perceived difficulty and stress were measured using single-item self-reports, with stress assessed only once, and tasks were intentionally set above curriculum level, which may have amplified challenge-related responses. Regulatory processes were inferred indirectly through behavioural and affective indicators rather than measured directly. The number of questions attempted did not capture the accuracy or quality of students' responses. A higher number of attempts could therefore reflect productive persistence, superficial movement between questions or unproductive floundering. Attempts should consequently be interpreted as a behavioural indicator of engagement across the task, rather than as evidence of successful task progress, conceptual understanding or learning. Interaction logs and transcripts were not included in the analysis, and the frequency, content and quality of support interactions were therefore not compared systematically across conditions. Consequently, scaffolding, co-regulation and learning partnership are used as theoretical lenses for interpreting the observed patterns, rather than as processes demonstrated by the study. Support-specific factors also warrant consideration. As support was provided by a single tutor, his individual style and physical presence may have shaped participants' interactions and responses to challenge. His presence may have offered reassurance or encouraged persistence, while obtaining help required direct social interaction. By contrast, students could consult the GenAI tutor without initiating a direct social interaction whenever they wished. Responses to the GenAI tutor may also have been influenced by novelty (Fryer et al., 2017) , while the Internet condition reflected the variable quality of open web resources. Finally, because the precise underlying model snapshot and behavioural configuration were not available to the researchers, and changes during the data-collection period could not be ruled out, the findings concern Khanmigo Lite as accessed between November 2024 and July 2025. They should not be generalised uncritically to other versions of Khanmigo Lite or to GenAI tutors as a category. Differences between these conditions may therefore reflect both the source of support and how that support was accessed. Despite these limitations, the findings have implications for how challenge is supported and experienced in educational contexts. For teachers, the results suggest that support should be treated as a pedagogical decision that shapes learners' engagement with difficulty, not simply as a means of providing answers. This points to a complementary role for AI tutors alongside human instruction, where AI may support learners in continuing to invest effort during challenging independent work, while teachers monitor whether difficulty is being resolved and provide responsive support when needed. For learners, the study highlights that responses to difficulty are not solely individual traits but are shaped by the support context, underscoring the importance of developing awareness of how different forms of help influence effort, persistence and stress. This suggests value in explicitly teaching helpseeking strategies, including how to engage productively with AI tutors as a way of working through difficulty rather than bypassing challenge. More broadly, the results underscore the value of attending to learners' behavioural and affective responses when evaluating the educational impact of AI.

items.abstract_text: This paper examined artificial intelligence (AI) in divestiture strategy and strategic decision-making of international oil companies (IOCs), with particular attention to Nigeria. The study aimed to examined how artificial intelligence improves the decision-making speed and quality of information used in divestiture strategies. A peer review qualitative data design was adopted. The study drawn evidence from peer-reviewed journals, and company’s official reports, which focuses on divestment cases involving Shell Petroleum Development Spin-off of its onshore outlets, Eni’ sale of Nigerian Agip Oil Company to Oando: Renaissance group, Total Energy’s spin-off of its portfolio, and ExxonMobil’s Spin-off of its Nigerian shallow-water subsidiary to Seplat Energy. The evidence was subjected to thematic content analysis on four decision domains: AI-driven asset valuation analytics, AI-driven human capitals analytics, AI-driven financial statement analytics, and post-divestment monitoring. The findings indicate that AI-driven asset valuation analytics, AI-driven human capitals analytics, AI-driven financial statement analytics, and post-divestment monitoring explained data quality, decision quality and decision-making speed. AI can integrate heterogeneous operational, financial, geological, market, regulatory and environmental information, identify patterns, generate scenarios and improve the speed and quality of strategic decisions. The paper concludes that AI-driven divestiture strategy with AI-driven human capitals analytics, AI-driven financial statement analytics improve strategic decision-making processes. It is recommended that IOCs should establish an AI-enabled portfolio intelligence platform that integrates AI-driven human capitals analytics, AI-driven financial statement analytics, and post-divestment monitoring data for decision support.

items.title: Do People Trust AI Assistants Even When They Are Consistently Wrong?
items.evidence: Preprint; source-checked v1, peer review unverified
items.abstract_text: People are increasingly using conversational AI systems to make decisions despite concerns around their reliability. How well do people calibrate to AI systems' accuracy in multi-turn conversations? We measure how people's reliance on LLMs' advice changes across repeated interactions, varying whether the AI assistant is helpful (100% accurate), unhelpful (0% accurate), or mixed (50% accurate). Across 4 experiments, we find people learn to trust helpful models more than unhelpful ones (67% vs 21% of the time), but only when they receive external feedback on the models' accuracy. Without feedback, people continue to be persuaded 48% of the time by a consistently unhelpful model (vs 38% for helpful). Rather than gaining trust in helpful models, participant reliance on LLM advisors tended to be high in early trials and only fell with evidence of inaccuracy. Participants trusted LLM advisors more than they trusted human advisors (83% vs 65%, Experiment 4), and LLMs benefited more from having a helpful track record than humans did. In contrast with previous work, we find limited evidence of an advantage for arguing for the truth (versus a falsehood). Truth advantages emerged only when participants were already very confident in their position, and did not emerge at all for static hints. Collectively, the results suggest that people may be swayed by LLM advice, even when it is consistently false, unless they have access to timely ground-truth feedback. Unfortunately, in many domains such feedback may not be available, leading to overreliance on AI.

items.abstract_text: Autonomous systems pose liability issues when automated decisions contribute to harm, failure, or non-compliance with regulations. Current legal AI studies primarily focus on classification, retrieval, question answering, and judicial prediction, and little has been done to translate legal and regulatory texts into structured signals that convey liability-relevant information. This research paper proposes a decision-support model for categorizing liability cues under European Union and Indian law. The source datasets were MultiEURLEX and IndicLegalQA, and a rule-based proxy mapping was developed to assign five labels: damage, defect, liability, regulation, and risk. This model is based on word-level and character-level TF-IDF, jurisdiction encoding, and a One-vs-Rest Linear Support Vector Machine classifier for multi-label classification. The final best configuration had an overall 91.33% subset accuracy, 96.08% Micro-F1, 87.81% Macro-F1, and 0.0201 Hamming Loss, compared to the best configurations of Logistic regression, Linear SVM, and Rand Forest. The framework aids initial legal and regulatory analysis and does not decide liability on doctrinal grounds or substitute for proficient legal analysis.

items.abstract_text: The determinants of the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-based virtual assistants in metaverse-enabled augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) training environments are the focus of this study, which is based on the need to improve the training experience of students who display anti-social behavior. An integrated approach based on the task-technology fit and the UTAUT2 models is adopted to investigate the factors that affect the training experience in AR and VR environments enabled by metaverse technologies. An online survey conducted in two languages—English and Arabic—yielded 310 participants. The data were then analyzed based on the hybrid approach of structural equation modeling and artificial neural networks. According to the study, the strongest predictor of the behavioral intention to use metaverse-based training systems is the performance expectancy factor, which is 94.1%, followed by the social influence factor, which is 67.5%, and the hedonic motivation factor, which is 66.6%. In addition, the effort expectancy and facilitating conditions factors did not affect the intention to use the training systems. In conclusion, the study revealed that the AI virtual assistant factors and the strategies adopted in the development of the training systems play an essential role in improving the training experience of students who display antisocial behavior in the classroom.

items.title: Teacher-regulated generative AI in structured group tasks: independent performance and metacognitive judgements in higher education
items.abstract_text: Introduction As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in higher education classrooms, an important question is whether it shapes not only students' task performance but also how they judge their own learning. This study examined whether participation in AI-supported structured group tasks was associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration compared with non-AI-supported structured group tasks. Methods A group-randomized, post-test-only classroom design was implemented in two undergraduate classes using Rain Classroom, a digital instructional platform. Students worked in pre-existing groups, and instructional condition was randomly assigned at the group level. In the AI-supported condition, students were permitted to use the platform's built-in AI learning companion during structured group discussion; in the non-AI-supported condition, they were instructed not to use it. After previewing the post-task assessment items, students completed a task-specific judgement form before responding to the assessment itself. The final analytic sample consisted of 126 students. Results Linear mixed models accounting for class and group-level clustering indicated significantly higher independent post-task performance in the AI-supported condition, B = 0.506, SE = 0.188, p = 0.013, 95% CI [0.117, 0.894], with a small descriptive standardized mean difference ( d = 0.196). No statistically significant between-condition differences were observed in predicted performance, confidence judgements, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. Discussion These findings indicate a modest between-condition difference in post-task performance without parallel statistically detectable differences in metacognitive monitoring.

reading.findings: In contrast to the significant difference in independent posttask performance, the adjusted between-condition difference in predicted score was not statistically significant. Neither confidence in anticipated performance nor confidence in understanding differed significantly between conditions. Thus, although the AIsupported group obtained higher actual post-task scores, the present data provide no statistically detectable evidence that AIsupported discussion also changed students' prospective estimates of performance or their immediate subjective certainty about performance and understanding. One explanation is that performance predictions and confidence judgements are shaped by more than informational support alone (Lichtenstein and Fischhoff, 1977) . In classroom settings, such judgements may reflect habitual self-evaluative tendencies, perceived task difficulty, prior academic experience, and personal standards for determining whether sufficient understanding has been achieved (Nederhand et al., 2021) . A single episode of AI-supported discussion may therefore support task preparation without being sufficient to produce a clearly detectable shift in students' prospective self-evaluations. The timing of the judgement form may also be relevant. Students completed it after viewing the assessment items but before answering them, a procedure designed to capture taskspecific judgements rather than general attitudes toward AI. Their predictions and confidence ratings may therefore have reflected a relatively cautious appraisal of the specific assessment they were about to complete rather than a broader sense of ease or familiarity associated with AI support. In this sense, the measures captured a more immediate task-specific judgement than broader self-report measures commonly used in studies of AI adoption or attitudes (Double, 2025; Schraw, 2009) . From a distributed cognition perspective, it is plausible that access to shared cognitive resources supported task preparation without necessarily changing students' personal estimates of their own performance. Because the study did not measure how individual students appropriated peer or AI contributions, this remains an interpretive possibility rather than a tested mechanism (Aarset and Johannessen, 2022; Atchley et al., 2024; Hollan et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2022 Kim et al., , 2025)) . Taken together, these findings show that higher observed performance in the AI-supported condition was not accompanied by statistically detectable differences in predicted performance or confidence. The confidence intervals around the prediction and confidence estimates all included zero and remained sufficiently wide to indicate uncertainty about the magnitude of any betweencondition differences. This study adopted a group-randomized, post-test-only classroom design to examine whether AI-supported structured group tasks were associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration compared with non-AI-supported structured group tasks. The study was conducted in two undergraduate classes within the same university course. Students completed the same instructional task under one of two conditions: an AI-supported condition or a non-AI-supported condition. Because the intervention was implemented through group-based classroom activity, instructional condition was randomly assigned at the group level, whereas the main outcome variables were measured at the individual level through a task-specific judgement form and an individual post-task assessment. The design was intended to preserve ecological validity while maintaining reasonable control over the role of AI in classroom learning by embedding AI as a regulated support resource during structured group discussion rather than as an unrestricted answergenerating tool. Because no pre-intervention measures of the study outcomes were collected, the design does not permit direct assessment of baseline equivalence or within-student change over time. Participants were undergraduate students enrolled in a university course taught by the researcher. During the semester, the researcher taught five sections of the course, from which two intact classes were randomly selected for inclusion in the study. The study was conducted in March 2026 in regular classroom settings and was embedded within normal teaching activities. All participants were second-year undergraduates majoring in Business English or Secretarial Studies. Age and gender were not collected as study variables. At the beginning of the semester, students in each class had already formed their own discussion groups for routine classroom activities. Group formation was based on students' free choice, and some students chose to work individually; as a result, group size ranged from 1 to 8 students. Of the 28 pre-existing groups, three were single-person groups: one was assigned to the AIsupported condition and two to the non-AI-supported condition. The remaining 25 groups consisted of two to eight students. Class was not used as a stratification factor. This resulted in 14 groups being assigned to the AIsupported condition and 14 to the non-AI-supported condition. analysis.results: In contrast to the significant difference in independent posttask performance, the adjusted between-condition difference in predicted score was not statistically significant. Neither confidence in anticipated performance nor confidence in understanding differed significantly between conditions. Thus, although the AIsupported group obtained higher actual post-task scores, the present data provide no statistically detectable evidence that AIsupported discussion also changed students' prospective estimates of performance or their immediate subjective certainty about performance and understanding. One explanation is that performance predictions and confidence judgements are shaped by more than informational support alone (Lichtenstein and Fischhoff, 1977) . In classroom settings, such judgements may reflect habitual self-evaluative tendencies, perceived task difficulty, prior academic experience, and personal standards for determining whether sufficient understanding has been achieved (Nederhand et al., 2021) . A single episode of AI-supported discussion may therefore support task preparation without being sufficient to produce a clearly detectable shift in students' prospective self-evaluations. The timing of the judgement form may also be relevant. Students completed it after viewing the assessment items but before answering them, a procedure designed to capture taskspecific judgements rather than general attitudes toward AI. Their predictions and confidence ratings may therefore have reflected a relatively cautious appraisal of the specific assessment they were about to complete rather than a broader sense of ease or familiarity associated with AI support. In this sense, the measures captured a more immediate task-specific judgement than broader self-report measures commonly used in studies of AI adoption or attitudes (Double, 2025; Schraw, 2009) . From a distributed cognition perspective, it is plausible that access to shared cognitive resources supported task preparation without necessarily changing students' personal estimates of their own performance. Because the study did not measure how individual students appropriated peer or AI contributions, this remains an interpretive possibility rather than a tested mechanism (Aarset and Johannessen, 2022; Atchley et al., 2024; Hollan et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2022 Kim et al., , 2025)) . Taken together, these findings show that higher observed performance in the AI-supported condition was not accompanied by statistically detectable differences in predicted performance or confidence. The confidence intervals around the prediction and confidence estimates all included zero and remained sufficiently wide to indicate uncertainty about the magnitude of any betweencondition differences. Given the limited number of analytic groups and the absence of an a priori power calculation, these non-significant findings should not be interpreted as evidence that the conditions were equivalent; rather, the present study did not detect parallel changes in students' immediate prospective judgements. The study also found no statistically significant differences between the AI-supported and non-AI-supported conditions in either calibration bias or absolute calibration error. The corresponding descriptive effect sizes were small (d = 0.227 for calibration bias; d = -0.144 for absolute calibration error). Thus, although students in the AI-supported condition performed significantly better on the post-task assessment, they did not show statistically detectable greater accuracy in judging their own performance than students in the non-AI-supported condition. This pattern is consistent with the distinction between task performance and metacognitive accuracy (Janssen and Lazonder, 2024; Schraw, 2009) . AI-supported discussion may assist task preparation without necessarily changing the processes students use to evaluate how well they are likely to perform. Performance and accurate self-monitoring should therefore not be assumed to develop in parallel. One explanation is that cognitive calibration requires more than informational assistance or discussion support (Janssen and Lazonder, 2024) . Better calibration may require explicit opportunities to compare judgements with outcomes, reflect on the basis of confidence, and evaluate the limits of one's understanding (Wang et al., 2024) . In the present study, the Rain Classroom AI learning companion supported group discussion but was not designed specifically to prompt metacognitive reflection, confidence checking, or prediction-feedback comparison. The instructional design therefore targeted task engagement more directly than calibration processes. Distributed cognition provides a contextual rather than causal interpretation of this result. The AI-supported task made information and interpretive resources available across peers, task materials, and the AI tool (Aarset and Johannessen, 2022; Hollan et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2022) , but the study did not directly assess whether or how these shared resources were internalized by individual students. It is therefore possible that collaborative resources supported task processing without producing a corresponding difference in individual metacognitive monitoring, but this mechanism remains to be tested directly (Atchley et al., 2024; Qiao et al., 2024) . The short-term nature of the activity may also be relevant. Calibration depends on the alignment between subjective judgement and actual performance and may require repeated cycles of prediction, action, feedback, and revision before measurable change becomes visible (Janssen and Lazonder, 2024; Wang et al., 2024) . A single classroom session may therefore be more likely to reveal an immediate performance difference than a stable change in monitoring accuracy. Because both predicted and actual performance were measured on bounded 0-10 scales, and actual scores showed substantial upper-end concentration, the derived calibration indices also had constrained score distributions, which may have reduced their sensitivity to between-condition differences. The non-significant calibration findings should therefore be interpreted cautiously. They provide no evidence that the present form of AI-supported discussion improved calibration accuracy, while the brief intervention and restricted score variability may have limited sensitivity to detect such differences. If improved judgement accuracy is an instructional goal, additional metacognitive scaffolding may be needed alongside AI-supported task activities. Taken together, this differentiated pattern suggests a theoretically important distinction between externally supported task processing and internally calibrated self-monitoring. In a structured collaborative task, AI may expand the informational and interpretive resources available to the group, but the present findings do not establish whether such support changes individual metacognitive monitoring.
analysis.discussion: This study examined whether AI-supported structured group tasks were associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration. The findings revealed a differentiated pattern across outcomes. Students in the AI-supported condition obtained significantly higher scores on the independent post-task assessment than those in the non-AIsupported condition. However, no statistically significant betweencondition differences were found in predicted score, confidence in anticipated performance, confidence in understanding, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. Taken together, the statistically detectable difference was concentrated at the level of independent task performance rather than extending to students' prospective judgements or metacognitive accuracy. This pattern underscores the importance of examining performance and metacognitive monitoring as related but distinct outcomes of AI-supported classroom activity. This study examined whether AI-supported structured group tasks were associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration in a higher education classroom. Using a group-randomized, post-test-only classroom design implemented through Rain Classroom, the analysis indicated that students in the AI-supported condition obtained higher scores on the independent post-task assessment than those in the non-AI-supported condition. However, no statistically significant between-condition differences were observed in predicted performance, confidence in anticipated performance, confidence in understanding, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. These findings indicate that, in the present instructional context, the AI-supported condition was associated with modestly higher performance on this task-specific assessment, without statistically detectable between-condition differences in performance predictions, confidence judgements, or cognitive calibration. Overall, the findings highlight the value of distinguishing task performance from metacognitive monitoring as separate outcomes when evaluating AI-supported classroom activities in higher education.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations of the present study should be considered when interpreting the findings, with the most consequential relating to study design, measurement, and statistical precision. First, no pre-intervention measures of content knowledge, confidence, or calibration were collected. Consequently, although random assignment occurred at the group level, it cannot be determined with certainty whether the two instructional conditions were fully equivalent on these variables prior to the intervention. This limits the strength of causal inference that can be drawn from the observed post-task differences. Future research could incorporate pre-and post-intervention measures in order to examine more directly how AI-supported structured group tasks influence change over time in both learning outcomes and metacognitive judgements. Second, the post-task assessment was intentionally brief and designed for classroom implementation. Although this format suited the practical constraints of a single class session and aligned closely with the instructional task, it should be interpreted as a task-specific indicator of learning rather than as a fully validated standardized measure. Because the assessment consisted of only four heterogeneous items, score precision may have been limited, and individual items may have had a relatively strong influence on total scores. Because item-level scores were not retained in the analytic dataset, item-specific performance patterns could not be examined retrospectively. The score distribution also showed notable upper-end concentration: 27.8% of the full sample obtained the maximum score, and ceiling concentration was particularly pronounced in the Class 1 AI-supported subgroup, where 69.0% obtained the maximum. This restricted variability may have reduced sensitivity for estimating between-condition differences in performance and, because calibration indices were derived from predicted and actual scores on the same bounded 0-10 scale, may also have constrained calibration-related outcomes. Although inter-rater reliability for the application/transfer item was excellent for the mean of the two ratings, ICC (A,2) = 0.935, 95% CI [0.890, 0.955], the brevity, heterogeneity, and upper-end concentration of the assessment remain important constraints. Future research could employ more extensive outcome measures with greater discrimination at the upper end. Third, no a priori power analysis was conducted. Together with the limited number of analytic groups, this means that the study may have had limited statistical precision for detecting small or moderate between-condition differences in performance predictions, confidence, or calibration. The non-significant findings should accordingly be interpreted as an absence of statistically detectable differences in this sample rather than as evidence of equivalence between conditions. Future studies should use larger samples, prospectively justified sample sizes, and repeated assessments to provide a more precise account of how AI-supported learning relates to both performance and metacognitive monitoring. Fourth, the study was conducted by the researcher acting as the course instructor. Although this arrangement supported implementation within an authentic teaching context, it also introduced the possibility of instructor-related bias. The dual role of researcher and instructor may have influenced instructional delivery, participant expectations, or intervention fidelity in subtle but unmeasured ways. Future research could reduce this source of bias by involving independent instructors, using multiple instructors, or adopting designs in which implementation and analysis are more clearly separated. Fifth, although the study examined performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration in addition to performance, it did not capture fine-grained interaction data on how groups actually used the AI support during discussion. For example, the study did not analyse the specific prompts students entered, the types of responses generated by the AI learning companion, or the extent to which different groups relied on AI in different ways. As a result, the present findings can describe between-condition differences, but cannot identify the detailed mechanisms through which those differences emerged. Future research could incorporate process-oriented data such as prompt logs, interaction traces, discussion transcripts, or response uptake patterns to move beyond whether conditions differ and toward a more precise understanding of how different forms of human-AI interaction relate to performance and metacognitive outcomes. Sixth, the AI support examined in this study was the Rain Classroom AI learning companion, embedded within a specific classroom platform and used under teacher-regulated conditions. The comparison in this study was therefore based on permitted vs. non-permitted use of a platform-embedded AI tool within a structured classroom task, rather than on unrestricted use of external generative AI systems. In addition, the intervention was relatively short in duration, as the study focused on a single classroom-based activity. As a result, the findings should not be taken as applying equally to all forms of generative AI or to more open-ended, sustained, or student-directed AI use. Future research could compare different AI systems, interaction conditions, and intervention durations in order to clarify how different AI affordances and instructional arrangements shape both learning outcomes and metacognitive processes (Atchley et al., 2024; Bauer et al., 2025; Janssen and Lazonder, 2024; Kim et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024) . Seventh, the study was conducted in a specific instructional context, namely a university course session on life and wellbeing, using a single case-based structured group task. Although this context provided an authentic classroom setting for examining AI-supported learning, the findings should not be assumed to generalize directly to other subjects, task types, or higher education contexts. The role of AI support may differ across disciplines, especially in courses characterized by different epistemic demands, problem-solving requirements, or assessment forms (Bond et al., 2024; Qian, 2025) . Future research could therefore examine whether the present pattern of findings is specific to this course theme and task design or reflects a more general feature of AIsupported structured group learning across disciplinary contexts.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Objective Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes are rapidly becoming normalized in clinical practice, yet governance frameworks focus on accuracy, privacy, consent, and medicolegal status. Risks to clinician capabilities have received less attention. Speak before the reveal is a proposed method in which clinicians verbalize critical cognitive steps, such as synthesis and plan, before note generation. Discussion Recent work distinguishes deskilling in senior clinicians, never-skilling from premature offload in trainees and mis-skilling, the internalization of AI errors and inappropriate use as sound practice. This Perspective builds on emerging evidence that reasoning before seeing AI output may protect unaided reasoning. Training implementation, evaluation, adherence challenges, validation methodology, and governance strategies for training bodies, health services, and scribe vendors are discussed. Conclusion Speak before the reveal is a low-cost, testable approach to maintaining clinical reasoning for individuals or organizations. Successful AI scribe adoption requires preserving clinicians’ ability to work without AI support.

items.title: Right Advice, Wrong Reasons: How Decision and Reasoning Alignment Shape Reliance on AI Advisors
items.evidence: Preprint; source-checked v1, peer review unverified
items.abstract_text: When people seek advice from AI on social situations, the system may recommend a decision they fully agree with but justify it through reasoning they disagree with. Conversely, it may offer reasoning they agree with, and yet reach a decision they reject. We distinguish decision alignment, whether an advisor recommends the option favored by a user's measured values, from reason alignment, whether its stated reasons align with the user's values. In this work, we ask how these two forms of alignment shape people's preferences for AI advisors and their willingness to use them in different roles. We conducted a within-subjects study (N=121) in which participants evaluated three AI advisors varying in decision and reason alignment across eight everyday moral dilemmas. Participants then chose which advisors they would consult, allow to draft messages for review, or allow to act on their behalf in new tasks. When seeking advice, participants most often preferred an advisor that reasoned through their prioritized values while recommending the opposing decision (40%). However, when participants had to pick advisors for new tasks, their preferences shifted toward advisors that also recommended decisions aligned with their values, rather than those that only shared their reasons. Also, as participants considered tasks that gave AI advisors greater autonomy, they became more likely to opt out of using any advisor, from 12% when consulting to 38% when allowing an advisor to act on their behalf. Our findings suggest that decision and reason alignment shape advisor preferences differently across contexts of AI use, and that alignment with a user's values does not necessarily imply willingness to delegate.

items.abstract_text: Abstract This article theorizes financial markets and democratic publics as collective information-processing systems embedded in shared communicative infrastructures, such that markets can even be said to be embedded in publics. Bringing the efficient market hypothesis into dialogue with the liberal marketplace of ideas and the Habermasian public sphere, I identify four epistemic conditions these traditions depend on: diversity, independence, aggregation, and correction. I argue that price discovery is epistemically embedded in the same media environment through which public opinions form. The attention economy of engagement-driven media brings this into view by degrading that environment: it privileges affective arousal over informational quality, correlates judgements, and suppresses correction, in effect creating corrupted marketplaces of ideas. The comparison also shows a specific difference between the domains: market correction through arbitrage operates through market transactions as well as media communication, whereas counterspeech and persuasion in publics are more reliant on media, arguably rendering publics more vulnerable to media impairment.

analysis.discussion: This article has argued that three major traditions of thought about collective information processing-the EMH, the marketplace of ideas, and the Habermasian public sphere-share the epistemic preconditions of diversity, independence, aggregation, and correction, though the meaning of these terms differs across traditions. For example, in the market-based traditions, the requirement is that individual errors be sufficiently statistically independent to cancel out in aggregation. In the Habermasian tradition participants must be free from coercion and strategic manipulation and oriented towards mutual understanding. I then argued that financial markets are epistemically embedded in publics: the judgements registered through trades are formed partly within the same communicative environments in which public opinion is produced. The attention economy, by overvaluing arousal, violates the epistemic preconditions of all three. Echo chambers correlate the biases of investors and citizens alike. The gamification of both trading and political communication rewards herding over independent analysis. The algorithmic distribution of content suppresses correction mechanisms (arbitrage, counterspeech, and rational persuasion) by rendering them invisible in an environment optimized for engagement. This impairment is not uniform: it is arguably comparatively limited in markets, because their corrective mechanisms operate through the market too rather than through media alone, and on which a majority of transactions involve sophisticated institutional traders. The comparison of the two traditions on publics, in turn, shows the attention economy moving publics away from the Habermasian model and towards a corrupted marketplace of ideas. This article has several limitations that also point towards future work. For example, the article has focused on the attention economy's destructive effects on collective information processing, but digital platforms also have constructive epistemic effects-lowering barriers to participation, enabling new forms of collective knowledge production, connecting previously isolated publics-that deserve attention and that complicate any straightforwardly pessimistic reading. There is also a tension here between theories that have claimed to be primarily descriptive of reality (EMH) and those that are more explicitly normative (Habermas) . But this difference is not clear-cut, considering, for example, the performativity argument-markets have, to an extent, been shaped by the EMH rather than the EMH merely describing it (MacKenzie 2006) . And although it is debatable if the marketplace of ideas theory had anything to do with it, in the performative sense, algorithmic media have nevertheless turned the marketplace metaphor into more of a reality in publics, as I have argued, so that the theory arguably now describes online publics more accurately than it ever described the print-era publics for which it was coined, although in a decidedly corrupt form, not in the way its defenders hoped. Moreover, even a supposedly descriptive theory may of course have normative implications, as the EMH clearly does (and readily admits from the very beginning, see Fama 1970) , and even a normative theory will be interpreted as describing the world (as has happened with Habermas to perhaps a larger extent than he ever intended). The EMH, particularly the claimed superiority of the market as an information-processing and valuation device, is in practice used normatively to justify market economies. This would merit further work. A place to start might be to note that while the attention economy degrades the three theories' ability to accurately describe and interpret the world, it does not necessarily degrade their normative force. Efficient markets, free marketplaces of ideas, and deliberative public spheres can still function as ideals, whose realization our institution-building attempts can be guided by. But theories of how information-aggregation mechanisms work empirically must evolve. The degradation of publics and markets could be termed more broadly as an erosion of social valuation. Besides information aggregators, markets and publics are also social systems for assigning worth; economic worth in the case of markets, political and moral worth in the case of publics (Boltanski and Th� evenot 2006) . When the epistemic conditions required for these systems to function are undermined by deterioration of the media, a society's capacity to evaluate is systemically impaired. This highlights the embeddedness of markets in publics and emphasizes why democratic publics and their functioning matter for social domains far beyond politics, as do markets and their functioning for domains far beyond finance.

items.abstract_text: Table Question Answering (TableQA) requires reasoning over natural language questions and structured tables and remains challenging due to noisy evidence and complex multi-step reasoning. Recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based approaches typically adopt decomposition–reasoning–validation pipelines that combine Chain-of-Thought (CoT) decomposition, Direct Prompting (DP), Python Agent (PyAgent) execution, and self-validation. However, these methods still largely rely on unconstrained LLM reasoning during decomposition, which may introduce unsupported sub-questions and irrelevant evidence expansion. We propose EV idence- A ware (EVA), a framework that explicitly grounds decomposition on question-relevant table evidence before reasoning begins. EVA first extracts evidence-aware relational structures that associate question semantics with supporting table attributes, thereby constraining sub-question generation within a grounded evidence space. EVA further introduces relation-guided validation and integrates both DP and PyAgent reasoning to improve robustness across different reasoning patterns. Experiments on datasets across multiple LLMs demonstrate that EVA consistently improves reasoning reliability and achieves strong performance across diverse TableQA settings.

items.abstract_text: As generative AI reshapes professional and educational practice, institutions face a challenge: how to support diverse learners, from non-coders to advanced students, in building confidence and practice with AI-supported problem solving. Most institutional responses bifurcate into conceptual workshops for general audiences or technical courses for computer science majors, leaving few spaces where mixed-ability learners can engage common AI tasks at levels matched to their prior experience. This experience report presents the LearnAI Framework, a two-layer model for just-in-time AI co-creation piloted at a comprehensive teaching university. The Wide-Exposure Layer embeds short presentations in existing courses to build AI awareness at scale, reaching students and faculty across 18 courses in five disciplines. The Customized Co-Creation Layer provides opt-in, one-on-one sessions where clients work with trained undergraduate tutors through a 5-Stage Pedagogical Script: Problem Framing, Tool-Task Mapping, Iterative Co-Prompting, Deployment and Verification, and Ethical Reflection. Over two semesters, 35 clients co-created 36 portfolio websites and over 20 deployed web applications. Interviews with five clients and two tutors suggest a recurring change in how clients described AI use, shifting from treating AI as a passive answer machine to engaging it as a collaborative tool under human direction. A small paired pre/post AI readiness dataset (N=7) provides preliminary descriptive context, and tutor accounts document how the pedagogical script was enacted and adapted across client types. We report on boundary cases including clients who felt overwhelmed and respondents who deliberately rejected AI use. This paper contributes a practical, adoptable framework with initial evidence from a single institution.

items.title: People prefer AI to human advice in multi-turn conversations but neither changes incentivised behaviour
items.evidence: Preprint; source-checked v1, peer review unverified
items.abstract_text: People increasingly ask AI chatbots for advice, yet large language models (LLMs) are sycophantic, overconfident, and can amplify human cognitive biases. In this article, we investigate how people perceive advice from humans versus LLMs and whether AI advice reshapes incentive-compatible donation decisions. Using Carrier, a new experimental platform, we designed an experiment where participants made a donation decision after discussing it with an AI chatbot advisor, another human, or receiving no advice. Participants judged LLM advisors to be significantly more rational, trustworthy, convincing, and sycophantic than human advisors. Analysis of chatlogs showed that LLMs were more engaged than human advisors: they shared more facts and more often stated their opinion and justified their recommendations. Despite this, donation decisions did not vary across conditions.

items.title: Lifecycle Narrative: Reconstructing the Development Process of a Machine Learning Model

items.abstract_text: Machine learning models are increasingly proposed for high-risk domains, such as healthcare and public policymaking. However, their growing complexity creates significant obstacles to transparency. This complexity arises from various factors; in this work, we focus on making the organizational development process of a model transparent. A model is often developed over many years and involves multiple version updates, carried out by different individuals, and based on varying subsets of data. To address these issues, we propose a new model reporting framework called a lifecycle narrative, characterized by three dimensions: first, how the purpose of the model has incrementally evolved over time; second, how the data used in the model and the model itself have been developed; and third, what inferences can be made with the model and what the consequences of its use are. We demonstrate these three dimensions using a case study of a high-risk application in healthcare. Our framework complements existing model reporting tools, such as model cards and datasheets, by reconstructing the full lifecycle of the model—a documentation requirement of the EU AI Act. Ultimately, the lifecycle narrative empowers external stakeholders, such as regulators, researchers, citizens, and national competent authorities, to holistically understand a model’s development process.

items.abstract_text: This study maps and synthesises two adjacent bodies of literature—research on ethnomathematics and culturally responsive mathematics instruction focused on Akan cultural practices, and research on artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education—to propose a culturally responsive, AI-supported instructional framework for Ghanaian classrooms. A systematic scoping review was conducted following the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) and PRISMA 2020 flow conventions. Six databases were searched for records published between 2005 and 2025, supplemented by hand-searching. AI was operationalised broadly, from intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning systems to generative AI from late 2022 onwards. Of 612 records, 25 studies were retained for qualitative thematic synthesis. The synthesis indicates that kente weaving, Adinkra symbolism, market transactions, and drumming patterns encode mathematical ideas such as symmetry, proportion, sequence, and logical reasoning. The AI-focused studies, most of which predate generative AI, suggest that these tools can support personalised, interactive, and contextualised learning. No included study combines the two strands in the Akan context; this absence is a central finding and motivates the proposed framework. Blending ethnomathematics with AI is associated with greater cultural relevance, engagement, and conceptual clarity, although digitising Indigenous knowledge raises ethical questions of ownership, representation, and community consent.

reading.interpretation: This review set out to map and synthesise the literature on integrating Akan ethnomathematics with AI and to propose a culturally responsive, AI-supported framework. The findings affirm that Akan culture is rich in embedded mathematical knowledge and that AI tools can plausibly amplify its pedagogical value. The following discussion interprets these findings, links them explicitly to theory, compares them with existing studies, and addresses ethical and practical considerations raised in the literature. 4.2.1. Cultural Context as a Foundation for Mathematical Cognition Learners frequently encounter abstract mathematics in isolation, which hinders understanding. The synthesis suggests that contextualising learning through familiar cultural practices—weaving, trading, and symbolic representation—facilitates meaningful connections. Understanding symmetry through kente or proportion through market transactions renders learning more intuitive and relatable, consistent with broader evidence that contextualised instruction supports transfer [27], [31]. 4.2.2. Artificial Intelligence as a Cultural Mediator A central theoretical contribution of this study is the conceptualisation of AI as a cultural mediator. Rather than delivering decontextualised content, AI can personalise, simulate, and visualise mathematical problems derived from cultural contexts. AI-driven kente-pattern platforms can help learners explore geometry through real-time manipulation of shapes and transformations, while conversational agents can generate adaptive assessments anchored in adinkra symbols. When embedded with curated cultural datasets, such systems act as bridges between tradition and innovation [12], [32]. Review Protocol and Search Strategy A review protocol was defined a priori, specifying the research questions, databases, search strings, and selection criteria. Six databases were searched for records published between 2005 and 2025: Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The search combined three concept blocks using  (“ethnomathematics” OR “culturally responsive mathematics” OR “Indigenous  AND (“artificial intelligence” OR “AI” OR “intelligent tutoring” OR “adaptive learning” OR “computer-assisted instruction” OR “learning analytics” OR  AND (“mathematics education” OR “conceptual understanding” OR “teaching” The two topical blocks were also run separately (each in combination with the mathematics-education block) so that studies addressing either strand in depth could be captured, given the near absence of studies addressing both. The database searches returned 610 records. Reference lists of key studies were additionally hand-searched; this citation searching contributed two seminal works that predate the search window but are foundational to the field [26], [27] and are flagged accordingly in Table 1. 3.3. Operational Definition of Artificial Intelligence and the 2005–2025 Window Because widely accessible generative AI tools such as ChatGPT only became publicly available in late 2022, it is essential to be explicit about what “artificial intelligence” means in a review whose search window opens in 2005. In this review, AI was operationalised broadly, following the taxonomy of Zawacki-Richter et al. [12] and Holmes et al. [11], to encompass: (i) intelligent tutoring systems; (ii) adaptive and personalised learning platforms; (iii) profiling, prediction, and learning analytics; (iv) automated assessment and feedback systems; and (v) generative conversational AI, the most recent addition to the family. The year 2005 was selected as the lower bound because it marks the period in which research on intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning matured into a substantial empirical literature (e.g., [28]) and in which ethnomathematics consolidated as an international research programme [5], [8]. Accordingly, studies published between 2005 and 2022 met the technology-related inclusion criterion by examining these earlier, pre-generative forms of AI and intelligent educational technology—not generative chatbots, which did not yet exist. Studies published from late 2022 onwards could additionally address generative AI. Table 1 identifies the specific technological focus of each AI-related study so that readers can verify this stratification directly. Two consequences of this definition are acknowledged https://doi.org/10.58421/misro.v5i4.1757 2605 openly: first, references in this review to conversational agents such as ChatGPT as candidate instructional tools are conceptual extrapolations from the evidence on earlier AI systems, not summaries of empirical trials of generative AI; second, no included study empirically evaluates generative AI in combination with ethnomathematics. Both points are revisited in the Limitations (Section 4.2.8). 3.4. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies were included if they (i) addressed ethnomathematics or culturally grounded mathematics instruction, or the use of AI as defined in Section 3.3 (or closely allied digital educational technology) in mathematics education or in African education systems; (ii) were peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, scholarly books, or authoritative institutional reports; (iii) were published in English, in principle between 2005 and 2025; and (iv) provided conceptual, empirical, or methodological insight relevant to at least one research question. Seminal works published before 2005 that were identified through citation searching and are foundational to either strand were eligible for retention and are explicitly flagged in Table 1. Studies were excluded if they were off-topic or non- educational, lacked any link between culture and mathematics or between AI/technology and mathematics education, were not peer-reviewed (e.g., blog posts, opinion pieces, or preprints), or were unavailable in full text or in English. On this basis, one otherwise relevant candidate source [1] was excluded from the corpus because it is a preprint; it is cited in this manuscript only as background context. 3.5. Study Selection and PRISMA Flow The selection proceeded in four phases—identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion. Of the 610 database records identified, 70 duplicates were removed, leaving 540 records, to which 2 hand-searched records were added (542 in total). Title and abstract screening excluded 125 off-topic or non-educational records, yielding 417 records for full- text assessment. A further 392 records were excluded at the full-text stage because they lacked a substantive link between culture and/or AI and mathematics education, were not peer-reviewed, or were unavailable in full text or in English, leaving 25 studies that met all criteria and formed the corpus for qualitative synthesis.
