The literature suggests that the cultural familiarity of these elements creates a cognitive bridge, supporting learners’ internalisation of mathematical concepts by situating them within familiar frameworks [27], [31]. 4.1.3. Relevance and Potential of AI Tools in Ethnomathematics-Based Instruction Across the corpus, AI tools emerge as promising means of supporting and expanding cultural mathematics instruction [11], [12]
analysis.discussion: This review set out to map and synthesise the literature on integrating Akan ethnomathematics with AI and to propose a culturally responsive, AI-supported framework. The findings affirm that Akan culture is rich in embedded mathematical knowledge and that AI tools can plausibly amplify its pedagogical value. The following discussion interprets these findings, links them explicitly to theory, compares them with existing studies, and addresses ethical and practical considerations raised in the literature. 4.2.1. Cultural Context as a Foundation for Mathematical Cognition Learners frequently encounter abstract mathematics in isolation, which hinders understanding. The synthesis suggests that contextualising learning through familiar cultural practices—weaving, trading, and symbolic representation—facilitates meaningful connections. Understanding symmetry through kente or proportion through market transactions renders learning more intuitive and relatable, consistent with broader evidence that contextualised instruction supports transfer [27], [31]. 4.2.2. Artificial Intelligence as a Cultural Mediator A central theoretical contribution of this study is the conceptualisation of AI as a cultural mediator. Rather than delivering decontextualised content, AI can personalise, simulate, and visualise mathematical problems derived from cultural contexts. AI-driven kente-pattern platforms can help learners explore geometry through real-time manipulation of shapes and transformations, while conversational agents can generate adaptive assessments anchored in adinkra symbols. When embedded with curated cultural datasets, such systems act as bridges between tradition and innovation [12], [32]. This mediating role positions AI not as a replacement for cultural knowledge but as an amplifier of it. It bears repeating that, for generative conversational agents specifically, this mediating role is a design proposition grounded in evidence on earlier AI systems (Section 3.3), not yet a 4.2.3. Operationalising the Theoretical Framework The proposed model operationalises Culturally Responsive Pedagogy by treating Akan cultural artefacts as legitimate mathematical content rather than mere illustration, thereby validating learners’ identities and challenging Eurocentric framings [24]. It operationalises constructivism by using AI tools to create inquiry-driven, experiential tasks—designing kente symmetries, simulating market exchanges—in which learners actively construct meaning and engage in dialogue and collaboration [25]. AI supports constructivist learning specifically by providing adaptive scaffolding, immediate feedback, and opportunities for iterative exploration that a single teacher cannot offer at scale. The https://doi.org/10.58421/misro.v5i4.1757 2613 two theories are thus complementary: CRP determines what content is meaningful, while constructivism determines how learners engage with it. 4.2.4. Comparison with Existing Studies The proposed model both extends and contrasts with prior work. Earlier ethnomathematics studies in Ghana and elsewhere demonstrate the cultural and cognitive value of Indigenous mathematics but generally stop short of integrating digital technologies [3], [4], [26]. Conversely, studies of AI in African education emphasise personalisation and access but rarely engage Indigenous knowledge [12], [14], [15]. By explicitly coupling Akan ethnomathematics with AI mediation, this review advances an integrative position that neither literature has fully articulated. Where some technology-in- education studies caution that AI may flatten local context, the present framework deliberatel y centres cultural authenticity as a design constraint, aligning with calls for decolonised and locally relevant EdTech [17], [18]. 4.2.5. Ethical Considerations in Digitising Indigenous Knowledge Digitising Indigenous knowledge raises questions that exte nd beyond conventional data privacy. The literature highlights issues of ownership —who holds the rights to cultural datasets derived from kente or adinkra —and of representation, since AI systems trained on incomplete or decontextualised samples risk misrep resenting Akan symbols and their meanings. Community participation is therefore essential: cultural custodians and educators should be involved in curating, validating, and approving content, and benefit - sharing arrangements should be considered so that co mmunities are partners rather than passive data sources [13]. Embedding these safeguards is a precondition for ethical implementation, not an afterthought. 4.2.6. The Risk of Cultural Simplification A further caution concerns cultural simplification. Kent e, adinkra, markets, and drumming are living cultural practices with deep historical and symbolic meaning; they are not merely teaching aids. Reducing them to convenient vehicles for mathematical content risks stripping away the very significance that make s them powerful for learners. The framework therefore advocates teaching the cultural meaning alongside the mathematics, so that learners appreciate, for example, both the symmetry and the symbolism of an adinkra sign. Maintaining this dual fidelity —mathem atical and cultural —guards against 4.2.7. Practical Classroom Challenges Implementation faces concrete barriers. Many Ghanaian schools, particularly in rural areas, have limited or unreliable internet access and few devices, constraining tools that require continuous connectivity [14], [16]. Teacher readiness is uneven, with gaps in both ethnomathematical methods and AI literacy [19], [20]. Language is a further consideration, since AI tools predominantly operate in English while many learners ar e more comfortable in local languages. The cost of AI subscriptions and devices may also be 2614 https://doi.org/10.58421/misro.v5i4.1757 prohibitive. These realities point to the need for offline-capable tools, sustained teacher professional development, localised and multilingual content, and phased, low-cost pilots. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the review is conceptual and literature-based; its conclusions are propositions to be tested, not empirical outcomes. items.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) have great potential to enhance productivity in many disciplines, such as software engineering. However, it is unclear to what extent they can assist in the design process of electronic circuits. This article focuses on the application of LLMs to switched-mode power supply (SMPS) design for printed circuit boards (PCBs). We present multiple LLM-based workflows that combine reasoning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a custom toolkit that enables the LLM to interact with the SPICE circuit simulator to receive physical feedback. Two benchmark experiments are presented to analyze the performance of LLM-based assistants on various design tasks. These include parameter tuning and topology adaption, as well as design optimization of SMPS circuits through optimal catalogue component selection to maximize circuit efficiency or balance multiple objectives like size, ripple, and component loss. Experiment results show that SPICE simulation feedback and current LLM advancements, such as reasoning, significantly increase the solve rate on 269 manually created benchmark tasks from 15% to 91%. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that most parameter tuning design tasks can be solved, while limits remain for certain topology adaption and multi-objective optimization tasks. Our experiments offer insights for improving current concepts, for example by adapting text-based circuit representations.

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has increasingly garnered attention within the global education landscape due to its potential to transform the teaching and learning process in a comprehensive manner. AI is capable of offering more personalised teaching approaches by adapting content and delivery methods according to individual students' proficiency levels, interests, and needs. It can analyse student performance in real time and provide immediate, targeted feedback, thereby enhancing students’ motivation to remain focused during learning sessions.This systematic literature review aims to critically examine and analyse the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the teaching and learning process, as well as its impact on student motivation. Scholarly databases such as Google Scholar, the Educational Resource Information Centre (ERIC), and Semantic Scholar were utilised to access relevant articles published within the last five years (2020–2025). A total of 156 articles were identified during the initial screening phase, and 13 were selected for synthesis as they met the specific contextual criteria of the systematic literature review, conducted in accordance with the stages outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) model.Findings from the review indicate a notable increase in both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation among students engaged in learning sessions that incorporate AI elements, particularly through the use of digital applications such as ChatGPT, Chatbot, Moodle, Ask AI, Image AI, Padlet, and others. These findings further substantiate the assertion that AI significantly contributes to enhancing students’ motivation during the teaching and learning process.The scope of this study specifically focuses on primary-level students to examine the influence of AI in the classroom context, thereby demonstrating the capacity of Artificial Intelligence to serve as a paradigm shift in fostering student motivation and cultivating a more productive teaching and learning environment.

A study by Yu, Yan & Cai (2024) found that information reliability is a key determining factor in shaping positive attitudes and the intention to continuously use ChatGPT among students. This indicates that students use ChatGPT not merely for technical convenience, but also because they trust the validity of the content presented. This reinforces the need for ChatGPT content to be continuously updated, reviewed, and monitored to ensure the accuracy of the information provided. More importantly, ChatGPT supports the principles of personalized learning. Students are no longer bound by the teacher’s schedule or pace of instruction; instead, they can learn at their own pace and style. This flexible learning experience aligns well with 21st-century learning concepts that emphasize student autonomy and self-directed approaches. Zhang (2024) noted that ChatGPT functions as a personal tutor, providing immediate guidance and feedback that enables students to correct errors and directly strengthen their understanding. This makes ChatGPT an effective learning aid in supporting students with varying ability levels. The Influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Usage on Increasing Student Motivation in PdPc Various recent studies show that AI generally has the potential to boost student motivation in teaching and learning. Hidir, Nazlena, Syahmi, and Farahin (2023) found that AI-based applications help students set learning goals, evaluate performance in real-time, and receive immediate feedback. Collectively, these factors drive an increase in intrinsic motivation because students better understand their progress and feel individually attended to. Furthermore, AI's ability to adapt content based on individual capability levels plays a crucial role in ensuring inclusive learning. Low-performing students do not feel left behind because content is tailored to their abilities, while high-achieving students are continuously encouraged to explore more challenging content. This situation supports student-centered teaching principles that are effective and responsive to diverse learning needs. A literature review by Hapsari, Ramadhan, and Ikramullah (2024) states that the use of AI in teaching and learning activities is proven to create a more engaging and innovative learning experience, which in turn increases student satisfaction and interest. This satisfaction and interest serve as key drivers of motivation, especially among primary school students who are still developing their attitudes toward learning. Overall, AI can no longer be viewed merely as a supporting technology; rather, it acts as a primary catalyst for transformation in teaching and learning approaches. The integration of ChatGPT and Chatbots has demonstrated great potential in enhancing the quality of the learning experience and fostering student motivation through personalization, instant feedback, and active engagement. Nevertheless, challenges such as reliance on machines, academic ethics issues, and a lack of AI literacy among teachers must still be addressed seriously. These include: • Most analyzed studies used quantitative or qualitative approaches in isolation without adopting a mixed-methods research design, which could potentially offer a more holistic view of students' experiences using AI. • The primary focus of past studies leaned heavily toward AI's effectiveness in terms of academic performance alone, whereas other affective dimensions—such as emotional engagement, learning resilience, and student identity formation—were • Rapid technological advancement means that past study findings may not reflect present realities, as the AI platforms and applications used by students evolve quickly Based on the identified limitations, several recommendations for future research are proposed to strengthen the existing literature: • Future research should employ a mixed-methods design to integrate quantitative data (such as motivation scores and academic achievement) with qualitative data (such as students' learning experiences) for a more comprehensive understanding of AI's • There is an urgent need to explore the long-term implications of AI use on students' affective and social domains, including technology dependency levels and the ability to think independently and critically. items.title: Biased Error Attribution in Multi-Agent Human–AI Systems Under Delayed Feedback
items.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Human decision-making is often influenced by cognitive biases, especially under uncertainty and risk. Prior works have studied biases in single-step decision environments with immediate outcomes or in interaction with a single AI agent. However, less attention has been given to (1) cascaded settings with delayed outcomes, where decision at one step influences future system states and (2) to interaction with multiple AI agents. To study this, we designed a naval battle strategy game where participants interact with two AI advisors. We find asymmetric responses to positive and negative outcomes, with significant changes after negative outcomes. Participants failed to identify the actions responsible for failures and misattributed responsibility across AI agents, leading them to modify decisions steps weakly related to the true cause of poor performance. We refer to this behavior as bias in error attribution. Our findings show how cognitive biases can emerge in human-multi AI teams in cascaded settings.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can both enhance and constrain employee creativity, yet the mechanisms underlying these divergent effects remain unclear. This study examines how augmentation and automation motivations for GenAI usage shape employee creativity through distinct knowledge-processing mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on dual-process theory and self-regulation theory, we distinguish augmentation and automation motivations for GenAI usage and propose distinct cognitive mechanisms linking them to creativity. We test the hypotheses using a multi-wave, multi-source field survey and a scenario-based experiment. Findings Augmentation motivation is positively associated with employee creativity through knowledge integration, whereas automation motivation is negatively related to creativity through knowledge dependence. Conscientiousness strengthens the positive indirect effect of augmentation motivation and attenuates the negative indirect effect of automation motivation on employee creativity. Research limitations/implications Augmentation and automation motivations may coexist and vary across tasks and use episodes. Future research could explore these dynamics, examine how other individual differences shape their effects, and assess whether the consequences of GenAI dependence vary across work contexts. Practical implications Organizations should encourage employees to use GenAI to generate and develop ideas rather than replace their own judgment. Training could help employees critically assess AI-generated suggestions and combine them with their own knowledge. Originality/value This research shifts attention from how much employees use GenAI to why they use it. By distinguishing augmentation and automation motivations, it explains when and why GenAI can enhance or constrain employee creativity through distinct knowledge-processing mechanisms.

items.abstract_text: Recently, the rapid growth of digital fake news has gained significant attention in both social media and artificial intelligence (AI) due to fake news can influence daily life deeply. This survey provides a review on AI-based fake news detection (FND), beginning by introducing the theoretical foundations like fake news definition, fake news ecosystem, related terms and fake news characteristics. Then, we introduce a taxonomy that separates AI-based FND methods into two categories which are model-centric models and process-centric frameworks. We then evaluate various model-centric models ranging from traditional models to machine learning, deep learning, and trending models. A significant portion of this work focuses on AI-based FND frameworks, which include dataset, data augmentation, information extraction, model validation and refinement, and results explanation and feedback. Finally, we discuss major challenges and trends to build more reliable information environments.

Improving model interpretability not only enhances user trust but also helps researchers identify biases and anomalies in data, facilitating model reinement and performance enhancement. One of the key advantages of LLMs over traditional methods is their ability to provide justiications for classiication decisions. LLMs can generate interpretable reasoning rules, allowing researchers to adjust these rules manually for beter adaptability and control. his transparency ensures that detection frameworks remain relevant and accurate in combating misinformation. Studies on ChatGPT's interpretability have demonstrated its capability to explain fake news classiications [52] , while argumentative LLMs use structured reasoning frameworks to enhance decision transparency. Systems like OE-Fact [134] , FOLK [144] , and FactAgent [82] provide real-time justiications for fact-checking, reducing opacity in decision-making. Moreover, frameworks such as MMIDR [148] , STEEL [75] , SNIFFER [113] , and EXMULF [6] extend explainability to multimodal misinformation, ensuring coherent analyses across text and images. Methods like HiSS [163] and MADR [65] enhance user trust by making each reasoning step traceable and veriiable. Feedback mechanisms play a crucial role in improving LLM-based fake news detection by continuously reining model predictions. hese mechanisms include human feedback alignment, agent-based feedback loops, and adversarial training. Fine-grained feedback, which provides sentence-level or paragraph-level corrections, enhances LLM performance by improving training signal density and eliminating irrelevant or inaccurate information. Automated feedback, such as ULTRAFEEDBACK [34] , addresses scalability issues by replacing human annotations with large-scale AI-generated critiques, reducing labeling costs while improving model alignment. Besides, ExFake [7] is composed of four modules working together to return the percentage of conidence of an input tweet and provide interpretable explanations to OSN users, it outperforms all the state-ofthe-art baselines of the FakeNewsNet benchmark on all the metrics in experiment. analysis.discussion: Fake news detection, as an emerging and evolving research direction, has gained wide atention across various application scenarios, particularly in an era characterized by widespread digital misinformation . With the rapid development of large language models, the research on AI-based fake news detection has made signiicant progress in recent years. A survey that synthesizes these advancements is both necessary and meaningful to guide future eforts in the ield. his survey introduces a novel taxonomy that categorizes existing methodologies into two distinct lines: FND Models (model-centric) and FND Frameworks (process-centric). We provide a holistic theoretical foundation by clarifying the fake news ecosystem-including its creators, dissemination paths, and distinctive characteristics-while tracing the historical trajectory of detection from early sociological analyses to advanced machine learning and deep learning architectures. We systematically compare diferent models and evaluate key procedural stages of the detection pipeline, such as datasets, data augmentation, information extraction, model reinement, model validation, and results explanation. Finally, we discuss the main challenges and trends. his survey aims to help researchers and practitioners gain a quick overview of state-of-the-art developments in AI-based FND and inspire future research towards building a more robust and trustworthy information ecosystem. Future research can focus on the creation of standardized performance benchmarks to allow for direct comparisons between various fake news detection models. hese evaluations should employ a consistent set of metrics like precision and the F1 score to build a clear baseline for performance. By testing models across multiple data sources, we can beter understand the generalizability of their techniques and identify which methods are efective for speciic types of data. It will provide the evidence needed to guide the development of future detection systems and improve the overall clarity of the research.

items.title: Exploring adaptive learning challenges and AI opportunities through educational professionals practices

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Despite its promise, adaptive learning faces significant technological, pedagogical, and infrastructural challenges that hinder its large-scale adoption. This study explores pedagogical obstacles from the perspectives of educators and instructional designers, focusing on their practices, perceptions, and specific needs. A mixed-methods approach combined a quantitative survey with qualitative data. Data were collected from 90 education professionals (teachers, instructional designers, and trainers) reached through LinkedIn and academic networks. Most participants (82.2%) identified situations requiring adaptation, yet only 55.6% had implemented adaptive measures. The qualitative analysis identified four main categories of adaptation practices. Participants expressed strong interest in AI-powered features to support instructional design tasks. The study proposes actionable recommendations to bridge the gap between technology and pedagogy, including the use of AI-assisted tools combined with human expertise, the development of adaptive interactive content and investment in professional development. This balanced approach aims to address critical barriers while maintaining educational quality and effectiveness, contributing to a better understanding of how AI can be integrated into adaptive learning systems to address current challenges.

A mixed-methods approach was adopted because our research questions are not identical in nature: three of them focus on observable and quantifiable facts (current practices, barriers, and expected characteristics), while one concerns perceptions and experiences (how professionals perceive and implement adaptation). A single method would not have allowed us to both quantify the extent of these practices and capture their diversity through concrete examples. The quantitative component was designed to assess the extent of the phenomena studied and identify trends. The qualitative component was introduced to capture, in the respondents' own words and based on their experiences, dimensions that a closed-ended list could not have anticipated. This qualitative aspect does not claim to be on an equal footing with the quantitative component: its role is to shed light on and contextualize the trends detected, not to replicate them. This method proved particularly relevant given that adaptation can involve multiple elements and varied approaches. The survey, based on the findings of the literature review, was designed to explore the main challenges and opportunities associated with adaptive learning. It consisted of 41 questions divided into several sections: • Demographics: Age, gender, country, city/region, primary role, years of experience, and area of expertise. • E-learning platform usage: Closed and open-ended questions on platforms used, usage frequency, and preferred features. • Perceptions of pedagogical methods: Likert scale questions on perceived effectiveness and open-ended queries about criteria for selecting teaching methods. • Challenges and needs in personalized learning: Open-ended questions on barriers to adoption and essential features of personalized learning solutions, including AI's role. • Consent and feedback: Participant willingness to evaluate and approve adaptive learning system recommendations. The questionnaire was pre-tested with a select group of education professionals to ensure clarity and relevance before wider distribution. analysis.discussion: The main objective of this research is to provide guidelines for the design of an adaptive learning system based on solid pedagogical practices, while addressing the current limits and challenges of adaptive learning and taking advantage of the potential of artificial intelligence in education. The results of this study highlight the importance and depth of the design phase in the pedagogical practices used by experts in the field, including needs analysis and the choice of effective teaching methods. The results also reveal an overall positive perception of adaptive learning, although its adoption remains moderate, due to several obstacles, including the lack of learner data and the time required to create personalized content. In the face of these difficulties, participants' interest in AI-assisted functions, while raising questions about privacy and the readiness of teachers, suggests promising perspectives for the future of adaptive learning. This study explored the pedagogical practices, perceptions, and challenges faced by education professionals regarding adaptive learning, as well as the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence (AI) to overcome barriers to its adoption. The findings, based on a survey of 90 professionals, reveal a generally positive perception of adaptive learning, which is recognized as a lever to enhance learner engagement and retention. However, its adoption remains limited due to major obstacles, including the lack of accurate learner data and the significant time required to create personalized content. In response to these challenges, participants expressed strong interest in AI-powered features that automate training plan structuring, resource generation, and real-time progress tracking, while also raising concerns about data privacy. From a theoretical perspective, this study contributes to the literature on adaptive learning and AI in education by providing empirical insight into the real-world obstacles faced by practitioners. In particular, it shows that the adoption of adaptive learning is hindered less by technological limitations than by practical and human challenges: the lack of reliable information about learners, the diversity of learning styles, and the time and resources required to design truly personalized content. Furthermore, it highlights a significant gap between the recognition of the importance of adaptation and its actual implementation, while revealing a strong interest in AI-tempered by genuine concerns regarding data privacy. Finally, the identification of four categories of adaptation strategies-content, pedagogical, technological, and evaluative and supportive adaptationprovides a framework for thinking about instructional design practices beyond the simple dichotomy between technological and human adaptation. From a practical standpoint, the findings of this study offer actionable insights for institutions, instructional designers, and policymakers seeking to promote the adoption of adaptive learning. They first highlight the need for sustained investment in teacher training, so that educators can integrate AI tools as allies in their practice, rather than as an additional burden. They also demonstrate the importance of designing adaptive learning systems as collaborative environments, where AI supports human pedagogical expertise without replacing it-an approach reflected in the concrete recommendations developed in this article: using AI to model learners and address data gaps, to structure content and reduce design time, to dynamically adapt resources to learner needs, and to implement human validation mechanisms that ensure teachers retain control over pedagogical decisions. Finally, the findings serve as a reminder that these systems must be designed from the outset to be ethical and privacy-respecting, rather than as an afterthe-fact fix. The value of this research lies in its focus on the perspectives of professionals whose voices are often sidelined. Yet it is precisely these professionals who are responsible for designing and implementing adaptive learning experiences in the field. By basing its conclusions on their actual practices, the obstacles they encounter, and the needs they express, this study helps bridge the gap between technological innovation and educational practice and, more importantly, enables professionals to participate in the design of future adaptive learning systems. However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the recruitment strategy, conducted via LinkedIn and academic networks, may have introduced a selection bias: participants who chose to respond are likely more familiar with digital tools and more open to innovation than the average teacher, which may lead to an overestimation of reported levels of AI adoption and readiness. Second, the relatively small and geographically concentrated sample (90 participants, primarily from Morocco and France) limits the ability to generalize these results to other institutional or cultural contexts. Third, the study relied on self-reported data collected via a single online questionnaire, which may introduce social desirability bias and does not allow for direct observation of practices. These findings open several avenues for future research. A key priority is to empirically test the collaborative human-AI approach outlined in the practical recommendations, through studies conducted in real educational settings. Extending this work to larger and more diverse samples would help test the generalizability of the adaptation categories and obstacles identified, while longitudinal studies would allow researchers to track how practices, perceptions, and adoption evolve as educators gain experience with AI tools. Finally, given the central role of professional development, future research should examine which training strategies most effectively enable teachers to integrate AI into their instructional design practices, ensuring that this integration remains pedagogically grounded, ethically sound, and sustainable over time.
analysis.limitations: While the study identified important trends and practical recommendations, several limitations should be noted: • Sample size and diversity: The sample of 90 participants is relatively small and lacks broad contextual diversity. • Selection bias: Online recruitment may lead to an overrepresentation of individuals who are comfortable with technology, thereby biasing perceptions of digital tools and artificial intelligence. This selection bias has significant implications for the interpretation of our findings. Specifically, the adoption rate shown in Fig. 2 (55.6% implementing adaptation measures) and the high levels of readiness and interest in AI features shown in Fig. 6 should be interpreted as likely being higher than what would be observed in the general sample of education professionals. It is assumed Future studies should expand recruitment methods and sample size for more representative and nuanced analyses of educational practices and perceptions. Artificial intelligence (AI) and associated technologies present promising opportunities to address adaptive learning challenges by automating certain pedagogical tasks [42] . Over 80% of participants expressed a keen interest in using AI for a variety of educational tasks, such as structuring training plans, generating resources, proposing activities and tracking learners in real time. This strong demand underlines the desire for tools capable of simplifying educational workflows. This high level of interest and readiness regarding AI features must, however, be qualified by the study's selection bias. Because the respondents self-selected into a study explicitly about technology-enhanced learning, they may represent an early-adopter subpopulation. Consequently, the enthusiasm for AI-assisted design and real-time monitoring reported here might not accurately reflect the general sentiment or readiness of the broader educational community, a factor that future research should address by using random sampling strategies. According to Acar [42] , generative AI can transform teaching by making it more efficient and accessible through the automation of certain pedagogical tasks. These tasks include generating resources such as lesson plans and customized case studies [43] , practice questions, resource recommendations and even automated creation of lesson plans and learning materials [43] , quizzes, simulations, personalized learning scenarios and educational games [40] , and monitoring online activity and analyzing digital traces [44] . AI has also revolutionized assessment processes, as demonstrated by the use of LLMs, which can provide precise, personalized feedback on complex work, similar to that of human experts [22] . This step forward helps to lighten teachers' workloads, while ensuring more detailed and faster assessment. In addition, the integration of the Internet of Things (IoT) with generative AI, as explored by Dong et al. [45] , enables even more personalized learning by collecting data on student interactions and adjusting feedback and assessments in real time. This combination enhances the engagement and flexibility of learning paths, while adapting to cultural diversity. However, these technological developments raise an important question: if AI takes over these automated tasks, what then will be the essential role of teachers or educational engineers in designing and creating courses? This is a crucial question as automation continues to advance in the educational field. While AI offers significant opportunities to improve teaching and learning, notably by automating certain tasks and providing personalized support, it also presents limitations that highlight the irreplaceable role of human educators. For example, Doughty et al. [46] show that although GPT-4 can considerably reduce the time and effort needed to create MCQs, it can make mistakes. These errors can include implausible or incorrect distractors or revealing the correct answer in the question statement. AI is often seen as a complement to teachers rather than a substitute for them. Chan and Tsi [47] point out that students appreciate the accessibility and instant assistance offered by AI, but that educators remain wary of over-reliance on technology, fearing the erosion of critical skills [48] . They insist on the need to balance the use of technology with human intervention to preserve deep learning experiences. This idea is reinforced by Pahi et al. [6] , which demonstrates that integrating human teaching assistants with generative AI like ChatGPT can enrich active, personalized learning. This hybrid model improves the quality of feedback while meeting the varied needs of students, by combining the technical clarity of AI with human empathy. Furthermore, the effectiveness of AI for initial learning does not necessarily guarantee long-term knowledge retention. Yang et al. [49] reveal that while language models are effective for initiating learning, knowledge retention is significantly better when AI is used to complement traditional learning methods, such as reading books. This hybrid approach promotes deeper, longer-lasting learning, emphasizing that AI needs to be thoughtfully integrated with traditional pedagogical practices. In summary, while AI can improve certain aspects of teaching, it does not replace human interaction and should be used as a complementary tool in a hybrid learning model.

items.abstract_text: This study employed a descriptive survey to investigate Yarmouk University students’ perceptions of AI as a tool for enhancing five specific EI skills. A self-administered questionnaire comprising 25 items was completed by a convenience sample of 384 students across five domains: AI’s role in stimulating motivation, developing social skills, developing self-awareness, developing empathy, and developing self-regulation. Both validity and reliability were established. Findings indicate that students perceived AI as moderately useful across all domains (overall M = 2.83, SD = 0.63). Statistically significant differences at α = 0.05 were found in all five domains based on gender, favoring males, though effect sizes were small (partial η² = 0.01-0.03). No statistically significant differences were found by college type. Although a significant multivariate effect emerged for academic level, none of the individual EI domains showed a statistically significant univariate difference. The results suggest that AI has emerged as a supplementary tool for developing aspects of EI among students, though its perceived effectiveness remains moderate. Implications for integrating AI into higher education to support emotional development.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how controllers in public healthcare envision human–AI collaboration in management control when dealing with uncertainty, complexity and equivocality, focusing on anticipated advantages and implementation challenges in an early-adoption setting. Design/methodology/approach We conducted an exploratory qualitative study with 14 controllers from Italian public healthcare organisations. Four closed-ended questions provided a preliminary picture of current AI adoption, while three scenario-based open-ended questions elicited prospective assessments. The framework method was used to analyse the data. Findings AI adoption remains limited and uneven, and is rarely embedded in everyday management control. Under uncertainty, controllers link AI to better forecasting and faster access to information, but worry about data quality, privacy and overreliance. In complex settings, they expect AI to help integrate diverse information and enable more systemic control, provided processes are standardised and human oversight remains. In equivocal situations, AI may support interpretation and communication, but its impact is limited by limited hands-on experience and the difficulty of codifying contextual nuances. Originality/value Based on the Jarrahi (2018) decision-making scenarios, the study develops a tentative conceptualisation of how public healthcare controllers envisage AI collaboration. The concerns of the participants inform three proposed arrangements: validation, recursive integration and contestable sensemaking. Their formulation and the accountability-augmentation principle are theoretical elaborations informed by prospective evidence and accountability research.

items.abstract_text: Purpose The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into Italian public administration raises a central question: can person-centred human resource management practices turn technology from a source of psychosocial strain into an enabler of continuous improvement? This paper explores how formalized and participatory governance of AI adoption, structured around three Kaizen principles, is associated with employee participation in digital change and with the technostress reported by public employees. Design/methodology/approach A theory-informed qualitative multiple-case study was conducted in five organizational cases, namely Italian public administrations engaged in digital transformation projects funded by the Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza (PNRR). In each organization, a manager–officer dyad (10 participants in total) took part in narrative interviews held between October and November 2025, focused on lived experiences of AI adoption, perceptions of human resource management and professional engagement. Transcripts were analysed through deductive, theory-driven content analysis based on the three Kaizen principles (process orientation, step-by-step improvement and human capital orientation) and on the technostress dimensions, followed by within-case and cross-case comparison. Findings Across 10 participant accounts embedded within five organizational cases, practices consistent with Kaizen were associated, within the accounts, with distinct narrative profiles of technostress and engagement. Accounts reporting all three principles described active co-authorship, professional empowerment and emerging roles; accounts reporting none described persistent techno-anxiety, disengagement and eroding professional identity. Among the creators, techno-insecurity is the one most closely tied to how adoption is governed, and is typically accompanied by techno-anxiety as an affective strain response, while overload, invasion, complexity and uncertainty appear in association with specific operating conditions. Intermediate accounts varied with the missing principle and its hierarchical level. Originality/value This paper develops the joint Kaizen–STS framework as an original analytical lens for AI governance in public administration. It provides qualitative evidence that Kaizen-consistent HR governance is associated with less salient technostress, particularly in the governance-related dimensions emerging from the analysis, and with stronger reported participation, professional agency and more favourable organizational conditions for continuous improvement. items.abstract_text: This research aimed to assess awareness of generative AI limitations, highlight its advantages, and identify potential threats from misuse, focusing on differences in opinions between future educators and students from non-education fields. The data were collected through surveying 931 undergraduate students of a private university in the Philippines. The researchers used a comparative-correlational research design with a qualitative strand. The study found moderate awareness of generative AI’s limitations (M = 3.31, SD = 0.94) and a moderate-to-cautious attitude toward its implementation (M = 3.15, SD = 0.87). Education students showed higher awareness than students from other majors (d = 0.40), while differences in usage, perception, and fear of skills deteriorating were negligible (d = 0.14–0.25) and, to some extent, neutralized in robustness checks. Differences between genders and years of study in perceptions were minor. The findings suggest that future teachers’ curricula should include a course on AI literacy and emphasize developing critical thinking skills to prepare students for implementing generative AI solutions in teaching practices.

items.abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a promising technology for supporting mathematical dialogue, feedback, and reasoning in mathematics education. However, research has paid limited attention to how university students’ geometric thinking develops through sustained interaction with GenAI, particularly in geometry transformation learning. This study aims to develop a Dialogic Geometric Thinking Framework that characterizes the dimensions and progression of university students’ geometric thinking during sustained dialogue with ChatGPT. A qualitative exploratory design was employed involving undergraduate mathematics education students enrolled in a Geometry Transformation course at an Indonesian public university. Data were collected from student–ChatGPT dialogue transcripts, students’ written solutions, and reflective interviews. The data were analyzed thematically using reflexive thematic analysis to identify recurring characteristics and relationships among dimensions of geometric thinking and to synthesize them into an integrated framework. The findings identified five interrelated dimensions of geometric thinking: conceptual reasoning, representational coordination, procedural justification, reflective regulation, and mathematical elaboration. These dimensions illustrate how students progressively articulate mathematical concepts, coordinate representations, justify solution procedures, evaluate their reasoning, and extend mathematical ideas during AI-mediated dialogue. The study resulted in a Dialogic Geometric Thinking Framework that provides a process-oriented perspective on the development of university students’ geometric thinking during interaction with GenAI. The framework offers an initial theoretical foundation for understanding and further investigating geometric thinking in AI-mediated mathematics learning. Keywords: geometric thinking, generative artificial intelligence, chatGPT, geometry transformation, mathematical dialogue.

While all 15 participants engaged in the learning activities and contributed to the complete dataset used to establish thematic saturation, 5 participants (P03, P05, P08, P11, and P14) were selected as representative exemplars in the findings to illustrate each of the five emerging framework dimensions vividly. Data were collected from three complementary sources: student-ChatGPT dialogue transcripts, students' written mathematical solutions, and reflective semistructured interviews. The primary data consisted of transcripts of students' interactions with ChatGPT while solving geometry transformation problems. Students were instructed to engage with ChatGPT as a conversational learning partner and were encouraged to ask questions, request explanations, verify solution procedures, justify mathematical arguments, and explore alternative solution strategies. The dialogue was conducted using ChatGPT and recorded in textual form for subsequent analysis. The second data source consisted of students' written solutions to geometry transformation tasks. These solutions were collected to examine how students expressed mathematical concepts, represented geometric objects, applied transformation procedures, and justified their solutions independently of the conversational interaction. The third data source consisted of reflective semi-structured interviews conducted after the learning activities. The interviews were used to clarify students' reasoning processes and their experiences during interaction with ChatGPT. The interview questions focused on students' decisions, interpretations of ChatGPT responses, evaluation of mathematical explanations, and reflections on changes in their understanding during the dialogue. The interview protocol was developed based on the principles for constructing qualitative semi-structured interview guides proposed by Kallio et al. (2016) . items.abstract_text: With the growing adoption of generative AI (GenAI) in higher education, concerns have emerged about excessive AI dependence and the inappropriate use of AI-generated content. However, few studies have examined the relationships among AI dependency (AID), cognitive offloading (CO), and AI-giarism (AIG). This study examined the direct and indirect associations among these constructs among 191 preservice physics teachers (PSPTs) from universities in Sulawesi, Indonesia, using a quantitative cross-sectional design and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results showed that AID was positively associated with CO (β = 0.664, p < 0.001) and AIG (β = 0.603, p < 0.001), while CO was positively associated with AIG (β = 0.242, p = 0.003). CO also showed a statistically significant indirect association between AID and AIG (β = 0.160, p = 0.003). The model accounted for 44.0% of the variance in CO and 61.6% of the variance in AIG. These findings indicate that AID is associated with self-reported AIG both directly and indirectly through CO within the specified model. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish causal relationships, and the self-reported outcome does not confirm actual incidents of academic misconduct. These findings highlight the importance of teacher education approaches that promote responsible AI use, independent reasoning, critical evaluation of AI-generated information, and transparent disclosure of AI assistance.

Among the AI-Giarism items, AIG6 recorded the largest mean (M = 3.717), while AIG1 had the lowest (M = 3.288). The standard deviations ranged from 0.888 to 1.200, indicating variability in participants' responses. The relatively high mean scores for some AIG items indicate varying levels of agreement with statements describing undisclosed AI use in academic work. However, these scores should not be interpreted as estimates of the prevalence or frequency of actual academic misconduct because they reflect participants' self-reported agreement with the statements rather than independently verified incidents. Furthermore, the interpretation of undisclosed AI use depends partly on institutional and course-specific policies governing AI assistance and disclosure. The measurement model showed satisfactory evidence of reliability and convergent validity. Cronbach's alpha ranged from 0.729-0.876, rho_A ranged from 0.735-0.880, and CR (rho_C) values ranged from 0.828 to 0.902, indicating acceptable internal consistency. The AVE values were 0.536 for AID, 0.509 for AIG, and 0.547 for CO; all values surpassed the recommended threshold of 0.50. The outer loadings ranged from 0.591 to 0.838. Although loading values for several indicators fell below the conventional threshold of 0.70, their retention should be considered alongside the overall reliability and convergent validity results, as well as their theoretical relevance to the respective constructs. Overall, the results provide evidence of internal consistency, reliability, and convergent validity for the measurement model. Table 3 presents the results of the heterotrait-monotrait ratio (HTMT) analysis for assessing discriminant validity. The HTMT values were 0.796 for AID-CO, 0.808 for AIG-CO, and 0.891 for AID-AIG. Although all point estimates were below the commonly used threshold of 0.90, the bootstrap interval results warrant a more cautious interpretation. For AID-CO, the interval ranged from 0.705 to 0.881, remaining below 0.90. For AIG-CO, the interval ranged from 0.702 to 0.911, with its upper bound slightly exceeding 0.90. The AID-AIG pair showed the greatest concern, with an HTMT value of 0.891 and an interval ranging from 0.819 to 0.959. Because the upper bounds for AIG-CO and AID-AIG exceeded 0.90, the results do not provide unequivocal evidence of discriminant validity for these pairs under the selected criterion. Thus, although AID and AIG are conceptually distinct, their empirical distinctiveness should be interpreted cautiously. Conceptually, AID refers to individuals' reliance on AI tools, whereas AIG concerns the use of AI-generated content without appropriate acknowledgment or disclosure in academic work. Although these constructs represent conceptually distinct aspects of AI use, their relatively high HTMT value suggests substantial empirical overlap. Therefore, the HTMT findings provide stronger support for the distinctiveness of AID and CO than for AID and AIG.
analysis.discussion: The findings reveal significant associations among AID, CO, and AIG among PSPTs. All hypothesized direct relationships were positive and statistically significant, and CO showed a significant indirect association between AID and AIG. These findings suggest that greater AID is associated not only with greater reported CO but also with higher reported AIG. The significant indirect effect further indicates that CO accounts for part of the statistical association between AID and AIG within the proposed model. Nevertheless, the findings should be interpreted in light of the study's cross-sectional design, which does not establish temporal or causal relationships among the constructs. Among the relationships specified in the structural model, the path from AID to CO showed the largest effect. This result is consistent with the central premise of cognitive offloading theory, which conceptualizes offloading as the use of external resources to reduce the cognitive demands associated with a task. Risko & Gilbert (2016) argue that people tend to offload cognitive work when external resources can make a task easier or reduce the effort required to complete it. In the context of GenAI, this process takes a different form because AI is not merely storing or retrieving information; it can generate explanations, solve problems, formulate ideas, and produce complete academic responses. These findings extend this perspective to PSPTs. Several AID items in this study capture behaviors such as seeking AI answers before attempting to solve a problem independently and relying on AI when facing academic difficulties. These behaviors closely correspond to the process of transferring cognitive effort from the learner to an external system. The relatively large effect size of AID on CO (f 2 = 0.787) therefore suggests that dependence should not be viewed merely as a preference for technological use. This association suggests that PSPTs who report greater dependence on AI also tend to report greater reliance on external support for cognitive tasks. However, the findings reflect respondents' self-reported tendencies rather than directly observed changes in problem-solving behavior. This interpretation is further supported by recent research on AI-based cognitive offloading in higher education. A large study involving 667 university students found that perceived AI value was associated with AI-based cognitive offloading, though the relationship depended partly on students' ability to evaluate AI outputs (Jiang & Chen, 2026) . This finding is relevant because it indicates that AI offloading is not inherently harmful; its consequences depend on how students use and evaluate the technology. Similarly, a recent systematic review synthesizing 67 empirical studies reported that ChatGPT may promote critical and creative thinking when it is integrated into inquiry-oriented, scaffolded learning activities, whereas unstructured use may be associated with cognitive offloading and lead to lower levels of cognitive engagement (C. Li et al., 2026) . AID also showed a substantial positive relationship with AIG. This finding suggests that students with greater reliance on AI may be more inclined to use AI in ways that involve submitting, paraphrasing, copying, or substantially rewriting AI-generated content without disclosure. Importantly, the result should not be interpreted to mean that AI use itself constitutes academic misconduct. Rather, the finding points to a distinction between using AI as an aid to learning and becoming dependent on it to produce academic work. Accordingly, AID should be understood as a construct distinct from inappropriate AI use. The observed association does not establish that students with greater AID necessarily engage in undisclosed or academically inappropriate use of AI-generated content. This distinction is particularly relevant because AIG is still an emerging concept in academic integrity research. Previous work shows that students do not necessarily perceive all forms of AI-assisted academic work in the same way (Chan, 2025) . Directly submitting AIgenerated content tends to be viewed more negatively, whereas less explicit forms of AI assistance, such as generating ideas or refining one's own work, are perceived more ambiguously. This ambiguity may complicate students' decisions about when AI use necessitates disclosure and where the boundary lies between acceptable assistance and inappropriate substitution of academic work. The present finding is also consistent with evidence that students' disclosure of AI use remains problematic even when institutions have explicit requirements. A previous study reported that 74% of students at one university failed to declare their AI use despite a formal requirement to do so (Gonsalves, 2025) . Ambiguity in existing guidelines, concerns about potential academic consequences, inconsistent rule enforcement, and peer influence emerged as important factors associated with non-compliance. Thus, AIG should not be viewed solely as an individual ethical failure. Institutional expectations, students' understanding of acceptable AI use, and the transparency of AI policies may also shape how students use and disclose AIgenerated content. CO was also positively associated with AIG, although its effect was smaller than that of AID. This finding is theoretically significant because it suggests that the way students allocate cognitive effort may relate to how they subsequently use AI-generated outputs in academic work. The items used to measure CO indicate reduced effort in independently finding solutions, reduced analysis of AI-generated solution steps, reduced use of conventional problem-solving approaches, and lower motivation to develop creative solutions. When these tendencies become established, students may become less inclined to critically inspect, reconstruct, or verify AIgenerated content before incorporating it into their coursework. One possible interpretation is that CO may also involve reduced independent scrutiny of AI-generated outputs, particularly when students rely on AI-provided solutions without evaluating them. However, this interpretation remains tentative because the study measured self-reported CO rather than directly observed verification behavior. This interpretation aligns with existing literature on cognitive offloading. Offloading can be an efficient strategy when the goal is to reduce unnecessary cognitive demands, but it can become problematic when external support replaces rather than complements internal cognitive activity (Chirayath et al., 2025) . Recent experimental evidence provides a useful illustration: lower levels of delayed knowledge retention were observed among university students who used ChatGPT for studying compared with those who learned without ChatGPT (Barcaui, 2025) , suggesting that reducing cognitive effort during learning may have consequences for longer-term learning. However, this evidence should not be interpreted as proof that AI assistance always reduces learning. AI's effects may differ depending on whether students use it as a cognitive scaffold or as a substitute for their own thinking. The smaller effect size of CO on AIG (f 2 = 0.085) is also informative. It suggests that reduced cognitive engagement alone may not be sufficient to explain AIG. analysis.limitations: The interpretation of these findings should consider several limitations. First, the crosssectional nature of the study prevents causal relationships from being firmly established. Although the structural model is theoretically consistent with a pathway from AID to CO and subsequently to AIG, longitudinal or experimental research is needed to determine whether increasing AID actually produces changes in CO and AIG over time. Second, because all variables were measured using self-report instruments, the reported results may have been affected by recall bias, socially desirable responding, and variation in students' interpretations of AI-related academic behaviors. The use of a common measurement method may have contributed to the observed associations among the constructs. In addition, potential conceptual overlap among AID, CO, and AIG warrants further examination to more robustly establish their distinctiveness. However, the present study does not establish that common-method variance or conceptual overlap inflated the estimated relationships. Future research could address these concerns by combining questionnaires with behavioral data, AI use logs, academic task performance, or qualitative interviews, and by further examining the discriminant validity of the constructs. Third, the participants were PSPTs from universities in Sulawesi, which provides a meaningful disciplinary and regional context but limits the applicability of the findings to other student groups. Replicating this study across diverse disciplinary, regional, and educational settings would help establish whether the identified relationships are context-specific or generalizable to university students more broadly. Furthermore, the observed relationships may be influenced by factors not accounted for in the present model, such as students' academic year, frequency of AI use, digital or AI literacy, academic pressure, and institutional AI policies. Because these factors were not examined as potential confounding variables, their possible influence on the estimated relationships remains uncertain. Future studies could measure and account for relevant variables to assess the robustness of these relationships. Finally, future research could investigate additional mechanisms, including academic self-efficacy, metacognitive awareness, and ethical judgment, to better understand the factors associated with students' reliance on AI, CO, and AI-related academic practices. Such research may help explain why some students use AI as a cognitive scaffold while others rely more heavily on it when completing academic tasks.

items.abstract_text: Purpose: This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) driven talent management practices and the performance of agri based enterprises in the Central Region of Cameroon, focusing on the mediating roles of workforce productivity and employee resilience. Research Methodology: A quantitative cross sectional survey design was employed, targeting 250 managers and human resource professionals. Data were collected with a structured questionnaire and analyzed with SPSS and AMOS through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and mediation analysis with 5.000 bootstrap resamples. Results: AI driven talent management was positively and significantly related to enterprise performance (r=0.523, p<0.01). Workforce productivity (β=0.18) and employee resilience (β=0.14) significantly mediated this relationship. Both the total indirect effect (β=0.32, p<0.01) and the direct effect (β=0.29, p<0.01) were significant, indicating partial mediation, with about 52 percent of the total effect transmitted through the two mediators. Conclusions: AI driven talent management enhances the performance of agri based enterprises both directly and indirectly through improved workforce productivity and stronger employee resilience. Enterprises should integrate AI strategically into talent management and support employees through change management. Limitations: The cross sectional design, self reported data, purposive sampling, and focus on a single region limit causal inference and generalizability. Contributions: The study provides empirical evidence from an underresearched African agricultural context and clarifies the mechanisms through which AI driven talent management translates into enterprise performance.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) companions are increasingly used by post-secondary students for emotional support, stress management, and self-management, yet their potential implications for primary care in this population remain unclear. Students may engage with AI companions before encountering purpose-built therapeutic chatbots, which are more often accessed through intentional health-seeking or professional guidance. This distinction may position AI companions as an earlier influence on self-management and subsequent help-seeking. Objective: To examine how artificial intelligence (AI) companions may influence stress regulation, sleep quality, symptom interpretation, and healthcare-seeking behaviour among post-secondary students, and to identify the principal benefits, risks, and unresolved questions relevant to primary care. Methods: A conceptual narrative review was undertaken using literature identified through Harvard University’s Hollis Library and Google Scholar. Evidence related to AI companions, academic stress, sleep quality, emotional support, healthcare-seeking behaviour, primary care, and digital mental health was synthesized using Stress & Coping Theory and the stress-buffering hypothesis as theoretical foundations. Results: AI companions may support stress appraisal, cognitive reframing, emotional reflection, symptom articulation, and self-management before clinical encounters. However, they may also contribute to emotional overreliance, misinformation, reassurance seeking, sleep disruption, and altered help-seeking behaviour. This review proposes conceptual mechanisms linking AI companion engagement with stress regulation, sleep, and pathways into primary care while identifying relational intensity as a clinically meaningful dimension of engagement beyond frequency alone. Conclusion: AI companions should be understood as adjunctive rather than substitutive support. Their clinical relevance is based on how they can shape patients’ experiences before obtaining primary care. Longitudinal research is needed to determine how patterns of engagement influence stress, sleep, and healthcare utilization over time.

items.title: AI-driven approaches for food risk assessment: current advances and future trends

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a tool to support food risk assessment and broader food safety activities in response to the growing complexity of global food supply chains, emerging foodborne hazards, and evolving food fraud practices. Unlike previous reviews that have largely focused on individual AI technologies or specific applications, this review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), transformer-based models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), multimodal learning, and emerging AI paradigms within a unified framework relevant to food risk assessment and food safety decision-making. The review examines their applications in hazard identification, contamination detection, predictive microbiology, risk classification, food fraud detection, surveillance, traceability, and decision-support systems. Particular attention is given to the strengths, limitations, interpretability, validation requirements, and implementation challenges associated with different AI approaches. The integration of AI with multimodal data sources, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, spectroscopy, biosensors, and advanced analytical platforms is also discussed as a means to improve risk prediction, monitoring, and early-warning capabilities. Key challenges include data quality and availability, model generalizability, limited external validation, computational requirements, interpretability, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging developments, including foundation models, federated learning, blockchain, digital twins, edge AI, and multimodal frameworks, are highlighted as promising directions for future research. Overall, this review provides a critical comparative framework for understanding the evolving role of AI in food risk assessment and related food safety applications, while identifying key scientific, technical, and regulatory priorities for future development and implementation. " Reference lists of key review articles and highly cited publications were also manually examined to identify additional relevant studies that may not have been captured during the database search. The study-selection process followed a structured screening procedure (Fig. 1 ). The initial search yielded 1,212 records across all databases. After removal of 312 duplicate records, 900 unique publications remained for title and abstract screening. During this stage, 641 records were excluded because they were unrelated to food safety, focused exclusively on agricultural production, lacked direct relevance to food risk assessment, lacked an AI component, or were editorials, conference abstracts, commentaries, or non-scientific publications. Consequently, 259 articles were selected for full-text assessment. Following detailed evaluation against predefined eligibility criteria, 173 studies were excluded because they lacked sufficient methodological information, did not report food-safety-related applications, focused solely on algorithm development without practical relevance, or provided insufficient validation data. Ultimately, 86 publications were included in the final review and qualitative synthesis. Studies were considered eligible if they were peerreviewed journal articles, conference proceedings, authoritative scientific reports, or review papers that described the application of AI technologies to food safety, food risk assessment, contamination detection, predictive microbiology, food fraud detection, traceability, outbreak surveillance, or decision-support systems. Publications were excluded when they focused exclusively on crop production, precision agriculture, or livestock management without a direct connection to food safety or risk assessment. Duplicate publications and studies lacking sufficient methodological details were also excluded. The selected studies were subsequently categorized into major thematic areas, including machine learning, deep learning, transformer-based architectures, explainable artificial intelligence, multimodal learning, predictive microbiology, contamination detection, food fraud and authenticity assessment, intelligent surveillance systems, and AI-enabled decision-support frameworks. For each study, information regarding the AI methodology, dataset characteristics, application domain, validation strategy, performance metrics, strengths, limitations, and practical implications was extracted and critically evaluated. Rather than providing a purely descriptive summary, this review emphasizes the comparative assessment of AI methodologies, highlighting their respective advantages, limitations, validation challenges, interpretability considerations, and practical applicability within food safety systems. Particular attention was given to emerging technologies, including transformer architectures, foundation models, multimodal AI, and explainable AI, as well as their integration with complementary technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), spectroscopy, blockchain, and intelligent sensing platforms. This structured methodology facilitated the development of a comprehensive framework illustrating how contemporary AI technologies can collectively support hazard identification, risk characterization, surveillance, regulatory decision-making, and proactive food safety management across increasingly complex global food systems. Explainable artificial intelligence approaches can generally be grouped into two types based on the way interpretability is achieved: intrinsic (interpretable) models and post hoc explanation methods. These approaches differ fundamentally in the trade-off between predictive performance and model transparency, and the choice between them depends on the complexity of the prediction task, regulatory requirements, and the level of explanation required by end users. Post hoc explainability approaches are developed to explain the predictions of sophisticated machine learning models after model training. Instead of altering the underlying predictive algorithm, these strategies provide explanations that help users understand how model predictions were derived while preserving the high predictive accuracy of sophisticated ensemble learning, deep learning, and transformer architectures. Thus, the post hoc methodologies have become the primary approach for explainability in modern AI-driven food risk assessment (Nagamalla et al., 2022) . SHAP is one of the most popular post hoc interpretability approaches, providing both global and local explanations by quantifying the contribution of individual predictors to model outputs. Also, LIME build simple surrogate models that explain individual predictions and are especially valuable for case-specific explanations. Feature relevance analysis ranks variables according to their value for prediction outcomes, which helps uncover critical contamination markers and risk factors. Visualizing attention in transformer architectures can identify the most important sections in text, genomic, and hyperspectral data, giving further insight into model behaviour (Arrighi et al., 2025) . But these approaches mostly uncover statistical correlations learned by the model, not causal linkages. Therefore, although they enhance transparency and enable interpretation, they should be used as additional tools to derive insights from the model and to inform decision-making, rather than as conclusive proof for regulatory validation or causal inference. Post hoc approaches are common, but they have some key limitations. Generated explanations are approximations of the underlying model and are not direct representations of its internal reasoning; hence, they may not always reflect the genuine decision-making process. This review critically examined the complementary roles of machine learning, deep learning, transformer-based models, and explainable artificial intelligence, highlighting their strengths, limitations, validation requirements, and practical applications within a unified food risk assessment framework. Although these technologies have demonstrated substantial potential for improving the accuracy, efficiency, and scalability of food safety systems, their widespread implementation remains constrained by challenges in data quality, external validation, interpretability, computational demands, and regulatory acceptance. Future progress will require standardized datasets, robust validation frameworks, trustworthy and explainable AI approaches, harmonized regulatory guidelines, and interdisciplinary collaboration among researchers, industry stakeholders, and regulatory agencies. analysis.limitations: Despite its considerable potential, the adoption of AI in food risk assessment remains constrained by several technical, regulatory, and operational challenges. Although applications such as contamination prediction, predictive microbiology, computer vision-assisted inspection, and intelligent surveillance have shown promising results, many advanced AI technologies remain at relatively early stages of validation and industrial implementation. A major limitation is the availability of high-quality, standardized datasets. Food safety data are often fragmented, heterogeneous, imbalanced, and region-specific, which can reduce model robustness, reproducibility, and transferability across food products, geographical regions, and regulatory environments. Another important challenge is the limited interpretability of advanced deep learning and transformer-based models. While XAI techniques improve transparency, current approaches primarily identify statistical associations rather than causal relationships. Consequently, explainability should complement, rather than replace, rigorous validation and expert assessment. Furthermore, many published studies rely on internal datasets and validation methods such as hold-out testing or k-fold cross-validation, which may overestimate real-world performance. Broader adoption requires independent external validation across diverse food matrices, production environments, and geographical regions to ensure model robustness and generalizability. Practical deployment presents additional barriers. Successful implementation requires reliable sensor networks, digital infrastructure, computational resources, technical expertise, and continuous model maintenance. Similar challenges have been reported in intelligent food processing systems and AI-assisted drying technologies, where sensor reliability, data quality, model transferability, and industrial scalability remain significant obstacles (Arora et al., 2024; Barthwal et al., 2024; Przybył & Koszela, 2023; Sapienza & Vedder, 2023) . In addition, integrating data from multiple sources, including laboratory analyses, environmental sensors, traceability platforms, and surveillance systems, remains challenging because of differences in data formats, metadata standards, and interoperability requirements. Regulatory and governance issues further complicate implementation. The lack of harmonized validation standards, performance reporting guidelines, and regulatory frameworks for AI-assisted decision-making limits confidence among regulators and industry stakeholders alike. Concerns related to data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, transparency, and accountability must also be addressed before AI can be widely adopted in food safety systems. Collectively, these challenges highlight the need for multidisciplinary collaboration to develop AI systems that are robust, transparent, trustworthy, and suitable for regulatory and industrial use.
