publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: This study examines the relationship between prompt engineering literacy and academic learning outcomes among tertiary-level students in Bangladesh, with particular attention to the ethical dimensions of artificial intelligence (AI) integration in higher education. Using a concurrent mixed methods design, data were collected from students across public, private, and National University-affiliated institutions through online forms, telephone surveys, and messaging-platform surveys, complemented by key informant interviews with students and educators. The findings show that students with stronger prompt engineering knowledge achieved substantially larger gains on a post-intervention knowledge assessment, and that this knowledge, together with the frequency and perceived usefulness of AI engagement, was the strongest independent predictor of learning outcomes, ahead of institutional type. Ethical concerns, most notably academic dishonesty, algorithmic bias, and overreliance on automation, were widely recognized by students, yet formal institutional guidance on ethical AI use remained rare and was almost entirely absent among National University-affiliated colleges. These results carry direct implications for policy and practice. They suggest that prompt engineering merits treatment as a foundational academic literacy rather than a technical add-on, that AI ethics training needs to reach under-resourced institutions as a matter of priority, and that closing the gap between how quickly students adopt AI and how slowly institutions govern it is now an urgent task for Bangladeshi higher education.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Graph neural network (GNN) detectors of AI-generated text report state-of-the-art accuracy, and the architectural claim that graph topology captures signals invisible to sequential classifiers is now common in the literature. We report the complete lifecycle of one such detector, from construction to falsification. AEGIS, a graph attention network over k-nearest-neighbour text graphs with multi-signal edge weights, reaches 98.50% accuracy on scientific abstracts with only 73K trainable parameters, outperforming five established baselines. We then subject our own system to the evaluation its headline number deserves: generation-time length control, format normalization, leakage-free splits, a tuned frozen-embedding probe as the calibrated null, and a 10 × 10 cross-generator transfer study over three seeds. Under this protocol the graph's apparent contribution collapses from +0.240 AUROC over a surface baseline to −0.0004 AUROC against the tuned probe, inside the measured replication noise floor, and the two detectors' transfer geographies are near-identical (ρ = 0.986). A single untuned regularization default manufactured a +0.027 phantom advantage. The structural differences the graph encodes are real, but they are a re-encoding of information already present in the embeddings. We distil the audit into a practical checklist for evaluating architectural claims in text detection, and argue that accuracy numbers and mechanism claims must be validated separately.

reading.limitations: Our corpus is English scientiﬁc abstracts; other domains, languages and text lengths may distribute the signal diﬀerently. The audit evaluates one graph architecture family (GAT over k-NN-plus-dependency graphs); graphs built from information gen- uinely external to the embeddings—citation networks, factual knowledge bases as in IDEATE—could in principle escape the redundancy argument, and deserve the same test rather than the same verdict. Our probe null is built on one embedding family; the direction of our conclusion is robust to this choice in our experiments, but magnitudes are instrument-relative. Finally, all evaluations are in-distribution with respect to the human corpus; adversarial and out-of-domain robustness are separate questions.

items.title: Multidimensional AI Literacy and Students’ Acceptance of AI-Enabled Learning Technologies: A Higher-Order Extension of the Technology Acceptance Model

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract AI-enabled learning technologies are becoming routine in higher education. However, acceptance research tends to explain adoption through beliefs about technology while paying less attention to the capabilities that learners bring to AI interaction. Although AI literacy has recently been linked to acceptance, it is often modeled as a global score or as separate dimensions, leaving unresolved whether related competencies operate collectively within the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) mechanism. This study tests a higher-order extension of the TAM using survey data from 528 students across three Indonesian universities who had prior experience with AI for learning. AI literacy was specified through awareness, usage skills, critical understanding, and ethics awareness and estimated using a disjoint two-stage partial least squares structural equation modeling procedure. The results support a coherent higher-order representation and show that AI literacy is most strongly associated with perceived ease of use and is also positively related to perceived usefulness and attitude. Within TAM, attitude shows a stronger direct relationship with behavioral intention than usefulness. These findings position AI literacy as a learner capability layer that complements technology beliefs in explaining students’ evaluations of AI-enabled learning technologies. The study contributes a measurement-to-mechanism perspective that maintains practical, critical, and ethical competence in acceptance research and suggests that implementation should consider learner capability alongside access and usability. Because the evidence is cross-sectional, self-reported, and multi-tool, the relationships should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

reading.methods: A cross-sectional, multi-institutional survey was conducted to examine students' acceptance of AIenabled technologies used for learning. The sample was criterion-based: respondents had to be active university students and had previously used at least one AI-enabled application in learning activities, so they evaluated technologies with which they had direct experience rather than hypothetical descriptions. Therefore, this study concerns a class of AI-enabled learning technologies rather than a single platform or an integrated digital learning system. Participation was voluntary and anonymous. The survey introduction explained the study purpose, use of aggregated data for academic research, the right to stop at any time without consequence, and that continuing the questionnaire would indicate consent. reading.findings: Descriptive statistics indicated generally favorable self-reports of AI-related capabilities and technology beliefs. AI ethics awareness had the highest mean among the four literacy dimensions (M = 4.01, SD = 0.70), followed by AI critical understanding (M = 3.84, SD = 0.65), AI awareness (M = 3.81, SD = 0.64), and AI usage skills (M = 3.72, SD = 0.71). A descriptive composite of the four dimensions had a mean of 3.84 (SD = 0.59); this arithmetic summary should not be confused with the standardized latent variable scores used to estimate the Stage 2 higher-order construct. Table 2 presents the full descriptive statistics.
reading.interpretation: Students' acceptance of AI-enabled learning technologies was associated not only with perceived ease, usefulness, and attitude but also with the multidimensional capabilities they reported bringing to their interaction with AI. In this three-university sample, awareness, usage skills, critical understanding, and ethics awareness formed a strong, reflective, higher-order AI literacy representation. This shared capability was most strongly associated with perceived ease of use and was also associated with perceived usefulness and attitude; within TAM, attitude retained the largest direct association with behavioral intention. Therefore, this study supports examining learner capability alongside technology beliefs when studying AI adoption in digital learning. It does not establish that increasing AI literacy causes acceptance or responsible use. For research and practice, the more defensible implication is to evaluate whether learners can understand, operate, question, and use AI appropriately as institutions implement AI-enabled learning technology. Longitudinal, experimental, tool-specific, and performancebased studies are needed to test the order and generalizability of these relationships.

items.title: Bridging textile design and AI: An innovative methodological approach for the Ghanaian Textile Designer

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose: The study aimed to investigate the feasibility of employing selected artificial intelligence (AI) software to generate contemporary textile designs. Focusing on bridging textile design and AI, with a methodological approach for the Ghanaian Textile Designer. With AI emerging as a transformative force in multiple industries, including textiles, the research sought to assess its capacity to enhance design processes and meet consumer preferences. Methodology/Design: Three AI software programs, including Playground, Leonardo, and Lexcia, were selected for the study. Each was provided with identical prompts to generate contemporary textile designs. The outputs were then systematically analysed to identify similarities, differences, and overall design quality. Findings: The results showed that while the software received identical prompts, the generated designs displayed notable variations, alongside some shared visual features. The AI-driven process proved significantly faster and more efficient than traditional methods and yielded designs consistent with consumer specifications. Practical and Social Implications: The findings suggest that AI tools can substantially improve productivity, creativity, and responsiveness in textile design. Introducing AI-based design tools to textile designers in Ghana could enhance competitiveness, foster innovation, and better align production with evolving market demands. Originality: This study offers an early exploration of the comparative application of multiple AI software tools for contemporary textile design, contributing novel insights into their feasibility, efficiency, and adaptability within the Ghanaian textile industry context.

The findings of this study demonstrate the feasibility and variability of AI-generated textile designs and carry significant implications for the textile industry and creative practice. The ability of AI to facilitate a faster, more efficient process and produce designs aligned with consumer specifications implies a shift towards more responsive and demand-driven manufacturing. This can lead to reduced time-to-market for new products and lower costs associated with the initial design phase. Additionally, the variation in outputs from different AI software, even with identical prompts, underscores that these tools are not autonomous replacements for designers. Instead, they function as powerful "co-creators" or "design assistants." The designer's role evolves from executing every detail to curating, refining, and imbuing the AI-generated options with artistic intent and cultural meaning. Finally, the observed variations in output suggest that each AI software has its own inherent "style" or algorithmic bias. This implies that designers can strategically select different AI tools to access a wider range of aesthetic possibilities and creative directions that may not have been initially conceived, thereby expanding the visual lexicon of contemporary textiles. By integrating AI, local industries can increase their productivity and innovate rapidly, potentially capturing new market segments with contemporary designs. Designers can use prompts infused with cultural symbols (e.g., "Generate a pattern inspired by Adinkra symbol 'Gye Nyame' in a modern colour palette") to create contemporary designs that are culturally grounded. This offers a pathway to preserve and evolve traditional aesthetics for a global audience.

items.abstract_text: While Enterprise sales systems have dashboards to track revenue, customers, and buying trends, reports often require reading between the lines to determine what's good and what's bad before deciding which accounts to focus on. In this research, an explainable Sales Intelligence framework is proposed that transforms transaction-level information into analytical evidence at the customer level and converts it into conversations to support decision-making. The following is an example of the framework: the UCI Online Retail dataset consists of 541,909 online retail transactions from a UK retail company from 1 December 2010 to 9 December 2011. Data preparation removes missing customer identifiers, invalid quantity/unit price data, and expired entries. This results in 397884 transaction lines, 18532 invoices, 4338 identifiable customers, 3665 products, 37 countries, and the following actual retained revenue (facts as of 31 December 2018): £8,911,407.90. Customer revenue, product activity, average order value, purchase frequency, and recency are calculated using deterministic methods to segment and assess account health. The proposed architecture leverages numerical computation and evidence retrieval to interpret AI-generated results and connect explanations/recommendations to verified transaction indicators, with an emphasis on algorithms. The proposed architecture interprets artificial intelligence results and connects evidence/messages and/or recommendations to certified transaction indicators, with an emphasis on algorithms. The study provides empirical results from the transaction analysis process. It proposes definitions of measures to evaluate an agent's future operational application, including numerical accuracy, retrieval precision and recall, F1 score, recommendation relevance, explanation agreement, error rate, and response latency. Validate data from the enterprise CRM and sales-interaction data (recommended).

analysis.discussion: It explains the importance of deterministic customer analytics and the need for customers to understand the attributes of conversational AI that make it explainable in enterprise sales intelligence. Converting transaction records into customer-based indexes yields a structured, customer-based understanding of commercial activity and purchasing behavior. Together with evidence retrieval and natural-language interpretation, these indicators can provide more user-friendly sales information and, in turn, support informed decisionmaking. One important aspect of the proposed framework is the split between AI-driven numerical computation and interpretation. The AI part accesses and clarifies the rationale behind the metrics for the customer, while the customer's analytical procedures define the metrics. This distinction will reduce unsupported revenue numbers, improve purchase-relationship recognition, and better track generated insights through a combination of revenue, purchase frequency, product activity, average order value, and recency details. They can help sales teams focus on top customers, track outdated accounts, and re-engage disconnected accounts. These categories, however, are analytical signals only and should not be used as absolute descriptions of customer International Journal of Advanced Artificial Intelligence Research (IJAAIR) https://aimjournals.com/index.php/ijaair 62 behavior; they should be considered alongside other business context. The other key principle, explainability, is also a focus, along with accountability in AI-powered sales decisions. Recommendations should be quantifiable in key customer metrics and transaction evidence, and users should be able to prove their impact before implementation. Therefore, the AI agent serves as a supplementary tool to support decision-making rather than replacing human judgment and traditional dashboards. The results are limited by the dataset and the proposed system's stage of development. The UCI Online Retail dataset excludes customer relationship history, sales interaction details, contract details, opportunity stages, and customer sentiment in addition to transaction data. For this reason, it cannot determine the root causes of shifts in buying behavior. Moreover, the planned conversational architecture has not yet been tested in operation. The retrieval accuracy, explanation quality, and relevance to recommendations need to be tested empirically with typical enterprise data from companies that sell products or services and validated against independent sources. 5.6 Future Research Future research should first adopt the proposed architecture and compare performance using the proposed reproducible analytical procedures. Document data preparation, customer identification, revenue calculations, segmentation thresholds, and customer "account health" classification as scriptable logic so it is reproducible and verifiable. The system should also be tested to ensure it produces consistent sales answers, in terms of numbers, whether it's asked in one way or another. Further research is needed to explore the effectiveness of evidence-based conversational AI with representative enterprise sales data. Such datasets should include relationship information, sales history, product information, opportunity details, and other organizationrelevant data. This would enable scientists to study the framework and determine whether it can support more detailed account evaluations than transaction reports provide. Conventional dashboards could also be compared with conversational sales intelligence systems to evaluate differences in how information is retrieved, tasks are accomplished, how accurately information is interpreted, and user experience. A human evaluation with sales representatives and managers would provide insights into whether the explanations and recommendations are practically useful for decision-making. Future investigations will also examine data privacy and access control, auditability, model reliability, and human oversight. For instance, in areas where sales information is critical and business decisions are being made, these factors are crucial to implementing AI-driven sales intelligence. Over time, this study would build continuity in the field by adapting the framework to other industries, assessing its success and effectiveness, and exploring its potential for enterprise sales management. The study presented a product-centric sales intelligence framework that merges customer-level analytics, proof-retrieval resources, and conversational AI to support explainable enterprise sales decisionmaking. The UCI Online Retail dataset, a daily retail dataset from a Norwegian online retail store, was used to build an analytical approach that generated customer insights such as purchase frequency, recency, average order value, product activity, and daily revenue. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. Written from the perspective of a primary school teacher and principal, this perspective paper examines three interrelated concerns of the author herself. These concerns arose from a wish to protect her pupils and led her to study the topic for her own professional development and to help her colleagues make teaching safer and better. They concern developing critical thinking towards AI-generated answers, protecting the personal data of minors, and the fear that excessive assistance from AI will weaken pupils' thinking. Drawing on a narrative, non-systematic review of recent research on cognitive offloading, the European and Greek regulatory framework, and illustrative examples from the author's own teaching practice and lesson scenarios for primary school, it argues that the fear of cognitive dependence is a plausible concern rather than an established finding for primary school pupils. The available evidence, which comes mainly from adolescents and adults, suggests that the form of AI support (whether it replaces the learner's effort or scaffolds it) may be an important factor. AI is regarded throughout as a valuable tool; the risk lies mainly in the way it is used. The classroom examples come from ordinary lessons whose only purpose was to teach pupils to question AI answers and to protect themselves when using AI. They were not planned as research, no research data were collected, and they are offered as the author's practitioner reflections, not as findings. The author's classroom experience illustrates that such activities can be implemented in ordinary primary school lessons, but their effects on pupils' critical thinking have not yet been evaluated. The paper relates the three concerns to long-standing educational principles, in particular Socratic questioning, Dewey's reflective thought and Vygotskian scaffolding. On this basis, it proposes a simple, as yet untested three-step classroom protocol (``think -- ask -- check''), age-appropriate data protection rules, and a role for school leadership, and outlines questions for future research.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.abstract_text: To address the growing computational demands of high-performance computing (HPC) and machine learning (ML) applications, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) have transitioned from single-chip designs to multi-chip module (MCM) architectures, driven by manufacturing constraints. Simultaneously, GPUs are increasingly deployed in cloud environments to accelerate a wide range of applications for multiple users. Spatial multitasking, which allows multiple applications to run concurrently on a single GPU by executing them on different sets of streaming multiprocessors (SMs), offers an efficient method for sharing GPU resources. However, effectively supporting multitasking in the emerging MCM-GPU architecture presents a significant challenge that remains an open problem. This article presents the key observation that the placement of co-executing applications in MCM-GPUs plays a critical role in system performance. Specifically, for certain multiprogram workloads, co-executing applications achieve better performance when located on the same GPU chip to maximize memory bandwidth utilization. Conversely, other workloads benefit from being distributed across different GPU chips to mitigate memory contention. To address this, we propose a Location-Aware Scheduler (LA-Scheduler) that identifies application characteristics and makes optimized scheduling decisions. The LA-Scheduler performs lightweight workload classification using a k-means-based clustering method and applies multitasking scheduling rules during runtime to determine the optimal placement of applications within the MCM-GPU architecture. Evaluation results show that the proposed LA-Scheduler improves system throughput (STP) by an average of 38.67% compared with single-task operation. Compared with the traditional methods intra-chip scheduling and inter-chip scheduling, the system throughput is improved by an average of 13.51% and 7.14% respectively.

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.abstract_text: Silicon Lifecycle Management (SLM) is essential for ensuring the reliability, security, and performance of modern computing platforms. Conventional SLM approaches rely on off-chip or software-only analytics, which lack on-die interpretability. We present X-OCTANE, an explainable on-chip telemetry-based anomaly notification engine. X–OCTANE is a hybrid explainability framework that integrates Causal-Preserving Mutual Information (CP–MI) with SHAP-based feature attribution for interpretable feature ranking and selection. The proposed feature rank-and-selection procedure retains competitive safety-oriented anomaly detection and bolsters security-specific in-field monitoring of compute platforms. For the 7 nm ASAP technology, X-OCTANE achieves competitive anomaly detection performance with less than 0.50% CPU die area and 1.0% non-idle power overhead. In addition, X–OCTANE improves anomaly-driven diagnosis accuracy by over 7% on average. Experimental validation using the PAMPAR benchmark suite on two separate experimental platforms demonstrates enhanced anomaly detection and diagnosis through the proposed explainable feature-rank-and-selection method. X–OCTANE establishes a scalable and transparent foundation for on-chip SLM analytics, unifying detection fidelity with causal interpretability.

items.title: Generative AI Writing Companions and L2 Learners’ Cognitive Writing Processes: A Conceptual Framework for Pedagogical Scaffolding

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) writing companions are changing how second-language (L2) writers plan, formulate, and revise texts. Yet improved textual fluency does not necessarily indicate deeper learning or stronger independent writing ability. This conceptual article develops a framework for interpreting AI-assisted L2 writing through the Cognitive Process Model of Writing, Cognitive Load Theory, and the Output Hypothesis. It argues that AI assistance may redistribute rather than simply reduce cognitive effort: linguistic suggestions can ease some local formulation demands, while evaluating, adapting, and verifying generated language creates additional monitoring demands. Whether this redistribution supports learning depends on the learner’s agency, the transparency of the task, and the instructional design. The article proposes a three-phase pedagogical model: supported conceptual ideation, autonomous drafting, and collaborative critical revision. Across these phases, AI support is deliberately varied so that learners can benefit from assistance without surrendering authorship, monitoring, or opportunities for linguistic retrieval. The paper is conceptual and does not report an empirical experiment. It therefore offers propositions and a research agenda rather than claims of measured effects. The framework can guide future classroom research, instrument development, and responsible integration of generative AI into L2 writing curricula.

items.title: Attention-Guided Stroke Location Inversion for Explainable Sketch Recognition

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has made remarkable progress in pixel and text domains, yet human sketches a uniquely sparse and sequential data modality remain largely unexplored from an interpretability perspective. The recently proposed SketchXAI framework introduced Stroke Location Inversion (SLI) to reconstruct stroke layouts from randomized configurations, but treats every stroke with identical optimization priority regardless of its structural relevance. We address this limitation by proposing Attention-Guided Stroke Location Inversion (AG-SLI). We initially evaluate a continuous formulation that scales per stroke gradients proportionally to self attention weights across a 30-category QuickDraw subset (86.13% classifier accuracy). Through a staged empirical protocol, we demonstrate that this continuous variant fails to replicate consistently, exhibiting sign-flipping median convergence speed changes (−47.8% to +40.0%) driven by localized sampling noise. Motivated by this instability, we introduce a refined, bounded, rank-based formulation: a fixed multiplicative gradient boost is restricted to the top 30% most attended strokes across the final four transformer layers, decaying linearly over the optimization trajectory. Benchmarked against standard machine learning optimizers across independent hard-case pools (n = 90), the refined mechanism achieves a median convergence depth of 10 iterations, significantly outperforming standard Adam (19 iterations) and SGD with Momentum (24 iterations). Furthermore, the framework limits non-convergence rates to 22.2%, improves spatial recovery (0.038 Final MSE), and yields a net 30.65% reduction in total job wall-clock time despite an updated O(N log N) per step complexity. We present this complete empirical journey including the initial non replication to establish a transparent baseline for reproducible, resource efficient optimization architectures in sparse visual domains.

reading.methods: We first review the SketchXAINet architecture and the original SLI formulation [10] . We then introduce our initial continuous attention guided formulation (Section 3.3), and, motivated by its empirical instability (Section 4.4), a refined rank-based formulation (Section 3.4) that forms our final proposed method. Figure 1 illustrates the overall workflow of the proposed AG-SLI framework, highlighting how the ViT encoder produces attention weights that guide the subsequent stroke location optimization. Rather than reporting a single experiment, we adopted an explicitly staged evaluation designed to distinguish genuine effects from small sample noise, motivated by the observation that convergence to threshold statistics on small subgroups can be highly variable. The evaluation consisted of the following stages: (i) An exploratory sweep of continuous AG-SLI over γ ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5} on 30 sketches; (ii) A confirmatory run of the same formulation on 100 independently sampled sketches; (iii) Two further independent hard case replications of continuous AG-SLI on fresh samples (n = 42 and n = 51); (iv) Design of the refined rank-based formulation (Section 3.4); and (v) Three independent replications of the refined formulation on hard case samples (n = 31, n = 32, and n = 90).
reading.findings: To illustrate what the quantitative convergence speed improvement (Section 4.5) looks like in practice, Figure 3 compares the recovery trajectory of the uniform baseline against the refined rank-based AG-SLI mechanism on a representative "bicycle" sketch, at iterations 0 (immediately after randomization), 20, 50, and 99. Under the uniform baseline, the two wheel strokes remain visibly detached from the bicycle frame even at iteration 99, producing a final configuration that only partially resembles the target category. Under rank-based AG-SLI, both wheel strokes have already relocated adjacent to the frame stroke by iteration 20, and the final configuration at iteration 99 forms a substantially more coherent bicycle silhouette. This example illustrates one concrete way in which faster confidence based convergence (as measured quantitatively in Section 4.5) coincides with a qualitatively more semantically coherent recovered sketch: the attention-guided mechanism prioritizes relocating the discriminative wheel strokes early in the optimization trajectory, rather than leaving their recovery to chance under uniform gradient updates. We emphasize that this single example is illustrative rather than representative of every sketch in our hard case sample: as reported quantitatively in Section 4.5, the improvement is a median effect observed across a population of hard sketches, and individual sketches vary in how clearly this pattern manifests visually.
reading.interpretation: This work introduces a robust, attention-guided optimization framework to resolve the uniform allocation inefficiencies inherent to baseline Stroke Location Inversion. Our initial, theoretically natural continuous formulation failed independent replication tests, illustrating how unbounded, sketch dependent scaling amplifies sampling noise and introduces oscillatory dynamics near coordinate junctions. By diagnosing these specific optimization instabilities, we designed a bounded, rank-based mechanism featuring multi-layer attention aggregation and explicit temporal decay. Our empirical evaluations confirm that the refined rank-based framework consistently cuts median optimization depth by 14.3% to 33.3% across independent evaluation cohorts. Wall-clock throughput profiling demonstrates that our rank gated sorting logic delivers a 30.65% net reduction in total test-time computational resource expenditure, proving its operational viability for real time, efficient visual sequence processing. items.title: Minds Meet Machines: The Joint Role of Trust and Intellectual Humility in AI Persuasion

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Research shows that AI models have a remarkable ability to change people’s minds following a short conversation, a notoriously difficult task for human communicators. Such persuasive paradigms provide a unique opportunity to examine which psychological characteristics predict receptivity to counter-attitudinal information. We focus on two characteristics: intellectual humility (IH), reflecting openness to revising one’s beliefs following new information, and trust in the information source (AI). To establish the role of a-priori dispositions that determine acceptance of new information, we ran two online studies, sampling British participants with a negative attitude toward legal immigrants (N = 294). We replicated previous findings showing significant and lasting attitude change following a brief exchange with GPT, but crucially, this effect was not uniform. In Study 1, attitude change was greatest among participants with higher initial trust in AIs and higher intellectual humility. Study 2 extended this finding by measuring both dispositions a week before the conversation with GPT, revealing the same pattern: opinion change was greatest among those who were both open to new information and trusting of its source. These findings highlight the centrality of recipient dispositions, suggesting that the relationship between source trust and persuasion depends on recipients' intellectual humility. More broadly, source trust may function as more than a heuristic cue, and its relationship with attitude change may depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the fallibility of their beliefs. Together, these findings extend perspectives on persuasion by highlighting the joint role of source trust and recipients' epistemic dispositions in belief revision.

items.abstract_text: Purpose Agentic AI systems execute procurement decisions, reroute shipments and renegotiate supplier contracts at speeds that preclude real-time human review. The existing literature offers limited analytical attention to the risks that arise when decision authority is delegated to agents. This paper develops a risk taxonomy for agentic AI in supply chains and traces the hierarchical dependencies and influence magnitudes among the identified risks. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of literature, analyzed through theories–characteristics–contexts–methods framework, produces the risk taxonomy. A hybrid modified total interpretive structural modeling and fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory methodology is then applied to structured expert judgments to establish the causal hierarchy and quantify inter-risk influence. Findings Three risks, namely workforce skill gap, data quality and reliability and ethical misalignment occupy the deepest level of the causal hierarchy. Lack of accountability and governance and data privacy emerge as terminal outcomes. All three analytical methods converge on a conclusion: agentic AI risks originate at the institutional layer, with technical risks acting as transmission mechanisms. Practical implications The findings indicate that effective governance requires that workforce capability, data integrity and objective-function alignment are addressed before deployment. The stratified agentic AI governance framework is proposed that translates hierarchical structure into a sequenced intervention architecture, providing practitioners with governance priorities organized by risk-propagation logic. Originality/value This paper contributes a systematically derived risk taxonomy and a causally weighted governance map for agentic AI risks in supply chains. Five propositions are derived from the causal structure and are advanced as a testable research agenda.

items.title: CardioTwin-AI: development and internal validation of a digital twin-based adaptive risk-aware learning framework for heart disease prediction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Heart disease is one of the most common causes of death in the world and early identification of individuals at elevated cardiovascular risk requires reliable risk-assessment methods that can support clinical decision-making. Many conventional machine-learning models focus primarily on disease classification or risk prediction and do not explicitly provide patient-specific virtual representations. This study introduces CardioTwin-AI, a Digital Twin-based Adaptive Risk-Aware Learning Framework (ARLF) to predict the presence or absence of heart disease. We propose a data-driven, patient-specific Digital Twin representation based on clinical attributes, in which the patient state is mapped to a corresponding virtual state and evaluated using state-level synchronization measures, including Twin Simulation Error (TSE) and Twin Fidelity Score (TFS) to quantify representation consistency. The deep feature representations are generated by feature engineering process based on autoencoder, and then analysed by the ARLF prediction model to estimate the probability of the presence of heart disease. It achieved high patient-state representation consistency between the source clinical state and its virtual representation, with a Twin Fidelity Score of 99.76% and a Twin Simulation Error of 0.002402. The proposed ARLF model achieved accuracy of 90.21%, precision of 90.32%, recall of 94.11%, F1-score of 92.18%, and ROC-AUC of 95.13% in the fixed held-out evaluation. The results indicate the potential of CardioTwin-AI for predicting the presence or absence of heart disease and assessing patient-state representation consistency, subject to further external validation and prospective clinical evaluation.

In the fixed held-out evaluation, CardioTwin-AI achieved 90.21% accuracy, 90.32% precision, 94.11% recall, a 92.18% F1-score, and a 95.13% ROC-AUC, with TSE = 0.002402 and TFS = 99.76%. Across repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation with 10 repetitions, CardioTwin-AI achieved the highest mean Accuracy, Recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC among the evaluated models. However, none of the pairwise comparisons remained statistically significant after Holm correction. Therefore, the results indicate promising predictive performance, but do not establish statistically significant superiority over the evaluated baselines. The framework's potential FIGURE 9 Calibration curve of CardioTwin-AI predicted probabilities on the independent test set. incremental contribution lies in integrating patient-state representation, feature augmentation, adaptive classification, and explainability within a unified computational framework. The present study remains at the research and development stage. The Digital Twin was evaluated using a static, publicly available dataset containing 918 patient records; it does not yet represent continuously updated physiological states or longitudinal disease progression. The fixed held-out evaluation and repeated cross-validation constitute internal validation and do not establish generalizability to independent patient populations, clinical utility, improved patient outcomes, or treatment benefit. Future work will evaluate CardioTwin-AI using independent external datasets and, where feasible, multicentre clinical cohorts; incorporate longitudinal electronic health records, wearable-sensor data, and additional clinical measurements where available; and investigate temporal modelling for updated patient-state representation and cardiovascular prediction over time. Prospective clinical evaluation will be necessary to assess generalizability and potential clinical utility before any clinical deployment is considered.

items.abstract_text: Purpose As artificial intelligence advances and its application scenarios continue to expand, human–artificial intelligence interaction grows increasingly close. While artificial intelligence brings convenience, it also raises concerns that it may weaken users' cognitive autonomy. To investigate this issue. This study aims to explore the composition of AI dependence and its impact on cognitive autonomy and specific aspects of creative performance. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on cognitive evaluation theory and the elaboration likelihood model to construct a dual-pathway model with instrumental dependence and affective dependence as core variables. The model explains the formation mechanisms of the two types of artificial intelligence dependence and their differential effects on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily examines their potential role in the elaboration dimension of creative performance. A two-stage mixed-method design was employed to test the model. Findings Study 1 found that perceived trust mainly had a positive effect on instrumental dependence. Different dimensions of interactivity differentially affected affective dependence and cognitive autonomy. Mediation analysis further confirmed the core mediating role of Dependence. Study 2, a small-sample exploratory experiment, re-tested selected hypotheses and found a possible negative effect of instrumental dependence on the elaboration dimension of creative performance. Research limitations/implications The main theoretical contribution of this study lies in revealing the dual-pathway formation mechanisms of artificial intelligence dependence and the reshaping effects of different types of dependence on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily explores the potential effects of dependence on elaboration performance. Originality/value The dual-pathway dependence model constructed in this study offers practical implications for understanding how long-term use of artificial intelligence affects cognitive autonomy.

items.abstract_text: The Research Topic begins with Achuthan's Artificial intelligence and learner autonomy: a meta-analysis of self-regulated and self-directed learning, which provides a broad empirical examination of the relationship between AI and learner autonomy. Synthesizing 32 empirical studies, 92 effect sizes, and 3,029 participants, the study examines the effects of AI-based interventions on SRL, self-directed learning (SDL), different dimensions and phases of SRL, and learning outcomes. The findings indicate positive effects of AI interventions on overall SRL and SDL, with particularly notable effects during the forethought phase, including goal setting and planning. At the same time, less consistent effects for behavioral regulation point to an important design challenge: supporting learners in knowing what to do and why to do it does not necessarily ensure that they will translate those intentions into effective action. The findings therefore provide encouraging evidence for AI as a scaffold for self-regulation while highlighting the importance of designing support across the full SRL cycle.Building on this macro-level evidence, Agustin's AI as a co-regulator: relational design for strengthening self-regulated learning addresses the theoretical mechanics of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in Winne and Hadwin's COPES architecture, this conceptual paper tackles a core dilemma in educational technology: how can AI assist learners without eroding the cognitive agency and productive struggle essential to self-regulation? Agustin introduces "productive metacognitive friction" -the deliberate structuring of challenge and discrepancy within AI interaction -as a design mechanism to prevent passive reliance. The article presents five relational design principles alongside an evaluation framework prioritizing learner autonomy, interpretability, process integrity, and long-term developmental growth across both formal education and workplace reskilling environments.Moving from meta-analytic synthesis and conceptual frameworks to empirical classroom research, Gu et al.'s Fostering feedback literacy by scaffolding self-regulated feedback: a comparative study of GenAI and human peers examines the operational mechanisms through which GenAI fosters feedback literacya key component of self-regulated learning. In a comparative mixed-methods study of first-year undergraduates in Hong Kong, the authors compare the developmental impact of GenAI-generated feedback against traditional human peer review. Their findings demonstrate that GenAI yields a statistically significant improvement in feedback literacy over human peer feedback alone. Qualitative evidence reveals that this advantage stems from GenAI's ability to scaffold distinct self-regulatory behaviors: providing immediate, non-judgmental spaces for goal setting, structured planning, critical evaluation, and real-time self-reflection. By removing the interpersonal friction and psychological safety concerns common in peer review, GenAI emerges as an effective tool for cultivating student feedback literacy.Finally, Chang et al.'s "Should I tell my teacher?" Student AI disclosure practices, stigma, and selfregulated learning in higher education examines the affective, social, and institutional factors that influence how learners adopt these tools in practice. Focusing on undergraduate students at a Canadian university, the authors explore the intersection of student AI disclosure practices, social stigma, and SRL processes. Their findings illuminate a key tension: while transparent disclosure to instructors correlates with proactive self-regulated learning behaviors (a "transparent-disclosure pattern"), fear of academic judgment and social stigmatization often triggers an "anxious-concealment pattern." Highly anxious students who use AI heavily are more likely to conceal their usage or restrict sharing to peer networks. This study highlights that technical scaffolds cannot succeed in a vacuum; institutional policies and pedagogical environments must account for emotional and social dynamics to prevent secrecy from undermining reflective SRL practices.Considered together, the four articles in this Research Topic illustrate that AI's role in self-regulated learning extends far beyond simple automation or content delivery. Achuthan's meta-analysis provides evidence of AI's potential to strengthen SRL and SDL, while also identifying limitations in behavioral regulation. Agustin's framework addresses this challenge conceptually by positioning AI as a co-regulator that supports learners without displacing their agency. Gu et al. demonstrate how such support can be enacted in feedback processes, whereas Chang et al. show how emotions, stigma, and institutional expectations shape learners' decisions about AI use. This collection highlights that realizing the promise of AI-supported self-regulated learning requires more than personalization or automation. Research and design must examine how AI can scaffold regulatory processes, support learner autonomy and human agency, and safeguard against cognitive over-reliance.

items.abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of online educational technologies, instructional videos have become a pivotal tool for flexible and efficient learning. The integration of visual aids, such as animations and dynamic elements, aims to enhance the learning experience; however, their effectiveness remains debated. This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static AI-generated images or manually animated versions of those images. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 undergraduate participants ( n = 10 per cell), comparing static versus motion-enhanced presentation conditions across male and female participant groups. Stable Diffusion XL generated the base images, and CapCut was used to add motion; the motion itself was not AI-generated. Participants viewed a 140-s mobile video on mortise-and-tenon structures, completed a 10-item accuracy test, and rated willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and mental effort. The ANOVA results provided no statistically significant evidence of a main effect of motion on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several subjective outcomes. For acceptability, the gender × motion interaction was statistically significant, but Bonferroni-adjusted simple-effect tests supported a gender-group difference only in the static condition. For mental effort, the interaction was also statistically significant; adjusted simple-effect tests indicated higher mental effort among female than male participants in the dynamic condition and higher mental effort in the static than dynamic condition among male participants. Given the small sample and multiple outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

For inclusive educational design, the goal is not to design "for males" or "for females," but to identify when motion helps or hinders different learners and to provide learner-controlled or adaptive options (Castro-Alonso et al., 2021) . This perspective motivates the present examination of whether responses to motion-enhanced AI-generated images differ across observed gender groups. This study employed a 2 × 2 between-subjects design, with two independent variables: "motion-enhanced AI-generated images" (static/dynamic) and "gender differences" (male/female). During the experimental design process, Illustrator software was used for graphic design, and CapCut was employed to produce the instructional videos. The experiment was conducted on an iPhone 11 device running iOS 15.7, featuring a 6.1 -inch Liquid Retina HD display. Participants watched an instructional video and subsequently completed a 10-item true/false test and a psychological evaluation questionnaire (collecting subjective data). Specifically, the dependent variables were learning accuracy, willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and perceived mental effort. Figure 1 shows the research framework of this study. Using purposive sampling, 40 undergraduate students (20 male; 20 female) were recruited via advertisement from a university in Shenzhen, China. A 2 (Gender: Male/Female) × 2 (Condition: Static/ Dynamic) between-subjects design was used. Forty participants were evenly distributed across the four experimental cells (Static-Male/ Static-Female/Dynamic-Male/Dynamic-Female), with n = 10 per cell. Stratified randomization was employed: participants were first stratified by gender, then randomly assigned to the static or dynamic video condition within each stratum. To control for prior knowledge, participants were explicitly screened to ensure they had no background in furniture design, woodworking, or architectural engineering, and specifically no prior knowledge of "mortise and tenon" structures. All participants possessed normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Before the experiment began, the researcher thoroughly explained the experimental purpose and safeguards. After fully understanding the relevant information, participants voluntarily signed a written informed consent form, confirming their rights to voluntary participation, informed consent, and withdrawal. Additionally, to avoid practice effects on the experimental results, all participants were first-time viewers of the experimental videos and were native Chinese speakers. All experimental protocols were approved by the Ethics Committee of Shenzhen Technology University under Approval No. SZTUYXLL2025113, a named institutional committee. Furthermore, written informed consent was obtained from all participants before participation. The experimental materials consisted of two versions of an online instructional video course on mortise-tenon structures. The visual assets were generated using a two-step workflow involving AI generation and manual editing to ensure both technical quality and pedagogical relevance. To ensure reproducibility and transparency, the AI-generated visual assets were created using Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) through the Automatic1111 web interface. A structured prompting strategy was employed to ensure high fidelity and structural accuracy. Positive prompts emphasized exploded views of mortise-tenon joints, traditional Chinese woodworking, an isometric perspective, and 8 k resolution on a white background. Negative prompts excluded distorted structures, artifacts, text, and cartoonish styles. analysis.discussion: Before discussing the implications of our findings, it is important to define the scope within which these results are most directly applicable. This study examined a specific type of instructional contentvisuospatially complex material (mortise and tenon structures) requiring understanding of three-dimensional relationships and assembly processes. The participants were higher education students with no prior domain knowledge, and the instructional videos were brief (140 s) and delivered on mobile devices. Therefore, our findings are most directly relevant to similar learning contexts: technical or procedural knowledge domains, novice learners, and short-format mobile learning environments. The present study investigated the effects of motion-enhanced AI-generated images in instructional videos on learning performance and subjective experience, with a particular focus on genderbased differences. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), this research aimed to elucidate whether dynamic visual presentations differentially impact male and female learners. The findings reveal a nuanced pattern: while motion effects alone did not significantly enhance learning accuracy, gender was associated with differences in objective performance and subjective evaluations. Significant interaction effects between gender and motion effects were observed for acceptability and mental effort, suggesting that responses to dynamic visual information may differ across gender groups; however, these differences should be interpreted cautiously because gender was not experimentally manipulated and relevant covariates were not measured. The present study yielded several noteworthy findings regarding the differential impact of motion-enhanced AI-generated images on male and female learners. A significant main effect of gender was observed, with male learners showing higher accuracy rates than female learners in this sample. However, this difference cannot be confidently attributed to spatial-processing ability, because the study did not measure baseline spatial ability, technology experience, general academic ability, or interest in the subject. Screening for prior woodworking knowledge does not ensure equivalence in these characteristics. Therefore, the accuracy difference may reflect unmeasured baseline differences, and this explanation should be treated as tentative. These findings address Q2 by indicating a difference between gender groups in this sample, but the underlying reasons remain unclear. This exploratory study examined learning performance and subjective responses to static versus motion-enhanced AI-generated images in a short mobile instructional video. No statistically significant evidence was found for a main effect of presentation condition on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several outcomes, but these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of inherent gender-based cognitive differences. For acceptability, a significant gender group × presentation condition interaction was observed. Bonferroni-adjusted simpleeffect tests indicated that female participants reported higher acceptability than male participants in the static condition, whereas the gender-group difference in the dynamic condition was not statistically significant. For perceived mental effort, the interaction was also significant: female participants reported higher mental effort than male participants in the dynamic condition, and male participants reported higher mental effort in the static than in the dynamic condition. The remaining adjusted comparisons were not statistically significant. These findings suggest that the effects of motion-enhanced visual presentation may vary across learners and outcomes rather than producing a uniform benefit. However, the small sample, absence of a formal manipulation check, limitations in measurement validation, multiple exploratory outcomes, and unmeasured learner characteristics constrain generalization. TAM-related perceptions and Cognitive Load Theory therefore serve as interpretive perspectives rather than as a tested integrated model. Future research should use larger samples, validated measures, appropriate analyses for bounded accuracy data, and learner-controlled or adaptive presentation based on measured needs and preferences rather than gender-based design prescriptions.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the findings of this study and should be considered when interpreting the results. First, no formal manipulation check or independent image-quality assessment was conducted. We did not collect expert or participant ratings of visual quality, structural accuracy, semantic consistency, motion salience, or informational equivalence between the static and dynamic conditions. Although images were informally screened for visible artifacts and structural accuracy before inclusion, this screening served only as a material-selection step and does not constitute formal validation. We therefore cannot conclusively verify that participants perceived the static/dynamic distinction as intended, nor can we fully rule out artifact-related confounding. Future research should include manipulation checks and systematic ratings of visual quality, structural accuracy, semantic consistency, motion salience, and informational equivalence. Second, the measurement instruments have several limitations. No formal pilot testing was conducted. The reliability coefficients reported in the original manuscript were drawn from prior source studies rather than calculated in the present sample; sample-specific reliability estimates are now reported in Supplementary material but should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size. The 10-item true/false accuracy test was reviewed for content validity by three experts, but no itemlevel analysis of difficulty, discrimination, or reliability was conducted. The acceptability scale was newly developed for this study and has not been formally validated; its factor structure, convergent validity, and discriminant validity remain unknown. The mental effort measure captures self-reported perceived effort and should not be interpreted as a pure measure of extraneous cognitive load. Future research should pilot-test all instruments, conduct item analyses, validate newly developed scales, and use measures that distinguish intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load more precisely. Third, the study does not test a full TAM model or provide measurement-model evaluation. TAM-related perceptions and Cognitive Load Theory are used as interpretive perspectives rather than as a tested integrated model. Willingness to continue learning is an intention-related evaluation, ease of understanding is perceived comprehensibility, preference is an affective evaluation of the video, and acceptability is a study-specific evaluation. No causal paths, factor structure, convergent validity, or discriminant validity are claimed. Future research should either validate adapted TAM constructs using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling or continue to use them as exploratory interpretive tools. Fourth, the sample size was small (N = 40; n = 10 per cell), and no a priori power analysis was conducted. Small or medium effects may therefore not have been detected. Nonsignificant results are reported as "no statistically significant evidence was found" rather than as proof that no difference exists, and 95% confidence intervals for nonsignificant effects are provided in Supplementary material. Future research should recruit larger and more diverse samples to detect small-tomedium effects. Fifth, several statistical issues require cautious interpretation. Learning accuracy was derived from 10 true/false items and is therefore bounded count data. A binomial generalized linear model would have been more appropriate than treating accuracy as a normally distributed continuous variable; however, the present study relied on ANOVA as an exploratory and comparability-oriented analysis, and no binomial GLM was conducted. In addition, because several dependent variables were examined, inflated Type I error cannot be ruled out; no formal multiplicity correction (e.g., Benjamini-Hochberg FDR) was applied, and interaction effects on secondary outcomes should therefore be interpreted as exploratory. Future research should use binomial or item-level mixed models for bounded accuracy data, report full assumption checks, apply appropriate multiplicity corrections, and provide effect sizes with confidence intervals. Accordingly, nonsignificant findings should be described as absence of statistically significant evidence rather than as evidence of no effect. Sixth, gender-related interpretations remain tentative. Gender was recorded as a binary category based on participant self-report; the source documentation does not specify whether this category reflects self-identified gender or biological sex, and no biological or essentialist interpretation is made. Gender was treated as an observed grouping variable, not as a causal or biological determinant. Baseline spatial ability, technology familiarity, general academic ability, anxiety, interest in woodworking, and prior experience were not objectively measured. Screening for prior woodworking knowledge does not ensure equivalence in these characteristics. The observed differences may therefore reflect unmeasured baseline differences, and they should not be used to prescribe different instructional treatments based solely on gender. Future research should include standardized measures of spatial ability, technology familiarity, and prior interest as covariates and should emphasize learner-controlled or adaptive presentation based on measured needs and preferences rather than gender-based design. Seventh, the qualitative component of this study is descriptive and lacks the methodological rigor expected of standalone qualitative research. The available record does not document participant selection beyond cell counts (three participants per cell, total N = 12; 6 male, 6 female), recording and transcription procedures, coding stages, number of coders, disagreement resolution, language and translation procedures, or criteria for thematic saturation. Interviews lasted 5-10 min and were conducted immediately after questionnaire completion. The interview comments are therefore presented as supplementary illustrations and should not be described as independently corroborating the quantitative findings. Future work should adopt established guidelines for rigorous thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) , employ multiple independent coders with systematic reliability assessment, and provide comprehensive documentation of the analytic process. Eighth, the experimental materials and context limit generalizability. The dynamic condition used a mixed-process approach: base images were AI-generated using Stable Diffusion XL, but motion effects were manually applied using CapCut. This differs from pure AI-generated videos, which may exhibit different motion characteristics, temporal artifacts, or semantic inconsistencies. Exact generation and animation parameters are also incompletely documented, limiting reproducibility. The study focused on a single domain-traditional woodworking structures (mortise-and-tenon joints)-selected for its high visuospatial complexity. items.title: From disclosure to epistemic accountability: preserving meaningful human control across the AI-assisted research lifecycle

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics
items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded across the scientific research lifecycle, while prevailing governance remains centered on disclosure of tool use and the assignment of responsibility to human authors. We argue that disclosure is necessary but insufficient because it does not establish that researchers understood, verified, challenged, and authorized the AI-assisted processes that shaped scientific claims. We define this disconnect as the epistemic accountability gap and develop the Lifecycle Epistemic Accountability Framework (LEAF) as a testable theory of how meaningful human control can be preserved across AI-assisted knowledge production. Drawing on a structured integrative review and critical interpretive synthesis, LEAF links four human-control capacities—competence, contestability, intervention authority, and traceable ownership—supported by evaluability by design, to five lifecycle checkpoints spanning evidence identification, study design and ethics, data processing and analysis, interpretation, and reporting or knowledge translation. The framework proposes that accountability improves when oversight is exercised prospectively at epistemically consequential decision points, documented through an audit trail, and calibrated to epistemic materiality: the extent to which AI assistance can alter the validity, interpretation, or consequences of a scientific claim. Six propositions specify testable relationships among disclosure, epistemic materiality, meaningful human control, lifecycle checkpoints, auditability, and defensibility of scientific claims. LEAF therefore shifts AI research governance from retrospective visibility to prospective, risk-proportionate control. We identify boundary conditions, implementation pathways, and an empirical research agenda for testing the framework across disciplines and resource settings. LEAF's distinctive explanatory mechanism is conditional: epistemic materiality escalates oversight, evaluability enables four human capacities, lifecycle checkpoints interrupt error propagation, and retained audit evidence makes consequential decisions answerable.

analysis.discussion: LEAF advances a theory of epistemic accountability. We synthesize established work on disclosure, human oversight, risk proportionality, lifecycle auditing, and scientific answerability into a conditional framework focused on the formation of knowledge claims. LEAF theorizes that disclosure is a visibility mechanism, whereas epistemic accountability emerges from the interaction of governance mechanisms, human capacities, system/workflow affordances, boundary conditions, and evidence of substantive epistemic engagement. This is an original theoretical integration and should be evaluated through the six propositions rather than presented as an established empirical result. For researchers, LEAF clarifies that accountability cannot be transferred to an AI system and cannot be satisfied by disclosure alone. Researchers must retain sufficient understanding to defend the evidence and reasoning supporting each consequential claim. This has implications for authorship, supervision, team composition, and continuing professional development. For journals, the framework supports a shift from binary questions about whether AI was used toward structured questions about where AI influenced the research lifecycle TABLE 10 Implementation roadmap for LEAF. The integration of AI into scientific research demands a corresponding evolution in governance. Disclosure remains fundamental, but it cannot demonstrate that researchers exercised the judgment required to preserve the integrity of AI-assisted knowledge production. The critical governance challenge is no longer simply identifying where AI was used. It is ensuring that competent and identifiable researchers retain meaningful control over the evidence, methods, reasoning, and decisions through which scientific claims are made. This Hypothesis and Theory article identifies an epistemic accountability gap between declared responsibility and demonstrable scientific control. To close that gap, LEAF reframes accountability as a continuous, lifecycle-based process. Five epistemic checkpoints require human evaluation and authorization before AI-assisted outputs influence subsequent research stages. Four human capacities-competence, contestability, intervention authority, and traceable ownershipare supported by evaluability by design as an enabling socio-technical condition. Risk-proportionate oversight and epistemic audit trails make the exercise of that control visible and reviewable. The article makes three principal contributions. First, it identifies the epistemic accountability gap between declared human responsibility and demonstrable human control. Second, it specifies meaningful human control through four human capacities supported by evaluability by design, while distinguishing those constructs from governance mechanisms, boundary conditions, and outcomes. Third, it introduces LEAF as a conditional theoretical mechanism in which epistemic materiality calibrates prospective checkpoint oversight, substantive human engagement interrupts error propagation, and audit evidence connects distributed authorization to defensible scientific claims. LEAF does not replace disclosure; it gives disclosure governance substance. Its core contribution is to shift attention from the presence of AI to the quality of human judgment surrounding its use. Institutions, journals, ethics committees, funders, and policymakers can use this framework to align transparency, reproducibility, accountability, and proportionate oversight across the research ecosystem. The framework now requires empirical validation and adaptation, particularly in resource-constrained settings. Nevertheless, it provides a theoretically grounded and operationally coherent basis for testing the next generation of AI research governance. Its central claim is that responsible AI-assisted science should be judged not only by whether AI use was disclosed, but by whether identifiable researchers were able-and institutionally enabled-to understand, challenge, justify, authorize, and take responsibility for the knowledge produced. used only to support language, organization, and structural refinement during manuscript development and revision. analysis.limitations: LEAF should be presented as a conceptual governance framework derived from heterogeneous evidence rather than from primary empirical evaluation. Direct evidence on meaningful human control across the scientific research lifecycle remains limited, and much of the supporting literature comes from healthcare, public administration, education, and broader human-AI decision-making rather than research practice itself (Hille et al., 2026; Lai et al., 2023; Zhai et al., 2024) . Transfer to science is therefore plausible, but it still requires testing across disciplines, institutional settings, and levels of epistemic risk (Currie et al., 2025; Van den Bosch et al., 2025) . The framework should also not be treated as a universally validated standard. Evidence for checkpoints, risk-proportionate oversight, and audit trails is promising, but their effects on accuracy, reproducibility, accountability, and trust have not been systematically established in research workflows (García-Llorente and Olmeda, 2026; Hille et al., 2026; Konda, 2026; Wong and Hsu, 2026) . Oversight should remain proportionate to epistemic materiality, disciplinary norms, local infrastructure, and downstream consequences rather than being imposed identically across all uses (Hille et al., 2026) . The same caution applies to the four formative dimensions and provisional Low-Critical governance bands of epistemic materiality, as well as to the meaningful-control constructs. They are theoretically specified tools for organizing empirical work, not validated psychometric scales or regulatory thresholds. Future studies should test inter-rater reliability and predictive validity of the materiality profile, potential weighting or non-linear combination of its dimensions, and the construct validity and contextual sensitivity of the four human capacities and evaluabilityby-design affordance before standardized assessment instruments or regulatory cut-points are adopted. Future research should pursue four priorities. First, comparative implementation studies should test LEAF against disclosure-only governance using outcomes such as error detection, reproducibility, review quality, time burden, and trust, because human-AI combinations are heterogeneous and often perform worse than the better solo performer in decision tasks (Vaccaro et al., 2024) . Second, validated indicators are needed for competence, contestability, intervention authority, traceable ownership, evaluability, and audit-trail quality, since existing MHC concepts remain vague and current measurement work is still early and context-bound (Van den Bosch et al., 2025) . Third, longitudinal research should assess how sustained AI use affects scientific judgment, skill retention, automation bias, and team accountability. Evidence from healthcare, diagnostics, and education already suggests over-reliance can degrade reasoning, increase error propagation, and erode training opportunities (Heudel et al., 2026; Sunday, 2025) . Fourth, studies in LMICs and fragile research systems should test feasibility and equity, because governance gaps, data poverty, weak infrastructure, and limited local leadership can cause AI governance requirements to reproduce or widen global disparities (Forsyth et al., 2026; Wahl et al., 2026; Yu and Zhai, 2024) . A further priority concerns organizational incentives. Formal checkpoints may fail when accountability is weak, enforcement is fragmented, or institutions do not protect people who challenge unsafe systems (Currie et al., 2025; García-Llorente and Olmeda, 2026) . Future work should therefore examine not only whether researchers hold formal authority, but whether staffing, hierarchy, training, and institutional culture allow them to exercise that authority without penalty (Currie et al., 2025; Resnik and Hosseini, 2026) . LEAF is most defensible, then, as a testable, context-sensitive framework rather than a settled standard. What matters next is empirical validation of its checkpoints, measures, and equity effects in real research environments. A direct empirical test could compare research teams assigned to disclosure-only governance with teams using LEAF for the same AI-assisted task. Outcomes could include undetected error rates, reproducibility, time to correction, quality of claim-evidence alignment, inter-rater assessment of defensibility, and completeness of provenance records. Factor-analytic and experimental work could separately validate the four human-control capacities and the enabling condition of evaluability by design, while multilevel studies could test whether institutional capacity, disciplinary norms, AI autonomy, and epistemic materiality moderate their effects. Evidence that LEAF adds no benefit beyond disclosure, or that stronger oversight fails to improve outcomes at higher materiality, would count against the framework's central propositions.

items.abstract_text: As digital technology becomes more deeply embedded in education, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly present in junior high school students' daily learning. This paper explores the "scaffolding" role of GenAI in students' self-regulated learning (SRL) and its possible influence on enhancing academic self-efficacy. Based on Zimmerman's cyclical phase model of SRL and learning scaffolding theory, the study systematically deduces the human-AI interaction process. The analysis suggests that GenAI acts as planning, monitoring, and reflective feedback scaffolds across the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases, effectively addressing the lack of personalized support in traditional autonomous learning. Furthermore, GenAI assistance contributes to the internalization of academic self-efficacy by accumulating direct mastery experiences and alleviating trial-and-error anxiety. Acknowledging the potential risks of cognitive offloading and academic misconduct associated with GenAI dependency, the paper proposes coping strategies such as cultivating students' critical GenAI literacy and implementing dynamic scaffold fading. This research provides theoretical support and practical guidance for educators to optimize GenAI-assisted self-regulated learning environments.

reading.overview: As digital technology becomes more deeply embedded in education, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly present in junior high school students' daily learning. This paper explores the "scaffolding" role of GenAI in students' self-regulated learning (SRL) and its possible influence on enhancing academic self-efficacy.
reading.interpretation: Based on self-regulated learning and scaffolding theories, this study systematically demonstrates GenAI's cognitive "scaffold" functions across the three phases of forethought, performance, and self-reflection, showing its capacity to bridge the gap left by insufficient personalized support in traditional autonomous learning. Meanwhile, GenAI significantly enhances junior high school students' academic self-efficacy and intrinsic learning motivation by helping them accumulate direct mastery experiences and creating a low-anxiety trial-and-error environment. However, technological empowerment and alienation risks inherently coexist. Faced with the potential hazards of "cognitive offloading" and academic misconduct, the effectiveness of GenAI scaffolds must be grounded in "fading" and "critical usage." Future educational practice should not evade technological intervention, but rather actively guide students away from the trap of technology dependency by deepening human-GenAI collaborative teaching models and cultivating students' digital literacy. This paper's conclusions are mainly based on existing theories and related literature and lack direct empirical testing tailored to junior high school students. Therefore, whether GenAI scaffolds can actually influence junior high school students' academic self-efficacy through pathways such as mastery experiences and learning emotions, as well as the specific intervention effects of different types of GenAI support, still requires further verification through experimental or longitudinal studies.
