items.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences
items.abstract_text: In the era of the attention economy, consumer attention has become an increasingly scarce and valuable marketing resource. With the rapid development of digital platforms and algorithmic recommendation technologies, the way firms acquire and utilize consumer attention has undergone significant changes. This paper uses a conceptual analysis examines how attention-based marketing mechanisms differ across products with different levels of consumer involvement. By integrating insights from attention-based marketing theory and consumer decision-making literature, this paper analyzes two distinct pathways through which attention is transformed into purchase behavior: low-involvement products primarily rely on attention repetition and mental availability to stimulate purchasing, while high-involvement products require deeper information processing and trust formation after attention is captured. The study further discusses how firms can allocate attention resources effectively by adopting broad attention strategies for low-involvement products and deep attention strategies for high-involvement products in the digital marketing environment. This paper contributes to a better understanding of attention allocation in marketing and provides both theoretical and practical implications for firms seeking to improve marketing effectiveness in the attention economy.

items.abstract_text: Against the backdrop of generative AI emerging as a core strategic asset for major powers, the rhetorical tropes of national security and industrial competitiveness are subject to strategic manipulation by divergent domestic actors. The deregulatory camp within the White House invokes industrial competitiveness to roll back security-focused executive orders; the security faction in Congress expands chip export controls in the name of national defense; state-level authorities counter federal overreach through consumer protection mandates; and Silicon Valley deploys a two-pronged lobbying strategy. Taking the 2023-2026 policy pendulum and BIS chip regulations as its analytical case, this paper demonstrates that domestic contestation spills over globally through transmission channels. This has produced a global AI governance landscape defined by fragmentation, hollowed-out soft law processes, and a three-bloc divide across the U.S., the EU, and China, while the shortening commitment half-life of U.S. policy positions has inflated the costs of multilateral cooperation. The study also identifies limited positive spillover effects. In response, the paper puts forward targeted strategies. The conclusion argues that U.S. internal regulatory divisions constitute a mechanism that externalizes domestic political costs as global governance uncertainty. Understanding this mechanism is a prerequisite for reshaping the multilateral AI order.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Education and Learning Reviews
items.abstract_text: Background and Aim: Evidence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary science education remains limited. This systematic review examined students’ conceptual understanding and engagement, teachers’ pedagogical strategies and challenges, and students’ critical thinking and scientific inquiry. Materials and Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, ERIC, Scopus, and Lens.org were searched for peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026. Two authors independently screened 187 unique records (Cohen’s κ = .78), identifying 20 eligible studies. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Framework synthesis integrated findings, informed by Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK). Results: Seven studies assessed AI capabilities rather than classroom implementation. Only two compared learning outcomes across conditions; none employed a randomized controlled design. Student perceptions and engagement were generally positive, whereas learning outcomes were mixed. A chatbot supporting self-regulated learning outperformed a rule-based chatbot, but ChatGPT-4o yielded smaller gains than peer collaboration. Teachers reported concerns regarding content accuracy, assessment reliability, and instructional readiness. Generative AI matched or exceeded student performance on structured examinations but demonstrated lower grading reliability than human assessors. Evidence concerning critical thinking was particularly limited. Richer reasoning was reported with dialogue-oriented tools or teacher guidance, whereas answer-seeking use of general-purpose tools was associated with weaker reasoning. Conclusion: Pedagogical structuring was recurrently associated with productive AI use, although causal inference remains limited. A provisional model warrants empirical testing. items.abstract_text: With AI agents increasingly involved in teamwork, whether AI can substitute human collaboration has become a heated topic in academia. Large-model-driven agents are now capable of participating in team brainstorming, task coordination, and collaborative problem-solving, and knowledge-intensive industries are beginning to form a large number of human-machine hybrid teams. Existing research mostly relies on theoretical reasoning and lacks empirical perceptual data from front-line practitioners. Drawing on a questionnaire survey of 158 employees with cross-industry teamwork experience, this paper explores practitioners' perceptions regarding the substitution of human collaborative behaviors by AI. The results show that AI can only partially substitute procedural and rule-oriented collaborative tasks, whereas social-emotional communication, conflict mediation and value judgment remain irreplaceable human strengths. Position, work experience and AI familiarity jointly shape individual perceptions of the substitution boundary. Most practitioners regard AI as an auxiliary tool rather than a leader of team collaboration. This study provides a practical reference for enterprises applying AI collaboration tools.

reading.interpretation: Focusing on the question of whether artificial intelligence is capable of substituting human collaboration, this paper draws upon questionnaire responses from 158 employees with practical team-coordination experience spanning diverse industries, alongside prior scholarly work, and arrives at three central conclusions: 1. AI agents can only partially substitute human collaboration and cannot achieve complete substitution. 2. In the current real-world workplace, the dominant model is AI as an auxiliary tool with humans holding the core of collaboration. The human-AI relationship manifests more as enhancement and assistance rather than AI replacing human collaboration participants. 3. An individual's perception of the boundary of AI substitution is jointly influenced by job authority and responsibility, workplace work experience, and familiarity with AI technology. This study also has limitations. First, all collected data are respondents' subjective attitudes and views rather than the objective performance observed in real experiments where AI and human groups complete collaborative tasks; subjective cognition may be biased. Second, the total sample size is only 158, which is limited in scale. As the questionnaire was distributed online via Questionnaire Star (Wenjuanxing), there is online sampling bias: some industries and positions are unevenly represented, and not all occupations can be included. Future research should conduct controlled experiments to compensate for the shortcomings of subjective questionnaires and increase the credibility of the study.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Cueing paradigms are commonly used to study the neural mechanisms of visual spatial attention control. In these paradigms, each trial starts with an external cue, which instructs the subject to pay covert attention to a spatial location in anticipation of an impending stimulus (instructed attention). Recent work has introduced a new type of cue which prompts the subject to spontaneously decide which spatial location to attend (willed attention). We studied the neural mechanisms of willed attention control by analyzing fMRI and EEG data recorded at two institutions (UF and UC Davis) using the same willed attention paradigm. The findings include: (1) both instructional cues and the choice cue activated the DAN, (2) the choice cue additionally activated a frontoparietal decision network consisting of dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), anterior insula (AI), anterior prefrontal cortex (APFC), dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), and inferior parietal lobule (IPL), (3) the decision about where to attend can be decoded in frontoparietal decision network in choice trials but not in instructional trials, and (4) EEG alpha oscillation patterns immediately preceding the choice cue, but not the instructional cues, predicted the postcue direction of attention and the frontoparietal decision network activity. Based on these findings we proposed a model of willed attention control suggesting how the direction of visual spatial attention was decided upon in the absence of external instructions.

analysis.discussion: Our results bear out the relationships proposed among the threat of AI, growth mindset, avoidance job crafting, and job burnout. The interaction between the threat of AI and growth mindset was negatively tied to both job burnout and avoidance job crafting, while avoidance job crafting was positively tied to job burnout, and its indirect effect showed up when growth mindset was low and disappeared when it was high. Together these results offer support for the moderated mediation Proceedings of ICFTBA 2026 Symposium: Driving Organizational Strategic Change for Financial Gains DOI: 10.54254/2754-1169/2026.BH38819 The findings carry two implications for theory. The findings identify growth mindset as a moderator in the relationship between threat of AI and job burnout, adding an internal psychological factor to a literature that has focused largely on organizational practices and leadership [5, 6], self-efficacy [7], and organizational self-esteem [8]. They also carry growth mindset research, much of which has been done in classrooms [10], over into how employees react to AI-driven technological change. Growth mindset, it turns out, matters for how employees appraise a threat and how they respond emotionally, and this widens the reach of implicit theory in organizational management. The results also place avoidance job crafting on the map as a behavioral route that connects the threat of AI to job burnout. Earlier studies looked mainly at the direct links between the threat of AI and employees' psychological states and work behavior [5, 16], paying less attention to the behaviors in between. What we find is that employees tend to answer AI-related pressure by shrinking their work roles and doing less in their tasks, and that this response cuts off their access to skill development, social support, and a sense of accomplishment, all things employees need to hold on to as resources. This pattern lines up with worries about the consequences of avoidance job crafting [14], and it suggests that conservation of resources theory can help make sense of how employees respond to AI-related pressure. When organizations bring in AI, they can shore up employees' belief that their skills can grow by giving them real chances to learn and to build AI-related capabilities. A growth mindset, then, should show up in training and development, not just sit there as a filter for choosing talent. Managers can also keep an eye out for signs of avoidance job crafting, such as repeated pullback from tasks, pushing responsibilities onto colleagues, or quietly disengaging. Regular conversations about workload and about what employees are worried about can help sort out what is driving these behaviors and whether the answer lies in more support, a better-designed task, or extra training. Support ought to continue all the way through an AI rollout. Because employees' concerns can touch on job security, skills, and professional identity, organizations can keep channels open for questions and feedback and keep watch on how employees are adjusting, and where burnout starts to show, more targeted support makes sense. 5.3. Research limitations and future research directions These findings need to be read against two limitations. The cross-sectional design is one of them: all variables were measured at a single point in time. The hypotheses lay out a proposed direction of association, but these data cannot pin down causal relationships among the threat of AI, avoidance job crafting, and job burnout. Future work could gather data at several points in time, measuring the predictors, the mediators, and the outcomes separately, so that the proposed sequence can be tested more rigorously. The other limitation is that every measure came from employees' own reports. The confirmatory factor analysis and Harman's single-factor test do speak to the measurement structure and to common method bias, but they cannot rule out subjective or recall bias, and employees may be reluctant to admit to avoidance job crafting because it looks like a negative behavior. Future research Proceedings of ICFTBA 2026 Symposium: Driving Organizational Strategic Change for Financial Gains DOI: 10.54254/2754-1169/2026.BH38819 could pair employees' responses with supervisor ratings or objective performance indicators, so that these relationships are examined through more than one source.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

analysis.methods: This study situates its empirical investigation within an advanced systems development course offered as a core course in the e-commerce major. Due to their characteristics of high cognitive complexity and strong demands for complex problem solving, systems development courses often impose substantial cognitive challenges on learners, particularly during multi-stage decision-making processes involving information integration, design iteration, and technical problem resolution. These challenges may easily result in information processing bottlenecks and cognitive overload among students ( Sweller et al., 2019 ). To address these instructional challenges and align with the TOPCARES competency framework, the course design integrates generative AI agents as cognitive partners throughout the entire systems development process. Specifically, AI agents are embedded across different project stages, including user story generation and requirement clarification in the initial phase, architecture recommendation and UML modeling assistance in the intermediate phase, and code generation, debugging, and iterative diagnosis in the implementation phase. This instructional design, which incorporates intelligent technologies into authentic project workflows, aims to achieve dual objectives of cognitive relief and learning enhancement. More importantly, it provides a realistic educational context for examining the underlying psychological and behavioral transformation mechanisms of human–AI collaboration. In this study, “Agentic AI” refers to the generative AI systems available to students during these course projects, as perceived by the respondents. The learning activities described above involved students using AI for task decomposition, requirement clarification, architecture and UML suggestions, code generation, debugging, and iterative feedback. The survey measures students' perceptions of these capabilities rather than objective system autonomy, general AI competence, or perceived usefulness. The specific platforms and their technical autonomy are not separately manipulated or experimentally verified; therefore, PAIC should be interpreted as a perception-based construct within this instructional context. To ensure the reliability and validity of the research instrument, all core latent constructs were measured using well-established and widely cited scales from international research, with necessary adaptations made to fit the specific context of AI-supported systems development learning. All items were assessed using a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The detailed measurement items are presented in Table 1 . The PAIC items focus on students' perceptions that the AI agent can decompose complex system-development tasks, provide coherent and technically executable solutions, and adjust assistance to the learning context. Thus, PAIC captures perceived agentic capabilities in the course setting rather than general satisfaction with AI or students' own AI competence.
analysis.discussion: Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) and Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), this study examines an integrated model of the associations among Perceived Agentic AI Capability (PAIC), cognitive and motivational variables, and Overall Student Engagement (OSE) in systems development courses. The findings provide evidence on how learners' perceptions of AI capability are related to cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and engagement in complex problem-solving contexts. Because the study used a cross-sectional self-report survey, the proposed relationships should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. First, the findings indicate that perceived agentic AI capability is more strongly associated with lower extraneous cognitive load than with higher academic self-efficacy. Within systems development courses, students may perceive AI agents as providing cognitive assistance through requirement analysis, code generation, error diagnosis, and feedback. This pattern extends research on generative AI education by highlighting the association between perceived AI capability and learners' reports of cognitive demands in complex project-based learning. However, the present design does not establish that AI capability perceptions cause changes in cognitive load. Second, academic self-efficacy shows the larger indirect association linking perceived agentic AI capability with student engagement when compared with the independent indirect association through extraneous cognitive load. This finding is consistent with research suggesting that generative AI may be associated with learner autonomy and confidence in learning processes ( Chan and Hu, 2023 ; Chiu, 2024 ). Third, the results are consistent with a sequential indirect association linking perceived agentic AI capability, extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and student engagement. This pattern is compatible with the proposed “cognitive relief–motivational enhancement” framework, but it does not validate a causal chain because all constructs were measured at one time point. Future longitudinal or experimental research is needed to examine temporal ordering and causal mechanisms. This study examines associations among perceived Agentic AI capability, extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development education. The findings indicate that higher perceived Agentic AI capability is associated with lower extraneous cognitive load and higher academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The bootstrap analysis identifies statistically significant indirect associations, including a sequential indirect association. The results are consistent with the proposed cognitive relief–motivational enhancement framework. The findings extend discussion of AI-supported complex learning beyond technology acceptance and learning performance, while highlighting the need for further longitudinal, experimental, and multi-source research. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the context-specific sample limits generalizability across disciplines, institutions, and cultural contexts. Second, the cross-sectional design and single-source self-reports constrain causal inference and may introduce common method bias. Future research could employ longitudinal or experimental designs and incorporate learning analytics, behavioral indicators, and independently assessed outcomes. Third, OSE is measured using one item for each of the behavioral, cognitive, and emotional dimensions and should therefore be interpreted as an overall self-reported engagement measure rather than a fully validated higher-order reflective construct. Future studies should use multiple items per dimension and further assess its measurement properties. Fourth, the non-significant multi-group results should be interpreted cautiously, as relatively small subgroup sizes may limit statistical power and do not definitively rule out potential moderating effects of prior programming experience or AI usage frequency. Larger and more diverse samples are needed to examine these potential differences. Finally, although the study involves group-based project work, the available data do not permit cluster-adjusted analysis. Future research should record course-section and project-group membership and account for potential within-group dependence.

items.abstract_text: This study investigates the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) among first-year English majors at Hanoi Open University. Using a mixed-methods approach, the research explores how Generative AI tools—such as ChatGPT and Bing Chat—serve as pedagogical "launchpads" rather than intellectual "crutches". Key findings show that AI feedback significantly strengthens the SRL cycle by helping learners decompose goals and providing immediate, non-judgmental diagnostic support. Notably, learners demonstrate high levels of "Technological Self-efficacy" and actively cross-verify AI outputs to mitigate the risk of "hallucinations." The study concludes that AI promotes independent thinking and adaptive help-seeking when positioned as a "debating partner." These results offer vital insights for higher education transitions, suggesting that AI-integrated frameworks can optimize self-learning capacity and cultivate the critical evaluation skills necessary for the Education 4.0 era.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping science education by expanding access to information, supporting adaptive instruction, enabling simulations, and providing timely feedback. This article examines the opportunities, challenges, and implications of AI integration for students’ critical thinking in the digital era. Using a narrative literature review, the study synthesizes foundational scholarship on AI in education, science learning, AI literacy, and critical thinking, alongside recent reviews and international guidance. The synthesis indicates that AI can support critical thinking when it is embedded in inquiry-oriented activities that require students to formulate questions, interpret scientific evidence, compare explanations, identify limitations, and justify conclusions. AI-supported simulations, conversational systems, and feedback tools may make abstract concepts more accessible and provide opportunities for iterative reasoning. However, these benefits are not automatic. Hallucinated information, algorithmic bias, privacy risks, unequal access, academic integrity concerns, and cognitive over-reliance may weaken learning if AI outputs are accepted without verification. The article argues that AI should function as a cognitive partner rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual work. Effective integration therefore requires scientific and AI literacy, teacher mediation, transparent assessment, ethical safeguards, and learning tasks that make reasoning visible. A human-centred approach can help science education use AI to strengthen, rather than displace, independent and evidence-based thinking.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Digital transformation is reshaping academic work through remote and hybrid arrangements, intensified digital connectivity and the expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI). These developments can support flexibility, autonomy and efficiency, but may also intensify workload, erode work–life boundaries and generate demands associated with continuous adaptation, academic integrity and professional responsibility. Existing evidence is fragmented across technostress, remote and hybrid work, digital readiness and AI-enabled academic work, leaving insufficiently explained how technological change becomes embedded in the organisation and experience of academic work and, through this process, relates to wellbeing. This conceptual paper addresses this gap by developing the Digital Academic Work Reconfiguration and Wellbeing (DAWR-W) Framework. The framework was developed through theory synthesis informed by a structured literature foundation of 40 empirical studies and complementary theoretical research. The synthesis distinguishes the characteristics through which digital transformation reconfigures the organisation, boundaries, demands, relationships and professional content of academic work from the psychosocial mechanisms through which academics experience these changes. The resulting framework identifies seven characteristics of digitally transformed academic work and six psychosocial mechanisms involving resource depletion and replenishment, recovery and psychological detachment, perceived control and autonomy, competence and adaptive capacity, relational connection and psychological safety, and professional meaning and identity. Organisational and institutional conditions shape how digital transformation becomes embedded in academic work, while boundary conditions and feedback processes recognise contextual variation and adaptation over time. The central contribution of the DAWR-W Framework is to position work reconfiguration, rather than technology exposure alone, as the occupational process connecting digital transformation with academic employee wellbeing. In doing so, the framework integrates previously fragmented digital-work phenomena within a common explanatory architecture and locates responsibility for sustainable digital academic work across both individual and institutional levels. It provides an occupation-specific foundation for empirical testing, work-design interventions, and digital and AI governance in higher education.

analysis.methods: The literature foundation was assembled through consideration of titles, abstracts and available full texts, guided by the relevance of each study to the conceptual purpose of the paper. Studies were eligible where they: (a) examined academic employees or provided separately identifiable findings concerning academic employees within broader higher-education samples; (b) investigated digitally mediated changes in academic work, including remote or hybrid arrangements, digital demands, digital adaptation or AI-enabled practices; and (c) provided empirical findings relevant to psychological functioning, wellbeing or psychosocial processes associated with these changes. Non-empirical publications, studies involving populations outside the intended occupational context and publications without sufficient relevance to digitally transformed academic work were not retained in the empirical foundation. The resulting literature foundation comprises 40 empirical studies, presented in Supplementary Table S1 . BW undertook the primary literature identification, eligibility assessment and conceptual synthesis, while NIM reviewed the final study selection and conceptual groupings informing the framework. The search strategy, eligibility criteria and final study selection were documented to support transparency in the development of the literature foundation. However, the original records do not provide a complete, independently reproducible account of intermediate screening decisions or exclusion categories. Accordingly, the authors have not retrospectively reconstructed screening counts or exclusion reasons that cannot be verified. The 40 retained empirical studies constitute the documented literature foundation informing the conceptual synthesis, rather than an exhaustive or systematically selected body of evidence. The paper is therefore presented as a conceptual theory synthesis, not a systematic or scoping review. Technological infrastructure establishes the material conditions under which digital academic work is performed. Unreliable systems, poor connectivity and inadequate technical support can increase the effort required to complete routine work. Gabr et al. (2021) , for example, found that poor Wi-Fi and insufficient technical training contributed to technostress among academic staff, while Mdluli and Ngo-Henha (2026) demonstrate the importance of organisational support and digital resources in adaptation to online work. Reliable systems, responsive technical assistance and opportunities to develop competence can therefore reduce avoidable demands associated with technological change. Infrastructure and workload design are interconnected but analytically distinct institutional conditions. Infrastructure concerns the reliability, accessibility and adequacy of the technological and technical resources through which academic work is performed. Workload design concerns how responsibilities, time and resources are formally allocated and recognised. Digital transformation may introduce additional activities involving platform adaptation, assessment redesign, online communication, troubleshooting and AI-related verification. Where these responsibilities become substantive features of academic work without corresponding adjustments to workload allocation or institutional support, the costs of implementation may be absorbed by individual academics. DAWR-W therefore positions infrastructure and workload design as institutional conditions capable of shaping digital work intensification, continuous adaptation and unrecognised digital work, rather than treating their consequences as matters of individual competence alone. The practical value of DAWR-W lies in directing institutional attention toward the organisation of academic work rather than treating technological adoption as an isolated indicator of digital transformation. Universities increasingly depend on digital platforms, remote and hybrid arrangements, and AI-enabled practices to support teaching, assessment, research and administration. However, the operational efficiency of these technologies does not necessarily indicate that their integration into academic work is sustainable. DAWR-W provides a conceptual basis for examining whether technological change redistributes responsibilities, modifies professional discretion, increases expectations of availability or introduces additional demands that are insufficiently recognised within existing institutional arrangements. A first priority is to identify additional or redistributed work. Technologies that improve efficiency in one activity may create learning, troubleshooting, communication, assessment or integrity responsibilities elsewhere. Sifat et al. (2026) , for example, demonstrate how AI adoption can generate additional academic-integrity and investigative work. Where such activities become recurrent, workload arrangements should recognise the time and resources they require. Reliable infrastructure, technical assistance and continuing capability development are equally important because inadequate technological conditions and training can themselves become sources of strain, as Gabr et al. (2021) demonstrate. A second priority concerns implementation and recovery. Academics should have meaningful opportunities to identify workdesign consequences when technologies affect teaching, assessment or professional judgement. Institutions should also establish communication and availability norms that preserve legitimate periods of disengagement. The objective is not to restrict digitally enabled flexibility, but to prevent accessibility from becoming an implicit expectation of continuous responsiveness. A third priority is digital and AI governance. Governance should move beyond acceptable-use statements to clarify decision authority, accountability, academic-integrity procedures, evidentiary standards, escalation routes and responsibility for implementation work. This is particularly important where academics are expected to interpret or enforce rapidly evolving AI-related requirements. Clear governance can reduce the extent to which ethical, procedural and workload uncertainty is transferred to individual academics. Individual competence, coping and adaptability remain important, but they should complement rather than compensate for sustainable work design. DAWR-W therefore supports a prevention-oriented approach in which avoidable work-system demands are addressed first, organisational resources are strengthened, and individual-level support is situated within those wider conditions. The practical question is consequently not only how academics can be helped to adapt to digital transformation, but how digital transformation itself can be designed so that the work to which academics are adapting remains sustainable. The Supplementary material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fsoc.2026.1987590/ full#supplementary-material
analysis.discussion: Digital transformation is reshaping academic work beyond the adoption of new technologies. It changes how responsibilities are organised, when and where work occurs, how relationships are maintained, the discretion academics can exercise and, increasingly, the boundaries of professional expertise and judgement. These changes can create flexibility and autonomy while simultaneously intensifying workload, weakening opportunities for recovery and generating new adaptation, integrity and professional demands. Treating digitalisation primarily as technology exposure obscures these divergent pathways. The DAWR-W Framework addresses this limitation by positioning work reconfiguration as the explanatory layer between digital transformation and academic wellbeing. It distinguishes changes in academic work from the psychosocial mechanisms through which those changes become consequential and locates both within the organisational and institutional conditions that shape digital implementation. In doing so, the framework accommodates positive and impaired functioning, contextual variation and adaptation over time without assuming that digitalisation is inherently beneficial or harmful. The framework also shifts part of the responsibility for digital wellbeing from individual adaptation toward the design and governance of work. Digital competence, coping and adaptability remain important, but their value depends partly on workload, infrastructure, professional discretion, boundary norms, organisational support and governance. Sustainable digital transformation therefore requires attention not only to whether academics can adapt, but also to the conditions of work to which they are being asked to adapt. DAWR-W provides a testable, occupation-specific and technologyagnostic architecture for examining these relationships as digital and AI-enabled academic work continues to evolve. Its central proposition is that the consequences of digital transformation for academic wellbeing cannot be understood adequately by asking how much technology academics use. The more consequential question is how technology changes academic work, how academics experience those changes, and how institutions shape the conditions under which that work is performed.
analysis.limitations: The DAWR-W Framework was developed through conceptual theory synthesis informed by a structured literature foundation rather than a systematic or scoping review. Structured searches of Scopus and Web of Science informed the selection of 40 empirical studies, guided by predefined eligibility criteria and conceptual relevance. The objective was to integrate empirical findings with established theoretical perspectives to develop a coherent explanatory framework, rather than to achieve exhaustive literature coverage or undertake formal evidence grading. Accordingly, DAWR-W represents a theoretically grounded conceptual integration whose proposed relationships require subsequent empirical validation. The empirical foundation also reflects differences in the maturity and methodological characteristics of the available evidence. Although research on technostress, remote working arrangements and workrelated recovery provides a relatively established basis for several proposed relationships, evidence concerning generative AI, professional identity, unrecognised digital labour and institutional AI governance remains comparatively emergent. Consequently, these newer pathways should be regarded as provisional theoretical propositions rather than established empirical relationships. Furthermore, the geographical and institutional diversity of the literature does not necessarily establish the framework's applicability across all higher education contexts. Differences in institutional resources, employment conditions, digital infrastructure and cultural expectations may influence how digital transformation is experienced and how its psychosocial consequences emerge. The predominance of cross-sectional research within several evidence streams also limits conclusions concerning temporal processes, causal direction and the proposed recursive feedback relationships. Longitudinal, comparative and mixed-methods investigations are therefore necessary to assess the framework's explanatory value, contextual applicability and potential refinement.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how knowledge workers make sense of GenAI-enabled co-production, with particular attention to authorship ambiguity and its implications for competence attribution, self-evaluation and meaningful work. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative approach based on in-depth interviews with 32 knowledge workers who work directly with GenAI tools, combining inductive coding with abductive interpretation. We used the Gioia methodology to analyze participants' reported experiences and interpretations of human–AI collaboration, with sensemaking informing the interpretation of emergent themes and aggregate dimensions. Findings The findings identify authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. When GenAI contributes to ideation, analysis, drafting, coding or other knowledge-intensive outputs, workers may find it difficult to distinguish their own contribution from that of the technology. Participants responded to this ambiguity differently. Some reconstructed their expertise around judgment, validation and contextualization and experienced GenAI as extending their professional capability. Others struggled to internalize successful outputs as evidence of their own competence and reported impostor-like experiences and reduced meaningfulness. The findings suggest that experiences of GenAI-enabled co-production depend on whether workers interpret and reconstruct their contribution. Practical implications Managers in comparable knowledge-intensive settings may consider making human judgment visible, clarifying legitimate uses of GenAI and recognizing contributions beyond output speed and quality. Originality/value This study identifies authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. It shows how uncertainty regarding the respective contributions of the worker and GenAI can complicate competence attribution and initiate sensemaking about professional contribution. By explaining how workers' interpretations of authorship ambiguity are associated with divergent identity and meaning outcomes, including enhanced capability, impostor-like experiences and changing meaningfulness, the study extends research on human–AI collaboration beyond its predominant focus on performance and productivity.

In the first stage (Figure 1a ), we train a 2D slice encoder, named SliceMIL, for a binary classification task. The aim is to produce a discrim-inative representation of input slices using a gated attention pooling mechanism [14] , which also provides an attention map focusing on the tampered region. Once SliceMIL is trained, it is frozen and used as the slice encoder. In the second stage (Figure 1b ), we train the entire HexMIL architecture: an input volume of K slices is decomposed into individual slices, each of which is processed by the SliceMIL encoder. The resulting representations are combined using a novel independent gated attention pooling mechanism, which generates a 1D attention vector highlighting the most likely tampered slices. This resulting volume-level feature vector is then processed by a classification head designed to determine whether the volume contains a tampered sub-volume. Since the model is trained on volumes of length K, and in real-world scenarios a CT scan may consist of a larger number K ′ of slices, HexMIL divides the entire volume into T sub-volumes of length K and assigns a probability to each sub-volume. Future work must assess the robustness of the framework against multi-center data and variations in CT acquisition protocols, which are known to introduce significant domain shifts in medical imaging tasks.

analysis.methods: The workflow of HexMIL is depicted in Figure 1 . The framework is trained in two sequential stages. In the first stage (Figure 1a ), we train a 2D slice encoder, named SliceMIL, for a binary classification task. The aim is to produce a discrim-inative representation of input slices using a gated attention pooling mechanism [14] , which also provides an attention map focusing on the tampered region. Once SliceMIL is trained, it is frozen and used as the slice encoder. In the second stage (Figure 1b ), we train the entire HexMIL architecture: an input volume of K slices is decomposed into individual slices, each of which is processed by the SliceMIL encoder. The resulting representations are combined using a novel independent gated attention pooling mechanism, which generates a 1D attention vector highlighting the most likely tampered slices. This resulting volume-level feature vector is then processed by a classification head designed to determine whether the volume contains a tampered sub-volume. Figure 1c illustrates the inference process. Since the model is trained on volumes of length K, and in real-world scenarios a CT scan may consist of a larger number K ′ of slices, HexMIL divides the entire volume into T sub-volumes of length K and assigns a probability to each sub-volume. The final probability assigned to the input volume is given by the maximum of these probabilities. Finally, the two attention maps are combined, yielding a 3D attention volume. In the sections below, we provide a detailed problem formulation and a description of our method.
analysis.results: We evaluate HexMIL's capabilities in generalization for both classification and localization of the AI-manipulated volume. We train the model using the manipulated volumes from a single architecture present in the M3DSynth [8] and CT-GAN [7] datasets as fake parts in each scenario, while testing with all the others excluded. Out-of-domain classification across generators. Table 1 shows the results obtained by HexMIL and all the baselines in the various out-of-domain classification scenarios. The results show a clear hierarchy but also a significant structure among the strongest baselines. HexMIL achieves the best overall classification performance with an AUC of 92.0 and an F1 score of 90.2, dominates all transfer directions in terms of AUC and nearly all for F1, which indicates robust crossgenerator generalization rather than gains limited to a few favorable pairs. Relative to the strongest baseline averages, which reach 82.9 AUC and 80.8 F1, this translates to absolute increases of +9.1 and +9.4 (approximately +10.9% and +11.6% relative improvement, respectively). At the same time, baselines show distinct strengths: ManTraNet leads the competitors in average AUC with 82.9, but its significantly lower average F1 of 73.7 suggests a strong ranking ability offset by weak calibration under distribution shifts. D 3 attains the second-highest average AUC of 80.7, yet its effectiveness varies across transfer directions, revealing a residual reliance on specific generative artifacts. NPR proves competitive in transfers from diffusion models but remains inconsistent in the most challenging cross-domain scenarios. Also specialized forensic detectors, such as TruFor and FreqNet, which use noise-sensitive fingerprints or high-frequency representations and have an average AUC score of 80.3 and 62.9, also have trouble when appearance and forensic statistics change at the same time across unseen generators. The results also show that single-level attention is not enough. Models like ResNet50-ABMIL and ViT-ABMIL do not have a second hierarchical stage and only use gated attention at the slice level. As a result, they perform much worse, with an average AUC close to 65. Finally, 3D CNNs (R3D-18, DenseNet121-3D) and Video Transformers (ViViT) underperform HexMIL by a large margin, reaching at most 72.9% AUC. This gap stems from the spatial sparsity of CT manipulations, as tampered sub-volumes occupy only a small fraction of the scan. While standard voxel-based architectures fail to isolate such sparse signals from healthy background tissue, HexMIL's hierarchical attention progressively focuses on the most discriminative patches and slices. Out-of-domain localization results. The localization results in Table 2 are particularly relevant because out-of-domain (ood) localization is generally more fragile compared to ood classification. Even in this context, HexMIL, despite not being trained in the localization of the manipulated volume within CT scans, achieves the best average ood localization performance, with a Intersection-over-Union (IoU) 42.4 and a Pointing Game (PG) 70.6, and leads in most transfer cells, while the stronger baselines optimize different and often complementary behaviors. MVSS-Net and ManTraNet are almost equal in average IoU (38.1 vs. 38.0), but ManTraNet records the highest baseline PG of 67.5, consistent with sharper anomaly peaks; TruFor remains competitive with an average of 36.6 IoU and 65.3 PG, performing strongly in specific diffusion-to-GAN transfers yet degrading elsewhere due to its sensitivity to joint changes in appearance and forensic residual statistics. Taken together, these results suggest that previous methods are typically strong along one axis at a time (classification, calibration, overlap, or pointing), while HexMIL is consistently strong across all axes. A plausible explanation is architectural: instead of a 2D slice-level evaluation followed by a late aggregation, HexMIL performs a 3D hierarchical aggregation of evidence with ante-hoc attention, preserving the inter-slice context and producing localization maps that are directly linked to the prediction mechanism.
analysis.discussion: We presented HexMIL, a hierarchical MIL framework that jointly addresses out-of-domain generalization and ante-hoc 3D spatial attribution for CT manipulation detection, trained with binary volume-level labels only. Across a rigorous crossgenerator generalization protocol, HexMIL outperforms all baselines by +9.1 AUC and +9.4 F1 in classification and achieves the best average IoU and PG in localization without any spatial supervision. Limitations. Fixed-length windowing may bisect manipulation regions in long scans; an overlapping or adaptive strategy could mitigate this. Generalization to anatomical sites beyond the thorax and to other modalities (e.g., MRI) remains to be verified; the underlying data originates from the LIDC-IDRI collection. items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Natural language processing and AI models are increasingly used to extract emotional signals from textual data; however, systematic validation of different computational paradigms in emotionally complex relational contexts remains limited. Such approaches may contribute to digital health research, particularly in the fields of digital mental health and couples therapy, where understanding emotional expressions within romantic relationships is especially relevant. Objective This study aimed to compare a lexicon-based approach (NRC Emotion Lexicon) and a transformer-based model (Pysentimiento) in detecting affective patterns within spontaneous romantic relationship narratives and to evaluate their criterion-related associations with a theory-driven measure of relational well-being. Methods In this cross-sectional exploratory study, 112 Spanish adults completed the Couple Flourishing Measure (CFM) and provided an open-ended description of their romantic relationship. Narratives were analyzed using both computational approaches to generate emotion and sentiment indices. Pearson correlations were computed between model outputs and CFM scores. Steiger Z tests were conducted to compare dependent correlations across models. Results Both approaches showed significant associations with couple flourishing, although the transformer-based model yielded stronger correlations for several affective dimensions, particularly positive sentiment ( r =0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.76) and negative sentiment ( r =−0.74, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.65). The lexicon-based approach showed smaller associations, primarily for negative emotions. Steiger Z tests identified significant between-model differences for disgust ( P =.04), joy ( P =.01), sadness ( P =.004), surprise ( P =.03), and positive and negative sentiment (both P <.001), but not for anger or fear. Conclusions In this sample, Pysentimiento showed stronger associations with couple flourishing than the NRC Emotion Lexicon across several affective dimensions, although differences were not consistent across all categories. These findings support the value of theory-driven external criteria for evaluating computational emotion detection in relational narratives and underscore the importance of context-sensitive interpretation when applying AI tools in psychologically sensitive domains. These findings also highlight the potential relevance of computational emotion analysis for digital health research, particularly in digital mental health and couples therapy research, although further validation in clinical settings is needed before clinical implementation.

analysis.methods: A total of 112 adults residing in Spain participated in this exploratory cross-sectional study. Participants were recruited through nonprobability convenience sampling, given the exploratory and methodological focus of the research. All participants had been in a romantic relationship for at least 6 months at the time of the study. No a priori sample size calculation was performed due to the exploratory nature of the study. An ad hoc questionnaire was designed to collect psychosexual and sociodemographic information from the participants. This instrument allowed us to obtain data on age, place of residence during the study, gender, duration of the couple’s relationship, and sexual orientation according to Kinsey et al [ 35 ]. In this study, we used the version validated in Spain by Saavedra-Roa et al [ 36 , 37 ]. It is a 16-item unidimensional instrument that is answered individually and assesses couple flourishing on a 7-point visual analog Likert scale, where 1=distressed relationship, 4=satisfied relationship, and 7=flourishing relationship. An example item is “Quality time with my partner alone is...,” where 1=distressed, 4=satisfied, and 7=flourishing. The scores ranged from 16 to 112, with higher scores indicating higher levels of couple flourishing. This instrument has been shown to have high reliability (α=.94), which was α=.95 for this study. A single open-ended question was used to capture the participants’ natural discursive responses. Individuals were asked to answer the question “How would you describe your couple relationship?” This prompt was chosen to encourage spontaneous and emotionally rich descriptions of the relationship, thus providing linguistic material suitable for subsequent computational emotion analysis. The narratives generated through this item served as the textual dataset for both NLP analyses (refer to the Data Analysis section). All participants completed an online survey administered via Qualtrics, which included sociodemographic and psychosexual information, the CFM, and an open-ended question regarding their perceptions of their affective-sexual relationship. The sampling was conducted between June 2023 and June 2024. Recruitment was conducted primarily through dissemination on social media platforms. Participants accessed the study via a link, provided digital informed consent, and completed the survey anonymously. The average response time of the battery was 28.08 minutes. All the narratives obtained from the open-ended question were processed in Spanish. Text processing differed between the 2 NLP approaches. For the lexicon-based approach, narratives were tokenized into words for comparison with lexicon entries, whereas the transformer-based approach was applied to the original, unprocessed responses. Subsequently, 2 NLP approaches were used to extract affective information from the narratives: a model based on the transformer architecture (Pysentimiento) and a lexicon-based model (NRC Emotion Lexicon, multilingual version 2022). Indicators of emotional polarity (ie, positive, negative, and neutral) and 6 basic emotions (ie, joy, sadness, anger, disgust, fear, and surprise) were obtained using Pysentimiento [ 15 - 17 ], an open-source model implemented in Python and based on the transformer architecture with support for Spanish-language text. For each narrative, the tool generated probabilistic scores ranging from 0 to 1, which estimated the presence of each emotion or sentiment dimension. Pysentimiento was applied to each participant’s complete, unprocessed response, and the resulting scores were retained at the participant level. Narratives were also analyzed using the Spanish version of the NRC Emotion Lexicon [ 12 ], a lexical resource that associates more than 14,000 lemmas with 8 emotions (ie, anger, fear, anticipation, trust, surprise, sadness, joy, and disgust) and 2 sentiment categories (ie, positive and negative). Each narrative was processed using the syuzhet package in R (version 4.4.1; R Foundation for Statistical Computing) [ 38 ], with words matched against lexicon entries. Lexicon matches were aggregated within each complete response to obtain participant-level scores for the 8 emotions and 2 sentiment categories. The unit of analysis was the complete open-ended response of each participant (n=112), rather than individual words or sentences. This unit was selected because the CFM was assessed at the participant level and the open-ended question elicited an overall description of the romantic relationship. Moreover, the relatively short narratives made further subdivision into sentences less appropriate for the study objectives. Correlations between the total scores on the CFM and the emotional and sentiment indices generated by both NLP models were examined using Pearson correlation coefficients ( r ). For each participant, the scores generated by both models were matched with their corresponding CFM total score, which served as a common external criterion for evaluating the associations between the affective indices and relationship flourishing. To determine whether the correlations obtained using Pysentimiento differed significantly from those obtained using the NRC Emotion Lexicon, Steiger Z tests for dependent correlations were performed for the emotion and sentiment categories shared by both models. This test was selected because the correlations were derived from the same sample and shared the CFM score as a common variable, while accounting for the correlation between the corresponding model-derived indices. Categories available in only 1 model were not included in these comparisons. The 95% CIs were estimated for the reported effects. Additionally, an exploratory ordinary least squares linear regression was performed to examine the trend in CFM total scores across dominant sentiment categories. Dominant sentiment was defined as the category with the highest predicted probability from Pysentimiento, with categories coded as ordered levels (1=negative, 2=neutral, and 3=positive). Missing data were handled using available-case analysis. All analyses were carried out using R [ 39 ] in the R Studio environment (version 2023.06.1+524; Posit PBC) [ 40 ]. Transformer models may complement traditional self-report measures and offer alternative ways to study affective processes using natural discourse data, thus expanding theoretical and methodological possibilities in this field [ 27 , 28 ]. The comparison suggests that different NLP approaches may vary in their suitability for relational contexts, with contextual language processing representing a potentially relevant methodological advantage when examining affective meanings in intimate narratives. In this context, these findings are particularly relevant to future research on clinical processes in couples therapy. Automated discourse analysis may provide additional information about affective signals that emerge spontaneously in interactions, which have traditionally been difficult to capture through manual coding or retrospective self-report measures [ 27 ]. Transformer-based models could be investigated for their potential to identify patterns of emotional communication associated with relational satisfaction or distress; detect moment-to-moment affective shifts during the process (ie, process-level markers); evaluate mechanisms of change, such as dyadic regulation, emotional responsiveness, or the emergence of shared narratives; and monitor therapeutic progress over time, potentially complementing traditional clinical assessments with context-sensitive indicators. However, these applications require direct empirical validation in therapeutic settings. These possibilities are consistent with recent advancements in psychotherapy-oriented NLP, in which sentiment-analysis models have been used to examine clients’ emotional expression across sessions [ 29 ] and to predict clinically relevant variables such as symptom severity [ 30 ]. Such potential applications are also consistent with findings by Steinbrenner et al [ 8 ], who demonstrated that NLP applied to psychotherapy transcripts could predict anxiety severity, suggesting possible applications for monitoring in therapeutic contexts. analysis.limitations: This study had several limitations. First, the sample consisted exclusively of participants residing in Spain, which limits the generalizability of the findings to other linguistic and cultural contexts. Second, although the transformer model showed stronger associations with CFM scores across several affective dimensions, these associations varied across emotion categories, indicating that the observed advantages were not uniform. This variability is consistent with challenges in computational emotion analysis previously discussed in the NLP literature [ 6 ]. Third, the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causal relationships between emotional discourse patterns and relational well-being. Fourth, the comparison was limited to 1 lexicon-based approach and 1 transformer-based model, restricting the generalizability of the findings to other tools within these computational paradigms. Fifth, multiple statistical comparisons were conducted without adjustment for multiple testing, increasing the possibility of type I errors. Therefore, individual statistically significant findings should be interpreted cautiously and require replication in independent samples. Finally, the analysis relied on a single open-ended narrative per participant and used CFM scores as an external criterion rather than independently annotated emotion labels. Consequently, the findings provide evidence of criterion-related associations but do not establish the accuracy of emotion classification. Furthermore, the use of nonprobability convenience sampling and self-reported data may have introduced selection and response biases, which should be considered when interpreting the findings. Future research should extend the comparison to other languages, populations, and various types of sexual-affective relationships, as well as explore the integration of transformer models with qualitative methodologies or longitudinal designs to examine the evolution of emotional discourse in couples over time and assess the temporal reliability of model-derived indices. It would also be relevant to evaluate the use of these tools in clinical or intervention contexts, carefully considering ethical aspects related to privacy and the analysis of sensitive narratives. Furthermore, future research should evaluate how these models can be integrated into the observational analysis of therapeutic sessions to study the interactional microprocesses and mechanisms of change throughout treatment.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background AI is increasingly embedded in health care and digital health applications, shaping clinical processes as well as how patients access information and participate in care. Research on bias in medical AI has largely focused on technical and performance-related disparities. Less attention has been paid to how such biases may affect patients’ access, understanding, trust, and opportunities for meaningful involvement in care. Objective This scoping review aimed to map how studies of bias in medical AI describe patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment and the digital divide and to identify gaps across technical, social, structural, and patient-centered perspectives. Methods This scoping review followed JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute) methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost databases were searched in August 2025 and supplemented by Google Scholar searches. Peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 onward were included if they addressed bias in medical AI and described patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment or digital inequality. Data charting focused on AI application types, bias dimensions, patient empowerment domains, digital divide–related factors, intersectionality, and debiasing strategies. Findings were synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results The search identified 497 records, of which 22 studies met the inclusion criteria. Bias was represented as a multidimensional sociotechnical phenomenon, with social bias identified most frequently (21/22 studies), followed by algorithmic bias (16/22 studies), structural bias (14/22 studies), and design-related bias (12/22 studies). Patient empowerment was most frequently addressed through involvement in care (n=13), followed by health literacy (n=9) and trust and assurance (n=7), whereas broader psychosocial and everyday-life domains were addressed less frequently. Digital divide–related factors were identified in 19 of the 22 studies, with digital literacy and usability barriers reported most frequently. Seven studies considered 2 or more social or structural dimensions of disadvantage. Although many studies discussed approaches that could mitigate bias-related barriers, explicit empirical evaluation of debiasing strategies in relation to patient empowerment or digital equity was largely absent. Conclusions Patient-related consequences of bias in medical AI extend beyond algorithmic performance and are reflected in access, understanding, trust, and involvement in care. Broader empowerment dimensions, multidimensional disadvantage, and empirically evaluated mitigation strategies remain comparatively underexplored.

analysis.methods: This scoping review was conducted to systematically identify, map, and synthesize the existing literature on bias in medical AI applications in health care, with a particular focus on patient empowerment and the digital divide. Given the exploratory nature of the research question and the conceptual heterogeneity of the field, a scoping review methodology was considered appropriate. The review was conducted in accordance with the JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute) methodology for scoping reviews and is reported following the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews). The completed PRISMA-ScR checklist is provided in Checklist 1 . As there is currently no dedicated registry for scoping reviews comparable to PROSPERO (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews) for systematic reviews, the review protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) to ensure transparency and reproducibility and is available online [ 38 ] The research question and eligibility criteria were structured using the PCC (population-concept-context) framework, as recommended for scoping reviews by the JBI. Regarding population (P), the population of interest includes individuals or population groups who may be affected by bias in the context of medical AI applications. Particular attention was given to marginalized or intersectionally disadvantaged groups, including but not limited to individuals differentiated by age, gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, disability, language proficiency, or migration background. Regarding concept (C), the core concept of this review comprises different forms of bias associated with the use of medical AI, including technical, algorithmic, social, structural, and intersectional biases. In addition, the review examines how these bias types are described in relation to patient empowerment and the digital divide. Regarding the context (C), the context included applications of medical AI across the patient journey, such as clinical decision support systems (CDSS), diagnostic tools, symptom checkers, conversational agents, LLMs, remote monitoring systems, and AI-based patient education tools. No restrictions were placed on geographic regions or health care systems. Eligibility was determined to be aligned with the PCC framework. An overview of all inclusion and exclusion criteria is provided in Table 1 . Studies were considered eligible when they addressed patient-related implications of bias in medical AI either explicitly or implicitly. Explicit relevance included direct discussion of patient empowerment, participation, or digital inclusion, whereas implicit relevance referred to studies describing patient-facing consequences such as access barriers, usability challenges, differential comprehension, trust, or unequal benefit from AI-supported health care. Purely technical studies without discussion of patient-related, ethical, or social implications were excluded. A structured literature search was conducted across the following databases in August 2025 to capture relevant medical, social science, and technical literature: PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost (including MEDLINE; APA PsychInfo; APA PsycArticles; ERIC; CINAHL Ultimate; Academic Search Elite; and additional social science and information science databases). Google Scholar was used as a supplementary source to identify additional relevant publications. The selection of databases was guided by the interdisciplinary scope of the review, aiming to capture biomedical, psychological, and social sciences perspectives on medical AI, bias, and patient-related outcomes. Together, PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost databases provide broad coverage of clinical, behavioral, and health services research relevant to the study objectives. The search strategy was developed based on an initial exploratory search and iteratively refined. Search terms were adapted to the specific syntax of each database ( Multimedia Appendix 1 ). The core search strategy combined terms related to medical AI, bias and equity, patient empowerment, and used Boolean operators: (“artificial intelligence” OR “machine learning” OR “natural language processing” OR “deep learning” OR “clinical decision support” OR “healthcare AI” OR “large language model*” OR LLM* OR ehealth OR “e-health” OR telehealth OR “tele-health”) (bias* OR inequit* OR inequal* OR discriminat* OR fair* OR intersectional*) (“patient empowerment” OR “shared decision*” OR “patient participation” OR “patient inclusion” OR “patient engagement” OR “patient involvement”) The search strategy was designed around the intersection of medical AI, bias and equity, and patient-related implications. Given the conceptual breadth and interdisciplinary nature of the topic, the strategy was iteratively refined during pilot searching to improve sensitivity to studies addressing patient-related consequences of bias. Limitations in the breadth of the search, including the databases covered and the potential omission of relevant studies using different terminology, are acknowledged in the Limitations section. The initial search strategy included an explicit digital divide component. During pilot searching, this approach was found to be overly restrictive and risked excluding studies in which digital divide-related aspects were addressed implicitly rather than as a primary analytical category. The search strategy was therefore iteratively refined to better capture the contextual breadth of the field. All records identified in the initial search were retained for screening and synthesis. Further details regarding these adaptations are provided in the section “Deviations From the Registered Protocol.” The reporting of the literature search was guided by the PRISMA-S (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses literature search extension) for search reporting. Full search strategies for all databases, including Boolean operators, database-specific syntax adaptations, and search limits, are provided in Multimedia Appendix 1 to enhance transparency and reproducibility. All identified records were imported into Rayyan (Rayyan Systems, Inc) [ 39 ] for screening and management. Duplicate records were removed before screening. Title and abstract screening were conducted independently by 2 reviewers using a blinded screening approach. Each reviewer assessed all records against the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus. Full-text screening was subsequently performed for all records deemed potentially eligible based on title and abstract screening, following the same independent and consensus-based procedure. For all included studies ( Multimedia Appendix 2 ), data were charted manually using a standardized data charting form developed iteratively by the research team ( Multimedia Appendix 3 ). Our literature search identified a total of 497 records, including 243 records from PubMed/MEDLINE and 254 records from EBSCOHost (see the PRISMA [Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses] flow diagram, Figure 1 ). In total, 358 records were then screened at the title and abstract level, where 250 records were excluded. Further, 233 records were excluded because they did not focus on patients (n=137) or did not involve the use of AI-based tools in health care contexts (n=96). A total of 107 records were sought for full-text retrieval, of which 4 could not be retrieved. Consequently, 103 full-text papers were assessed for eligibility. During full-text screening, 82 papers were excluded, primarily because the lack of patient focus became evident during full-text review (n=52), or the missing involvement of medical AI applications (n=29) became evident. Overall, 22 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final synthesis [ 7 , 12 , 19 - 21 , 45 - 61 ]. Table 3 shows an overview of the included studies’ characteristics. The included publications were predominantly published between 2016 and 2025, reflecting the recent and rapidly evolving nature of research on medical AI, bias, and patient-related outcomes. Studies originated mainly from North America, Europe, and Asia, with the United States (8/22, 36.4%) and European countries (8/22, 36.4%) most frequently represented, followed by Asian countries (5/22, 22.7%) and Canada (1/22, 4.5%). Regarding study design, the literature comprised a heterogeneous mix of quantitative (n=12), qualitative (n=5), and mixed methods studies (n=4), alongside one systematic review. Quantitative designs most commonly included observational cohort studies, cross-sectional surveys, randomized controlled trials, and feasibility or usability evaluations, while qualitative approaches primarily involved interviews, focus groups, and exploratory design studies. This diversity reflects the exploratory and interdisciplinary nature of research at the intersection of medical AI, bias, and patient-related outcomes. A wide range of medical AI tools was examined across the included studies ( Table 3 ). The most frequently represented application type was conversational agents or chatbots (7/22, 31.8%), followed by LLM-based applications (4/22, 18.2%), and decision support AI (3/22, 13.6%). Diagnostic AI, robotic systems, and other ML- or NLP-based applications were each represented in 2 studies (2/22, 9.1%). One study examined a surveillance system (1/22, 4.5%), while 1 study investigated patient and public perceptions of medical AI without focusing on a specific AI tool (1/22, 4.5%). Across studies, medical AI tools were deployed for a variety of clinical aims ( Table 3 ). The most common application was clinical decision support, including assessment, screening, and diagnostic support (8/22, 36.4%). Other frequently reported aims included long-term patient support and self-management (5/22, 22.7%), patient education and health information (4/22, 18.2%), and medical history collection or symptom monitoring (4/22, 18.2%). Only 1 study focused on mental health-related medical AI applications. Several studies included mixed stakeholder samples, incorporating perspectives from patients, clinicians, or members of the general public (4/22, 18.2%). Only 1 study focused explicitly on a pediatric population.
