The findings indicate that bias was predominantly represented as a multidimensional sociotechnical phenomenon rather than as a purely technical problem. Social bias was the most frequently identified category, followed by algorithmic, structural, and design-related bias, with several bias dimensions frequently co-occurring within individual studies and across different medical AI application types. This pattern suggests that patient-related consequences of bias cannot be understood solely in terms of algorithmic performance but also need to be considered in relation to design choices, social conditions, and the contexts in which AI systems are implemented. Patient empowerment was addressed across the evidence base in heterogeneous ways. Involvement in Care was the most frequently represented empowerment domain, followed by health literacy and trust and assurance, whereas broader psychosocial and everyday-life dimensions, including social support, perceived health, managing daily life, and illness perceptions and experiences, were less frequently represented. Digital divide-related factors were identified in 19 of the 22 studies, with digital literacy and usability barriers emerging most prominently. Intersectional or multidimensional dimensions of disadvantage were considered in 7 studies but remained comparatively uncommon. Similarly, while many studies discussed potential approaches to reducing bias-related barriers, explicit empirical evaluation of debiasing strategies in relation to patient empowerment or digital equity was largely absent. Taken together, these findings show that current research recognizes many of the social and patient-related implications of bias in medical AI, but these dimensions are not yet addressed with equal conceptual or methodological depth. The evidence base is particularly concentrated on participation, information-related dimensions of empowerment, trust, and usability, while broader dimensions of empowerment, intersectional disadvantage, and empirically evaluated bias mitigation remain less developed. By integrating bias, patient empowerment, and digital equity within a single analytical perspective, this review therefore highlights both the multidimensional nature of bias in medical AI and important gaps in how its patient-related consequences are currently conceptualized and evaluated. Consistent with recent reviews on bias in medical LLMs and health care AI more broadly, the reviewed studies suggest that bias in medical AI cannot be understood solely as a technical performance issue [ 34 , 35 ]. Existing reviews have primarily emphasized demographic performance disparities, data imbalance, algorithmic fairness, and mitigation strategies [ 34 , 35 , 62 ]. However, our synthesis extends this perspective by showing how bias becomes relevant for patient empowerment through design choices, usability assumptions, language accessibility, trust, and structural conditions of deployment. Across the included studies, bias emerged across multiple sociotechnical layers throughout the AI lifecycle, including data practices, algorithmic design, user interfaces, institutional contexts, and human-AI interaction [ 27 , 28 , 41 ]. While algorithmic biases, including concerns related to sampling and unequal performance across demographic groups, were frequently discussed in the included studies [ 45 , 57 , 61 ], our results highlight the relevance of design and structural bias for patient empowerment. This finding is in line with other research in this area emphasizing how interface design, usability assumptions, and default interaction patterns may privilege certain users while disadvantaging others [ 41 , 43 ]. In this scoping review, design bias was identified across several patient-facing medical AI application types [ 19 , 53 , 55 ]. These systems often assumed a baseline level of digital literacy, language proficiency, and physical or cognitive ability, thereby potentially reproducing existing inequities rather than mitigating them. As argued by Leslie [ 27 ] and Cross et al [ 3 ], such biases are not incidental but reflect deeper structural conditions in which AI systems are developed and deployed. An important contribution of this scoping review is the attempt to clearly distinguish patient empowerment as an explicit research goal from empowerment-related aspects that emerge as a by-product of AI implementation. Because the inclusion criteria encompassed both explicit and implicit relevance to patient empowerment, empowerment was not necessarily conceptualized or operationalized as a distinct outcome across the included studies. Instead, empowerment-related aspects were frequently reflected in indicators such as engagement, satisfaction, trust, or technology acceptance. This pattern mirrors concerns raised in previous work on patient empowerment, which has shown that the concept is frequently used inconsistently and measured with heterogeneous instruments [ 17 , 22 , 23 , 63 ]. The literature reviewed in this study suggests that this conceptual ambiguity persists in medical AI research, where empowerment is often inferred from engagement, satisfaction, trust, usability, or information access rather than examined as a multidimensional construct involving knowledge, control, participation, and evaluative capacity, as originally described by Funnell et al [ 26 ]. By explicitly distinguishing between empowerment as a conceptual condition and empowerment-related domains as descriptive categories, this review advances prior work that has primarily documented definitional heterogeneity. Our findings indicate that medical AI research frequently approaches empowerment through engagement, information provision, or technology acceptance [ 17 , 63 ]. Without sufficient support for patient control and evaluative capacity [ 26 ], such interventions may result in a form of “thin” or superficial empowerment that may coexist with persistent inequities. By applying the thematic categorization proposed by Mora et al [ 23 ], our analysis makes visible which dimensions of patient empowerment are prioritized in current medical AI research and which are less frequently represented. Involvement in Care was the most frequently represented domain, followed by health literacy and trust and assurance. These domains were particularly evident in AI-based patient education [ 12 , 21 ], decision support systems [ 57 ], and LLM-based information tools [ 50 ]. These findings align with the broader digital health literature, which has long emphasized information access and shared decision-making as core components of patient empowerment [ 63 ]. analysis.limitations: This scoping review has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, the literature included was highly heterogeneous with respect to study designs, AI applications, clinical contexts, and reported outcomes. This heterogeneity limited the comparability of findings and precluded quantitative synthesis or robust cross-study comparisons, particularly regarding empowerment-related outcomes. Second, no formal methodological quality appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies was conducted. Such an assessment was not part of the mapping-oriented objective of this scoping review, which focused on conceptualizations, thematic patterns, and evidence gaps, rather than on estimating intervention effectiveness or the certainty of evidence. Consequently, the findings should be interpreted as descriptive patterns within the identified evidence base rather than as evidence of causal effects or effectiveness. Third, although the search strategy was iteratively refined in line with the mapping-oriented purpose of the review, it may not have captured all potentially relevant literature. The strategy prioritized studies at the intersection of medical AI, bias, and patient-related implications, and relevant studies addressing equity, digital inclusion, or empowerment only indirectly may therefore have been missed. In addition, the search focused primarily on biomedical, psychological, and health services databases and did not include major multidisciplinary and engineering-oriented sources such as IEEE Xplore, Scopus, or Web of Science. Consequently, the resulting evidence map should be interpreted as a structured mapping of the identified patient-centered literature rather than as evidence that all potentially relevant research on bias in medical AI has been captured. Finally, there is a risk of overinterpreting patient empowerment in studies where empowerment-related aspects were inferred indirectly from measures such as technology acceptance, satisfaction, or engagement. Increased use of or positive attitudes toward medical AI do not necessarily translate into meaningful empowerment, particularly when patients’ control, resources, understanding, or evaluative capacities are not explicitly assessed. The empowerment-related findings should therefore be interpreted as thematic mapping of potentially relevant dimensions rather than as evidence that the included AI applications produced patient empowerment.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Watershed environmental governance increasingly combines dense sensing infrastructure with institutions whose attention, authority, and coordination capacity remain limited. We develop the cognitive orchestration layer as a theory-building concept for examining how large language model (LLM)-based agents may connect sensing, assessment, decision advice, institutional response, and feedback without displacing domain models or public authority. Methods The Agentic Framework for Watershed Governance (AFWG) specifies three enabling pathways, three institutional interfaces, and four propositions. A purposively selected set of eight publicly documented cases is used to illustrate functional configurations, source limitations, and research gaps; it is not a systematic review or empirical evaluation. Results The cases document sensing, assessment, and decision-support functions, but do not establish improved decision quality, sustained institutional use, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO is retained as an adjacent-domain design illustration, not an existence proof of full-loop closure: human authorization remains necessary, and its reported performance has not been independently replicated. Discussion Transfer to watershed governance is plausible only where domain models remain authoritative, outputs carry provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain authority to authorize consequential actions, and institutional audit and failure handling are built into deployment. AFWG therefore offers a bounded conceptual framework and a falsifiable research agenda, rather than a claim that agents have already closed the watershed response loop.

It is not described as an existence proof of full-loop closure. The peer-reviewed paper describes a hierarchical multi-agent system integrated with Zhejiang's joint flood-and-typhoon command arrangements, spanning provincial departments and lower-level emergency-management organizations (Wang et al., 2026) . The architecture includes situation awareness, task decomposition, domain-specialist agents, provenance links, confidence communication, cross-agent validation, and human review. These features make the case useful for refining AFWG's institutional interfaces. The MAESTRO performance figures are author-reported/ developer-assessed results, not independently replicated findings (Wang et al., 2026) . The study reports 98% agreement with expert alert levels across 100 typhoon scenarios; this is warninglevel agreement, not environmental prediction accuracy. It also reports a reduction in decision latency of more than 85%, not an independently verified reduction in public-authority response time. analysis.methods: MAESTRO is retained because it makes authorization, provenance, confidence, multi-agent coordination, and institutional embedding unusually explicit. It is not described as an existence proof of full-loop closure. The peer-reviewed paper describes a hierarchical multi-agent system integrated with Zhejiang's joint flood-and-typhoon command arrangements, spanning provincial departments and lower-level emergency-management organizations (Wang et al., 2026) . The architecture includes situation awareness, task decomposition, domain-specialist agents, provenance links, confidence communication, cross-agent validation, and human review. These features make the case useful for refining AFWG's institutional interfaces. The MAESTRO performance figures are author-reported/ developer-assessed results, not independently replicated findings (Wang et al., 2026) . The study reports 98% agreement with expert alert levels across 100 typhoon scenarios; this is warninglevel agreement, not environmental prediction accuracy. It also reports a reduction in decision latency of more than 85%, not an independently verified reduction in public-authority response time. Supplementary Section S5.4 and Supplementary Table S13 report r = 0.9975 between LLM evaluations and expert-consensus scores at the macro level; this is evaluator concordance, not a correlation with disaster outcomes. The provenance caveat does not mean that the study lacked evaluation safeguards. Its Supplementary Section S5 describes anonymized, shuffled report assessment and separation between the people generating reports and those scoring them. These measures reduce particular assessment biases within the authors' study; they do not establish replication by an external research team or a causal reduction in disaster losses. Accordingly, we use these results only to characterize the reported technical evaluation, not to validate AFWG or infer watershed effectiveness. The sources describe different deployment stages rather than necessarily conflicting dates. Wang et al. (2026) report integration or operation from mid-2024, whereas an official Zhejiang account records a formal launch on 16 April 2026 and use for that flood season (Zhejiang Provincial Department of Emergency Management, 2026). A later formal announcement does not, by itself, confirm or disprove earlier operation. We therefore distinguish the publicly announced launch from the paperreported earlier use, which lacks independent corroboration in the inspected material. Neither date supplies an independently validated operational benchmark. Under the manuscript's definitions, MAESTRO does not close the agent-executed response ring. Its outputs are recommendations, and human authorities retain the power to issue warnings and mobilize action. The case may illustrate how an agent participates in a broader socio-technical loop that institutions can close, but it cannot simultaneously be coded as autonomous full-loop closure. In Table 6 , sensing, assessment, and decision advice are sourcereported; feedback and audit features are architectural provisions; response remains human-authorized. The cited study acknowledges limitations including the absence of prospectively defined impact indicators and a counterfactual design, restricted application domains, an incomplete cost-benefit analysis, the time required for integration, and a focus on early warning (Wang et al., 2026) . The present analysis also distinguishes internal evaluation safeguards from external validation and early operation from formal launch. MARSHA/WildfireGPT is a peer-reviewed consultative hazardadaptation prototype (Xie et al., 2025) . In its 2025 report, the OECD described FEMA's Planning Assistant for Resilient Communities (PARC) as a generative-AI initiative intended to assist governments with hazard-mitigation planning and the preparation of draft plan elements (OECD, 2025, Box 5.58) . This is a secondary description of the initiative, not an independent operational evaluation. These systems identify different institutional tasks, not comparable effect estimates. Their implications for AFWG's authorization and feedback interfaces are developed in Section 5. The Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fenvs.2026.1974405/ full#supplementary-material .

The layer coordinates access to observations, validated domain models, knowledge, and workflow services, but it does not replace those models or public authority. The eight illustrative cases document reported functions in sensing, assessment, retrieval, model coordination, and decision advice. They do not demonstrate sector-wide prevalence, sustained use, improved decision quality, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO provides a useful adjacent-domain design illustration, but its metrics are author-reported, its public chronology requires a distinction between mid-2024 paper-reported operation and formal launch on 16 April 2026, and human authorization leaves the agent response ring open. Our conclusion is therefore conditional. LLM-based agents may improve the cognition-to-institution handoff when validated scientific models remain authoritative, tool access is constrained, outputs communicate provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain the authority to authorize consequential actions, institutional agreements govern cross-boundary action, and independent audit and failure recovery are built in. Whether these conditions improve loop performance or environmental outcomes remains an empirical question. Six implementation measures follow. First, procure orchestration through a staged gateway: sandbox evaluation, supervised pilot, limited operational release, and independent review before scale-up. Second, assign every recommendation a named receiving official, legal authority, deadline, escalation path, and override field; no consequential work order should be issued without an auditable authorization record. Third, require a model-and-data register listing approved domain models, rule versions, retrieval corpora, tool permissions, update dates, and documented uncertainty ranges. Fourth, create a minimum feedback schema linking alert, recommendation, authorization, action, implementation status, field observation, override, incident, and outcome identifiers across agencies. Fifth, establish an independent audit function with log access, red-team testing, supplier separation, anomaly review, and authority to suspend the system. Sixth, publish a standard evaluation dashboard covering assessment latency, citation completeness, error and abstention rates, human review time, override rates, authorized response time, feedback completeness, and environmental outcomes. These measures translate interface-based deployment, open evaluation data, and parallel auditing into procurement and operating requirements rather than general appeals.

Two boundary decisions illustrate the rule. In particular, internal consistency cannot establish the reliability of judgments at the assessment-decision and decisionresponse boundaries. Figure 3 is a case-by-ring matrix for the included set only; it does not depict density or prevalence, or establish the absence of cases outside the bounded scan. This paper has six limitations. First, it does not estimate causal effects. Second, the original eight cases are purposive illustrations without a population frame or a complete historical screening log; the supplementary searches extend the evidence considered but do not create a population frame. Third, many deployment claims are source-reported and lack independent outcome evaluation. Fourth, MAESTRO is adjacent-domain evidence, and the separate accounts of early operation and formal launch do not establish independently validated performance. Fifth, the interpretive mapping has not undergone independent human double coding. Sixth, the institutional adaptations developed here are design arguments, not validated cross-national findings. The Chinese observations establish particular integration and warning-response problems, not their national prevalence or the effectiveness of an agentbased remedy. The revision strengthens transparency through documented source-verification and topic-based searches, record-level exclusions, explicit appraisal of additional studies, claim-level mapping, and metric-specific provenance. The resulting evidence supports the bounded design arguments developed here. Empirical validation would require a defined sampling frame, independent coding, accessible evaluation data, and comparative or quasiexperimental designs. Test P1. Using the quasi-experimental design afforded by the River Chief System's assessment reform, compare response latency and five-ring completion rates before and after the orchestration layer is embedded in a basin, to assess whether continuous cognitive support compensates for declining institutional attention. Test P2. Compare response-ring latency and completion rates between deployments closely integrated with the responsibility chain and those outside it, to assess the moderating role of institutional integration. Test P3. Conduct process tracing of cross-boundary waterpollution or flood events, contrasting how knowledge orchestration affects coordination costs under different dataownership arrangements. Test P4. Compare indicator behavior and data quality between deployments with and without institutionalized auditing, observing whether strategic responses emerge and whether auditing suppresses them. Test institutional adaptation. The adaptations developed in the preceding discussion provide specifications to evaluate, rather than leaving institutional transfer undefined. Compare whether recipient-and-authority mapping, joint authorization, and participatory feedback function as intended within comparable workflows. MAESTRO, PARC, and MARSHA/WildfireGPT should not be ranked by raw speed or agreement figures because their tasks, institutional roles, and evaluation designs differ. Comparative studies should instead examine matched mechanisms such as lawful routing, handling of disagreement, authorized action, and review of outcomes.

items.abstract_text: The study aimed to check the association of ChatGPT use and critical thinking on academic integrity. The research design is cross-sectional correlational study to collect data from university students aged from 18 to 23 years old. The sample size was 600 students taken via purposive sampling from the University of Gujrat, Pakistan. Standardized psychological scales of ChatGPT usage scale, critical thinking evaluation scale, and academic integrity scales were used. Our findings showed that ChatGPT has no significant effect on academic integrity but has positive effect on critical thinking. While critical thinking has positive effect on academic integrity. It showed that ChatGPT doesn’t directly change cheating behavior, but it can boost critical thinking for students, and that improved critical thinking is what increases academic integrity. Implications of the findings are discussed.

analysis.discussion: The study aimed to explore the relationship between ChatGPT use, critical thinking skills and academic integrity among university students. The present research aimed to check whether the ChatGPT and critical thinking skills both positively influence on the academic integrity among students, or ChatGPT have no influence on academic integrity or the critical thinking skills have positively influenced on academic integrity. H1 stated that there is significant relationship between ChatGPT use, critical thinking, and academic integrity among university students: The first hypothesis was supported as the results indicate a significant positive correlation between ChatGPT and critical thinking skills, indicating that students use ChatGPT information by using their critical thinking skills by evaluating and analyzing the information. The students at university show positive relations that mean they not just use ChatGPT to do assignments and academic tasks but also use it for enhancing their critical thinking skills in their academic tasks. The present results are consistent with the study by (Suriano et al., 2025) , that investigates how students interact with AI chatbots like ChatGPT and the factors like attitude, trust, engagement, and knowledge about AI plays the role. The researchers found students' trust in AI. Eventually, engagement with AI influences critical thinking skills than simple knowledge of AI. The study suggests that AI chatbots can focus on the development of critical thinking skills but only when students are actively engaged and analyze information carefully rather than accept it without reflecting it. The study relates in a way that proper use of ChatGPT may increase the critical thinking skills in students. The present results are consistent with previous studies (Nugroho &Trisusana, 2024; Syahsaputra, & Ni'matuzahroh, 2026) whose findings showed that many students use AI for writing assignments, understanding topics, summarizing information and generating ideas. Students believe that using AI for writing and help is acceptable but using it for completing assignments was disheartening and dishonesty. Therefore, they used their metacognitions to evaluate positive use of the AI tools. Another study examined how ChatGPT impacts secondary students' critical thinking skills by using survey-based quantitative approach. The data were collected from 300 students. The results show that most students believe that AI tools like ChatGPT improve their critical thinking skills as compared to those who haven't used it or used it often less. The research also found a positive relationship between ChatGPT use and critical thinking skills (Zafar et al., 2025) . H2 stated that critical thinking mediates the association between ChatGPT use and academic integrity.The results in figure 1 indicate that ChatGPT usage was not significantly associated with academic integrity (beta = .07, p = .15), whereas critical thinking significantly and fully mediated the relationship between ChatGPT usage and academic integrity (beta = .23, p < .001). Previous research suggests that students commonly use ChatGPT for brainstorming, paraphrasing, writing assistance, and information retrieval, but concerns remain regarding plagiarism, overreliance, and inaccurate references. Ethical and responsible use including transparency, source verification, proper citation, and plagiarism avoidance facilitate students to protect academic integrity (Kanashina, 2026; Shishakly, 2025) . ChatGPT needs to be treated as a supportive learning tool in critical thinking rather than a replacement for students' own reasoning and academic work (Sallam, et al., 2024; Susnjak, 2023; Tlili, et al., 2023) . The systematic review of literature showed how integrating AI technologies like ChatGPT can change practices of assessments. AI tools support learning, but at the same time they also challenge academic integrity, originality, and exploring students' original abilities. Traditional assessments approaches like essay writing are more vulnerable for generative AI misuse, which may push educators to think again about how students are being evaluated. The research also demonstrates using AI resistant methods like oral exams and multi-stage assessments is the better way to understand and measure critical thinking. It also explains the institutional policies and digital literacy practices to encourage the proper use of technology (Ncube et al., 2025) . The first limitation is that this study used self-report questionnaire and the second is the sample size. The sample size was small so can't generalize results this on the population and the self-report questionnaire might introduce biasness. The first strength of this research is that it added to existing literature and studied the interrelation between ChatGPT, academic integrity and critical thinking. The second strength of this study is that it only conducted in Western context, this study never happened before in Pakistan context. Future researchers will use longitudinal study design to see the impact of these variables over time. Future research will expand the sample size and replicate the study across multiple universities to improve generalizability of findings.In conclusion, this study provides evidence that ChatGPT, critical thinking and academic integrity among university students are strongly correlated with each other. The path analysis in structure equation model confirmed that ChatGPT is not directly influence on academic integrity but critical thinking has significantly positively mediated with ChatGPT and academic integrity.
